instructions: For each slate, rank journeys A–D from best to worst for an observer under exactly these conditions (one ranking per slate; ties allowed only if truly equal). Do not open `hidden` until you have ranked every slate: it holds the engine's own score, pool rank and pick reason.

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Measuring the Depths of Perseus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Which of these is closest, and how do we know?
journeys.hook: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last.
journeys.story: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Algol to Andromeda Galaxy, all in the sky around Perseus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Perseus

stops.name: Algol

getThere.text: Find Algol by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Algol quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A bright white star in Perseus. Every few days it fades to about a third of its light for some hours, then recovers.
card.see: Algol is one of the brightest stars of Perseus. At full light it matches Almach in Andromeda; at the bottom of an eclipse it matches ε Persei. Use the app’s predicted minimum, then look twice a few hours apart. Your eyes are enough; binoculars only make the comparison stars easier to pick out.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars plus a third, more distant companion. The pair circles every 2.87 days and we see the orbit almost edge-on. When the dim orange companion slides in front of the hot blue-white star, less light reaches us. That is an eclipsing binary: the stars do not change, our view of them does.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep down about one binocular field (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Alpha Persei Cluster is one of the nearest young star clusters (open clusters within about 600 light-years).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Alpha Persei Cluster is about 566 light-years away, about 6 times farther than Algol.

card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus. Dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. This is a cluster that only binoculars or the eye can take in whole. Note how similar the bright members look.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, roughly 90 million years ago. Mirfak itself is a member, a supergiant that has already left its long, steady adult life. The others are hot blue-white stars still burning hydrogen. Because the family is so close, it spreads over several Moon widths; a farther cluster just like it would shrink into a small knot.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster)

getThere.text: Move about 14° (two fields) down and to the left, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Alpha Persei Cluster at about 566 light-years, Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) at about 1,210 light-years.

card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north. A large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the "Muscleman". Use the widest field you have; a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster sit close together on the sky, but not in space. Stock 2 is about 1,200 light-years away; the Double Cluster is over 7,000. It is also much older, a few hundred million years, so its hottest blue stars are gone. Two clusters side by side on the sky can belong to completely different parts of the galaxy.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae
stops.class: F8pIa-0 to M3 (variable) · yellow-hypergiant · yellow-hypergiant variable

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) down and to the left (about 18°).

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae holds a record: one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. Before we go on: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: ρ Cassiopeiae lies about 8 times farther than Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster).

card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia. It looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most powerful stars you can see by eye.
card.see: Start at Caph, the end of the W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-southwest to a faint yellowish star: ρ Cassiopeiae. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of the cluster NGC 7789 between them. Compare ρ with nearby stars; it slowly changes.
card.understand: ρ Cas gives off more than half a million times the Sun’s light. Most bright-looking stars are nearby; this one is visible from enormous distance because of sheer power. It is in a short, unstable stage that only the heaviest stars reach: swollen, restless and losing mass in bursts. In 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) up and to the left, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Andromeda Galaxy is the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: From about 9,170 light-years to about 2,480,000 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 300 times farther.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Cassiopeia
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from γ Cassiopeiae to VV Cephei, all in the sky around Cassiopeia.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-west, around Cassiopeia

stops.name: γ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Find γ Cassiopeiae by eye, about 60° up in the north-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find γ Cassiopeiae quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Some stars spin so fast that they flatten into squashed balls, hotter at their poles than around their waists.

card.glance: The middle star of Cassiopeia’s W: a hot blue-white star that gives no hint of its secret in binoculars.
card.see: γ Cas is the center of the W. In binoculars it is a plain blue-white point. Swing to orange Schedar at one end of the W for a color contrast. Over the decades γ Cas has sometimes outshone Schedar and sometimes fallen below it, so make your own comparison tonight.
card.understand: γ Cas is a young star many times heavier than the Sun, spinning so fast that its equator barely holds on. Gas leaks off the equator and settles into a thin disk that glows like a neon sign. That disk adds bright colors to the star’s spectrum, and as it grows or thins out the star’s brightness changes. Stars like this are called Be stars, and γ Cas was the first.

stops.name: Schedar

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just left of γ Cassiopeiae, in the same view, and you have Schedar.

stops.whyHere: Schedar shows the next idea you need. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Same W, opposite colors: γ Cas is a hot blue-white star, Schedar a cooler orange giant. Swing between them and compare.

card.glance: The bright orange star at the southern end of Cassiopeia’s W.
card.see: Binoculars bring out a clear orange tint. Swing to γ Cas at the center of the W and back to compare the colors.
card.understand: Schedar has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant with a cooler, orange surface.

stops.name: η Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. η Cassiopeiae is already in the field, just right of Schedar.

stops.whyHere: η Cassiopeiae adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: η Cassiopeiae is about 600 times less luminous than Schedar, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A pale yellow star in Cassiopeia’s W with a faint orange companion that steady, high-power binoculars can sometimes split.
card.see: η Cas sits between Schedar and γ Cas in the W. The companion is only 13 arcseconds away and far fainter, so most hand-held binoculars show one star. Brace 10× or larger binoculars on something solid and look for a tiny orange dot pressed against the yellow glare.
card.understand: The bright star is close to a twin of the Sun, slightly hotter; the companion is a cooler, smaller orange dwarf. They orbit each other slowly: since observers began recording the pair in 1779, the companion has swung a long way around. A true orbiting pair like this lets astronomers weigh both stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: Take three field-widths down, toward Cepheus; δ Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: δ Cephei holds a record: the prototype of the Cepheid variables (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. δ Cephei is about 2,000 times more luminous than η Cassiopeiae.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: From δ Cephei, slide down and to the right roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: δ Cephei gives off about 1,950 times the Sun's light, VV Cephei about 57,000–89,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Starlight Postmarked Long Ago: Andromeda
journeys.drivingQuestion: How old is the light hitting your eye right now?
journeys.hook: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when.
journeys.story: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Capella to γ Cassiopeiae, all in the sky around Andromeda.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Andromeda

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, about 65° up in the north-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Capella quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings.
card.see: Look for a creamy, slightly golden tint: warmer than Rigel or Sirius, not as orange as Aldebaran. No binoculars or ordinary telescope can split it; the two stars are far too close. Just south of Capella, find the small triangle of stars called the Kids.
card.understand: Capella is two giant stars, each about two and a half times the Sun’s mass, circling each other every 104 days. Timing that orbit lets astronomers weigh them directly. The weights reveal the two are at different stages: one is already burning helium in its core, the other is only now swelling into a giant.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Mirfak

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three binocular fields, toward Perseus.

stops.whyHere: Mirfak holds a record: the brightest star of the Alpha Persei Cluster (within the cluster). Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Mirfak is about 506 light-years away, about 10 times farther than Capella.

card.glance: A bright yellow-white star in Perseus, ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains: the Alpha Persei Cluster. Mirfak itself looks a shade yellower than its siblings. This is one of the finest binocular views in the sky; it suits wide, low-power binoculars better than telescopes.
card.understand: These stars were born together and share one age. Mirfak started out heavier than most of its siblings, so it burned through its core hydrogen first and has already swollen into a yellow supergiant. Its lighter brothers and sisters are still in their long, steady adult phase, shining blue-white. One family, two stages of life, side by side.

stops.name: NGC 752

getThere.text: Move about 20° (three fields) up and to the left, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: NGC 752 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Mirfak at about 506 light-years, NGC 752 at about 1,410 light-years.

card.glance: A broad, even scatter of faint stars bigger than the full Moon, next to the orange pair 56 Andromedae.
card.see: Start at the wide orange double 56 Andromedae and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. There is no bright center; let your eye relax over the whole field. Notice there are no standout blue-white stars here.
card.understand: In a young cluster the brightest stars are hot blue-white heavyweights. Here they are all gone: after more than a billion years, only stars a little heavier than the Sun remain on their long, steady adult life, and a few have swollen into giants. Its members are also drifting apart, slowly mixing into the Milky Way.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about two and a half binocular fields (about 15°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Andromeda Galaxy is the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Andromeda Galaxy lies about 2,000 times farther than NGC 752.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: γ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Sweep right about three binocular fields, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: One gentle stop to close the loop.
stops.transitionText: Andromeda Galaxy and γ Cassiopeiae look like neighbors, but γ Cassiopeiae is about 5,000 times closer than Andromeda Galaxy.

card.glance: The middle star of Cassiopeia’s W: a hot blue-white star that gives no hint of its secret in binoculars.
card.see: γ Cas is the center of the W. In binoculars it is a plain blue-white point. Swing to orange Schedar at one end of the W for a color contrast. Over the decades γ Cas has sometimes outshone Schedar and sometimes fallen below it, so make your own comparison tonight.
card.understand: γ Cas is a young star many times heavier than the Sun, spinning so fast that its equator barely holds on. Gas leaks off the equator and settles into a thin disk that glows like a neon sign. That disk adds bright colors to the star’s spectrum, and as it grows or thins out the star’s brightness changes. Stars like this are called Be stars, and γ Cas was the first.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: From Cloud to Cinder over Taurus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Could you watch a star's whole life in one patch of sky?
journeys.hook: Follow one star's whole life, from glowing cradle to scattered ashes, in one sweep of sky.
journeys.story: Follow one star's whole life, from glowing cradle to scattered ashes, in one sweep of sky. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Christmas Tree Cluster to Kabdhilinan, all in the sky around Taurus.
journeys.regionLabel: In the south-east, around Taurus

stops.name: Christmas Tree Cluster

getThere.text: Look 35° up in the east. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Betelgeuse, aim at it, then follow the hop to Christmas Tree Cluster.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

card.glance: A bright star at the base of a small triangle of fainter stars, like an upside-down Christmas tree.
card.see: Go a little under halfway from Betelgeuse to Procyon, then about three and a half degrees north. The bright star S Monocerotis marks the trunk; a narrow triangle of fainter stars points south to the tree’s tip. With north up, the tree hangs upside-down. The nebula is a photo target.
card.understand: These stars formed a few million years ago, and their birth cloud is still around them. S Monocerotis, the bright trunk star, is far hotter and heavier than the Sun, and its light eats into the surrounding gas. A dark finger of dust, the Cone Nebula, sits at the tree’s tip where gas is still collapsing into stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Meissa

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) up and to the right, toward Orion.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Christmas Tree Cluster showed you one stage of a star's life. Meissa is the stage that follows.

card.glance: The head of Orion: a tight little triangle of stars where you expect a single one.
card.see: Point at Orion’s head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn the faint naked-eye smudge into a compact group: Meissa and two close neighbours in a triangle, with a dozen fainter stars around them. The ring of gas around the group shows only in long-exposure photos.
card.understand: Meissa is an O-type star, among the hottest kinds there are, at the center of the cluster Collinder 69. The family formed about five million years ago. Since then the light and winds of its hot stars, and probably a supernova, have pushed the leftover gas outward into a huge ring, leaving the young family in the open.

stops.name: σ Tauri

getThere.text: Move about 15° (two and a half fields) up and to the right, toward Taurus.

stops.whyHere: Pay attention here; σ Tauri upsets an easy assumption. Quick background: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: Look for what time has done: Meissa at about 3.4–7 million years, σ Tauri at about 625 million years.

card.glance: A wide, easy pair of white stars about 1° south-east of Aldebaran.
card.see: Look about 1° south-east of Aldebaran. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 7.4 arcminutes apart. Compare their brightness: nearly equal.
card.understand: Both stars are white A-type stars, hotter than the Sun. Wide pairs like this one may be true companions drifting together, or just a chance alignment; only distances and motions can tell.

stops.name: θ Tauri

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the right of σ Tauri, in the same view, and you have θ Tauri.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: θ Tauri is θ² is the brightest true member of the Hyades (Hyades members (Aldebaran is a foreground star)).
stops.transitionText: Fast-forward. θ Tauri shows the stage that comes after σ Tauri.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair in the Hyades V: one white star, one yellow-orange.
card.see: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair. Binoculars split it at a glance: almost 6 arcminutes. Compare the colors: θ² is white, θ¹ yellow-orange. Defocusing slightly makes the contrast stronger.
card.understand: Both stars were born in the Hyades about 625 million years ago, so they started out together. θ¹ has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a yellow-orange giant. θ² is still hot and white, near the end of its long, steady adult life. A small difference in their starting mass is enough to put them in different chapters.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Kabdhilinan

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) up and to the left, toward Auriga.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Kabdhilinan is about 50 times more luminous than θ Tauri.

card.glance: The orange star at Auriga’s south-western corner.
card.see: Look at the pentagon of Auriga: its south-western corner is ι Aurigae, distinctly orange next to yellowish Capella.
card.understand: ι Aurigae is a luminous orange giant about 450 light-years away. Its surface is near 4,200 K, cooler than Capella’s stars, so it looks more orange.

conditions.message: The Moon is 53% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 26° from it; it sets at 03:02.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Old Light in Boötes
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Old news from space: each stop's light is older than the last.
journeys.story: Old news from space: each stop's light is older than the last. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Arcturus to Great Hercules Globular Cluster, all in the sky around Boötes. R Coronae Borealis is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Boötes

stops.name: Arcturus

getThere.text: Find Arcturus by eye, about 45° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. One thing first: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: The brightest star of spring: a strong orange-gold light at the end of the curve you follow from the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Follow the curve of the Dipper’s handle away from the bowl; the first bright star you meet is Arcturus. In binoculars its orange-gold color is obvious. Later, carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare the two colors. Defocusing slightly makes the warm tint even richer.
card.understand: Arcturus has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 25 times the Sun’s width; that large glowing surface is why such a cool star shines so brightly. It weighs about the same as the Sun but is billions of years older and poorer in heavy elements. It also moves quickly across our line of sight, which marks it as a member of the Galaxy’s older, thicker disk passing by.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Izar

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths left (about 10°); Izar is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. Quick background: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Arcturus at about 37 light-years, Izar at about 203 light-years.

card.glance: An orange star in Boötes; binoculars show one star, though telescopes reveal a lovely color pair.
card.see: In binoculars Izar is orange, like a dimmer copy of Arcturus ten degrees away. Its blue-white companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Izar lies about 200 light-years away, five or six times farther than Arcturus. To look even this bright from so far, it must pour out roughly three times as much light as Arcturus.

stops.name: ν¹ & ν² Boötis

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths left (about 17°); ν¹ & ν² Boötis is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: ν¹ & ν² Boötis adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: From about 203 light-years to about 974 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 5 times farther.

card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes: one orange, one white.
card.see: In binoculars the two sit side by side, orange ν¹ and white ν², nearly equal in brightness. Defocus slightly to make the color contrast pop.
card.understand: ν¹ is an orange giant nearly 1,000 light-years away; ν² is a white star about 440 light-years away. They have nothing to do with each other and line up only from where we stand. The orange one must give out far more light to look as bright from twice as far.

stops.name: R Coronae Borealis
stops.class: G0 Iep (hydrogen-deficient carbon star) · binary-interacting · r-crb variable

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) down and to the right, toward Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: R Coronae Borealis lies about 2 times farther than ν¹ & ν² Boötis.

card.glance: When at normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the bowl of the Northern Crown; at other times, missing altogether.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a bit fainter than the faintest stars of the crown. If you cannot find it, the star may be in one of its fades. Either answer is a real observation; note which you saw.
card.understand: R CrB is a strange supergiant almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Every so often its outflowing gas cools enough for carbon to condense into soot grains. A cloud that forms on our side blocks the light, and the star dims by up to thousands of times. Months or years later the soot drifts away and the star returns.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep left about two binocular fields, toward Hercules.

stops.whyHere: Great Hercules Globular Cluster holds a record: the brightest globular cluster in the far-northern sky (globular clusters north of declination +30°).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Great Hercules Globular Cluster is about 24,200 light-years away, about 10 times farther than R Coronae Borealis.

card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on one side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. On the line between η and ζ Herculis, about a third of the way from η, sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star. It brightens toward the center. Binoculars won’t split it into stars; that takes a telescope. Compare it with a nearby star of similar brightness: one is a point, the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of stars that all formed together in the young Milky Way. M13 holds roughly half a million Suns’ worth of stars in a ball about 120 light-years wide. Its stars are about 12 billion years old, more than twice the Sun’s age, and they contain far less iron and other heavy elements than the Sun because they formed before many generations of stars had enriched the gas. Globulars swarm around the galaxy in a vast halo, not in the flat disk.

image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Splitting Stars over Boötes
journeys.drivingQuestion: Are double stars real partners or chance alignments?
journeys.hook: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from δ Boötis to Alphecca, all in the sky around Boötes.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-east, around Boötes

stops.name: δ Boötis

getThere.text: Look 40° up in the east. Find Alphecca by eye, then hop up and to the left to δ Boötis.

stops.whyHere: We start here because δ Boötis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Boötes with a faint companion that binoculars split cleanly.
card.see: In 10x binoculars look just beside δ Boo for a much fainter point, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away; it splits cleanly when you hold steady.
card.understand: The bright star is a giant about 11 times the Sun’s width; its companion is a Sun-like dwarf. Gaia measures the same distance for both, about 120 light-years, so they belong together and orbit very slowly.

stops.name: ν¹ & ν² Boötis

getThere.text: Sweep left about one binocular field (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: ν¹ & ν² Boötis shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. ν¹ & ν² Boötis is about 30 times more luminous than δ Boötis.

card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes: one orange, one white.
card.see: In binoculars the two sit side by side, orange ν¹ and white ν², nearly equal in brightness. Defocus slightly to make the color contrast pop.
card.understand: ν¹ is an orange giant nearly 1,000 light-years away; ν² is a white star about 440 light-years away. They have nothing to do with each other and line up only from where we stand. The orange one must give out far more light to look as bright from twice as far.

stops.name: 16 & 17 Draconis
stops.class: B9.5 V + B9 V + A1 Vnn · main-sequence

getThere.text: From ν¹ & ν² Boötis, slide left roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Draco.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet 16 & 17 Draconis is about 20 times smaller than ν¹ & ν² Boötis.

card.glance: A wide, nearly equal pair of white 5th-magnitude stars 90″ apart in Draco; easy in any binoculars.
card.see: Two matched white points sit 1½′ apart. A telescope would show one of them is itself a 3″ pair.
card.understand: Catalogues list a third star 3″ from one of the pair; whether all three are bound together is not settled.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alkalurops

getThere.text: Take three field-widths up and to the right, toward Boötes; Alkalurops is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alkalurops adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Alkalurops shows the same idea as 16 & 17 Draconis. Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.

card.glance: A white star in Boötes with a faint companion binoculars can split; the companion is itself double.
card.see: In 10x binoculars a much fainter star sits just south of μ Boo, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away. Hold steady to separate it from the glare. Its own two stars need a telescope.
card.understand: The bright star is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass. The companion is a pair of Sun-like stars orbiting each other closely, and all three share the same motion through space.

stops.name: Alphecca
stops.class: A1 IV + G5 V · main-sequence · eclipsing-algol variable

getThere.text: Sweep right about one and a half binocular fields, toward Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: The answer stop: Alphecca is where tonight's question comes together.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: Alphecca, next to your memory of Alkalurops.

card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star of the arc; binoculars fit the whole crown in one or two fields. Use it as the reference point for the two strange variables nearby.
card.understand: Alphecca is really two stars, a white one and a Sun-like one, that eclipse each other every 17 days, but the dip is far too small to notice by eye.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Ursa Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Dubhe to Alkaid, all in the sky around Ursa Major.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north, around Ursa Major

stops.name: Dubhe

getThere.text: Find Dubhe by eye, about 65° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Dubhe quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer.

card.glance: The bright yellow-orange pointer star at the top of the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the bowl; Merak is the lower one, five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is distinctly yellow-orange and Merak white. Sweep between them a few times and compare. A faint star sits about a fifth of a Moon-width from Dubhe, but its true companion is far too close to see.
card.understand: Dubhe is a giant that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 26 times the Sun’s width, cooling to a yellow-orange glow. It lies about 120 light-years away, half again as far as Merak, and it does not share the motion of the five middle Dipper stars. So the Big Dipper is not one group: most of it is a family, and Dubhe is a passer-by seen in the same direction.

stops.name: Merak

getThere.text: Same field of view: Merak sits just above Dubhe.

stops.whyHere: Merak adds the next piece of the story. Quick background: Star families do not stay together forever; they loosen and drift apart, yet their stars keep moving in step.
stops.transitionText: Dubhe and Merak point to Polaris together, but they are strangers: Merak belongs to the Dipper’s family, while Dubhe is a passer-by half again as far away. Compare their colors as you swing between them.

card.glance: The lower pointer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl: white in binoculars, beside yellow-orange Dubhe.
card.see: Merak and Dubhe are the pointers to Polaris. In binoculars Merak is white and Dubhe yellow-orange: a sibling and a stranger side by side. About two degrees southeast, under dark skies, the Owl Nebula is a faint challenge.
card.understand: Merak is a hot white star about two and a half times the Sun’s mass. In 1909 Ejnar Hertzsprung noticed that it and several other Dipper stars move together; modern measurements confirm a family drifting through space about 80 light-years away. Dubhe, five degrees off, is not part of it.

stops.name: Megrez

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths right (about 10°); Megrez is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Megrez is the faintest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism).
stops.transitionText: Stay in the family. Megrez and Merak grew up in the same nursery.

card.glance: The faintest Big Dipper star, where the handle joins the bowl.
card.see: In binoculars Megrez is white. About one and a half degrees northeast lie the two faint stars of Winnecke 4 (M40); brace the binoculars to see them.
card.understand: Megrez is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass, born with Merak, Phecda, Alioth and Mizar about 400 million years ago. Interferometry shows it spins fast enough to be flattened.

stops.name: Alioth

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Alioth is already in the field, just right of Megrez.

stops.whyHere: Alioth holds a record: the brightest star in Ursa Major (Ursa Major).
stops.transitionText: From the bowl’s corner into the handle: Alioth shares Megrez’s birth date and its path through the Galaxy.

card.glance: The brightest Big Dipper star, first in the handle next to the bowl; plain white and steady in binoculars.
card.see: Alioth is the handle star touching the bowl. In binoculars it looks white and steady; its light changes by only about two percent as it turns, far below what eyes can notice. Sweep along the handle to Mizar and Alcor to see three family members in one short glide.
card.understand: Alioth is a hot white star born with the other stars of the Ursa Major family. Its outer layers are unusually calm, so some elements sink while others float up, and a weak magnetic field herds them into patches. As the star rotates every five days, the patches swing toward and away from us, and its light flickers very slightly.

stops.name: Alkaid

getThere.text: Move about 10° (one and a half fields) right (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: Alkaid holds a record: the hottest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism). One thing first: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Alioth at about 106 times the Sun's light, Alkaid at about 598 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Alkaid ends the handle. In binoculars it looks crisply blue-white, a clear contrast with yellow-orange Dubhe at the other end of the Dipper. About three and a half degrees to the southwest, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 degrees, three times hotter than the Sun’s, which is why it looks blue-white. Hot stars like this are heavy and burn through their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go. It lies about 100 light-years away and travels in a different direction from the five family stars in the middle of the Dipper.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Ursa Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Cor Caroli to Mizar & Alcor, all in the sky around Ursa Major.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Ursa Major

stops.name: Cor Caroli

getThere.text: Find Cor Caroli by eye, about 70° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Cor Caroli is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A white star alone under the Big Dipper’s handle; braced 10x binoculars may show a faint partner almost touching it.
card.see: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Dipper’s handle. Hold 10x binoculars very steady, or use a tripod, and look for a much fainter companion right beside it. In 7x binoculars it usually stays merged. Its white color makes a good contrast with red La Superba about seven degrees to the north.
card.understand: The brighter star is hot and white, with a strong, lopsided magnetic field. That field holds elements such as silicon and europium in large patches on its surface. As the star turns every five and a half days, the patches swing in and out of view and its light and spectrum change slightly. Astronomers named this whole class of variable star after it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Groombridge 1830

getThere.text: Move about 12° (one and a half fields) up, toward Ursa Major.

stops.whyHere: Groombridge 1830 holds a record: one of the fastest-moving stars across the sky that binoculars can show (stars brighter than about 9th magnitude). Quick background: Globular clusters are ancient balls of stars that swarm around our galaxy in a wide halo, well away from its flat disk.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Groombridge 1830 is about 500 times less luminous than Cor Caroli.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star in a quiet corner of Ursa Major, findable in binoculars with a chart.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about 16 degrees due south of Phecda, the bowl star nearest the handle. In binoculars it is a faint yellowish point with no visible hint of its speed. Note its position against nearby stars; in a lifetime of careful sketches it would visibly creep.
card.understand: Most stars near the Sun circle the Galaxy with us in its flat disk, like cars in the same lanes. Groombridge 1830 follows a steep, looping orbit through the halo, the old, thin swarm of stars around the disk, so it cuts through our lane at high speed. It contains far less iron than the Sun, a sign it formed early, before generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy’s gas.

stops.name: La Superba

getThere.text: From Groombridge 1830, slide down and to the left roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Canes Venatici.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: La Superba is one of the very few carbon stars visible to the unaided eye (dark-sky naked-eye stars).
stops.transitionText: Size check: La Superba is about 800 times larger than Groombridge 1830.

card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, head about a third of the way toward Megrez, the star joining the Dipper’s handle to its bowl. Faint to the eye, it is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember. Keep looking: red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare. Then swing to white Cor Caroli for contrast.
card.understand: Late in life, a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. Carbon-rich molecules and soot block blue light, so what escapes is deep red. The star is cool, about 2,700 degrees, and it is shedding gas and dust that have piled up into a shell about three light-years across.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alkaid

getThere.text: Sweep down about one and a half binocular fields, toward Ursa Major.

stops.whyHere: Alkaid holds a record: the hottest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet Alkaid is about 200 times smaller than La Superba.

card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Alkaid ends the handle. In binoculars it looks crisply blue-white, a clear contrast with yellow-orange Dubhe at the other end of the Dipper. About three and a half degrees to the southwest, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 degrees, three times hotter than the Sun’s, which is why it looks blue-white. Hot stars like this are heavy and burn through their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go. It lies about 100 light-years away and travels in a different direction from the five family stars in the middle of the Dipper.

stops.name: Mizar & Alcor

getThere.text: Take one field-widths up and to the left (about 7°); Mizar & Alcor is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Mizar & Alcor is the first star found to be double from its spectrum alone (Mizar A) (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: Alkaid ends the Dipper’s handle, but unlike Mizar next door it is not family: hotter, younger and heading its own way.

card.glance: Bright Mizar and fainter Alcor at the bend of the Big Dipper’s handle: a pair you can split by eye, wide apart in binoculars.
card.see: Look at the middle star of the Dipper’s handle; keen eyes see little Alcor beside it. Binoculars spread them less than half a Moon-width apart, with a fainter star nearby making a small triangle. Mizar’s own close companion needs a telescope at moderate power, so don’t expect to split it here.
card.understand: Mizar and Alcor are not a chance alignment. Both lie roughly 80–90 light-years away and drift together, and each is itself multiple: Mizar is two pairs of stars, and Alcor has a small red-dwarf companion found in 2009. That likely makes six stars in one system. They also share their motion with Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth, all born together about 400 million years ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 05:55.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Variable Hearts of Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do some stars brighten and fade?
journeys.hook: Stars are not as constant as they look. Tonight you'll see why.
journeys.story: Stars are not as constant as they look. Tonight you'll see why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from P Cygni to δ Cephei, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Cepheus

stops.name: P Cygni

getThere.text: Look 65° up in the east. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Sadr, aim at it, then follow the hop to P Cygni.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find P Cygni quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A modest 5th-magnitude star about 2° south-west of Sadr, at the heart of the Northern Cross.
card.see: From Sadr, slide about 2½° south-west, toward Albireo. P Cygni is a plain white point against the Milky Way, easy in binoculars. Nothing about the view hints at its power; the story is in the distance.
card.understand: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable, one of the heaviest kinds of star. It is so bright that the push of its own light almost overcomes gravity, so it sheds mass in a strong wind and sometimes in eruptions. Stars like this are only a short step from the end of their lives.

stops.name: 31 Cygni
stops.class: K4 Ib + B4 IV-V · binary-interacting · eclipsing-long-period variable

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one and a half binocular fields (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. A short reminder before you look: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: 31 Cygni, next to your memory of P Cygni.

card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue companion beside it: a binocular colour trio with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter 7th-magnitude star closer in. The colours are easier than Albireo's because the gaps are wider.
card.understand: A hot blue star orbits the orange supergiant and slips behind it every 10.4 years, a slow eclipse too shallow to notice by eye.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about three binocular fields, toward Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Garnet Star holds a record: one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Garnet Star.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: RW Cephei

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about one binocular field (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: RW Cephei is one of the largest known stars in the Milky Way (known stars in our galaxy).
stops.transitionText: Depth check: RW Cephei is about 8 times farther than Garnet Star, though they share this patch of sky.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-southwest of δ Cephei. Binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so compare it with neighboring stars and note what you see; you are watching a star that can be veiled by its own dust.
card.understand: RW Cep is a cool hypergiant, a heavy star in a swollen late stage. Images from the CHARA interferometer show a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During its recent fade, one side of the disc looked darker than the other: a dust cloud, probably formed from gas the star had just thrown off, was blocking part of its light.

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just left of RW Cephei, in the same view, and you have δ Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: δ Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variables (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: RW Cephei measures about 900–1,800 times the Sun's radius; δ Cephei about 28–48 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Splitting Stars over Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Are double stars real partners or chance alignments?
journeys.hook: Doubles, colors, and a pair that may not be a pair at all.
journeys.story: Doubles, colors, and a pair that may not be a pair at all. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from 61 Cygni to Sheliak, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Cygnus

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the east. Find Deneb by eye, then hop down and to the right to 61 Cygni.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A faint naked-eye star in a dark sky, south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find it about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart. Compare their colour with white Deneb; then remember that the faint pair is well over a hundred times closer.
card.understand: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in a year. 61 Cygni is about 11 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours. The two stars are orange dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun, orbiting each other. They look faint not because they are far but because they give out little light; Deneb looks bright despite being enormously farther.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: 31 Cygni
stops.class: K4 Ib + B4 IV-V · binary-interacting · eclipsing-long-period variable

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two binocular fields (about 13°).

stops.whyHere: 31 Cygni shows the next idea you need. Quick background: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: 31 Cygni is about 30,000 times more luminous than 61 Cygni, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue companion beside it: a binocular colour trio with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter 7th-magnitude star closer in. The colours are easier than Albireo's because the gaps are wider.
card.understand: A hot blue star orbits the orange supergiant and slips behind it every 10.4 years, a slow eclipse too shallow to notice by eye.

stops.name: 16 Cygni B

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) up and to the left (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: 16 Cygni B is one of the first stars known to host a planet on a highly stretched orbit (exoplanet discoveries of the 1990s). One thing first: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. 16 Cygni B is about 4,000 times less luminous than 31 Cygni.

card.glance: One of a matched pair of 6th-magnitude yellowish stars 40″ apart, near δ Cygni on the swan's western wing.
card.see: Use the chart from δ Cygni (Al Fawaris): about 5° north lies a pair of equal faint stars, 40″ apart, which 10× binoculars split on a steady mount. Both have the same soft yellow-white tint. 16 Cyg B is the slightly fainter one, to the south-east.
card.understand: Both stars are close copies of the Sun: similar temperature, similar mass. Studying the tiny pulsations of their surfaces, the Kepler spacecraft dated them at about 6.8 billion years, older than the Sun. Around B circles a planet heavier than Jupiter on a strongly stretched orbit, perhaps pulled into that shape by its sibling star A.

stops.name: Double-Double
stops.class: A4 V + F1 V (ε¹); A8 Vn + F0 Vn (ε²) · main-sequence

getThere.text: Sweep up about two and a half binocular fields, toward Lyra.

stops.whyHere: Double-Double holds a record: the best-known "double" star.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: Double-Double, next to your memory of 16 Cygni B.

card.glance: A pair of matching white stars just north-east of Vega; any binoculars split them easily.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two equal white stars, like headlights in the distance. Sharp-eyed observers can sometimes see them as an elongated star without optics. Do not expect binoculars to split each star again; that needs a telescope at high power.
card.understand: Each of the two stars you see is itself a pair, a couple of arcseconds apart, circling each other over centuries. The two pairs share the same distance and drift through space together, so the four stars probably form one gravitationally linked family. Pairs like these matter: timing their orbits is how astronomers weigh stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Sheliak
stops.class: B8.5 Ib-II + disk · binary-interacting · eclipsing-beta-lyrae variable

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one binocular field (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Sheliak holds a record: prototype of the β Lyrae class of eclipsing binaries (variable-star classification).
stops.transitionText: The Double-Double's pairs take centuries to orbit. A few degrees south, Sheliak's two stars nearly touch and circle every 13 days.

card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's parallelogram; it changes brightness every few days.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat (γ Lyr) are the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, 2° apart: an ideal comparison. Some nights the two look equal; at deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly fainter. Note which is brighter tonight and check again in a few days. Binoculars also show a 7th-magnitude companion 46″ away.
card.understand: Sheliak is two stars orbiting every 13 days, so close that one has swollen into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner. The partner is wrapped in a thick disk of that stolen gas, which hides it from view. As they circle edge-on to us, each passes in front of the other, so the light rises and falls continuously.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Polaris to Garnet Star, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Cepheus

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Find Polaris by eye, about 35° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Polaris quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: From Polaris, slide right roughly two fields of view, toward Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Errai is one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003 (history of astronomy). A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Errai is about 200 times less luminous than Polaris.

card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of Cepheus’s house-shaped outline, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the “house” of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris. In binoculars it is a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen; compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the house’s other corner.
card.understand: Errai is a star a little heavier than the Sun that has finished its long hydrogen-burning life and is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 astronomers noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its velocity, a hint of a planet. Doubts about the star’s own variations left the claim in limbo until 2003, when a planet with a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed.

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Move about 11° (one and a half fields) up (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Alfirk holds a record: the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Errai gives off about 12 times the Sun's light, Alfirk about 17,000–22,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: From Alfirk, slide right roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: VV Cephei holds a record: one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky).
stops.transitionText: Size check: VV Cephei is about 100 times larger than Alfirk.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Same field of view: Garnet Star sits above and to the right of VV Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Garnet Star is one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Two red supergiants a few degrees apart. The Garnet Star lives alone; VV Cephei has a hot partner it eclipses every 20 years, which lets astronomers measure it.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Hercules: Light from Every Century
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when.
journeys.story: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Vega to Zeta Herculis, all in the sky around Hercules.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Hercules

stops.name: Vega

getThere.text: Find Vega by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings; binoculars show a white jewel in a field of faint stars.
card.see: Vega is the brightest point near the zenith. In binoculars it stays a hard white spark; notice the faint stars around it that your eyes alone miss. Look 2° east-north-east for a close pair, the Double-Double, and a little farther south for the long parallelogram of Lyra.
card.understand: Vega is in the long, steady middle of its life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, exactly as the Sun does. It is about twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight makes it burn hotter: its surface is near 9,500 K, so it looks blue-white rather than yellow. Heavier stars also spend their fuel faster, so Vega's steady phase will be much shorter than the Sun's.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Eltanin

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two binocular fields, toward Draco.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Eltanin is the star that revealed the aberration of starlight, proof that Earth moves (history of astronomy (Bradley, 1729)).
stops.transitionText: Vega's light left it about 25 years ago; Eltanin's about 150 years ago, in the age of steam.

card.glance: The brightest star in the dragon's head, a lopsided quadrangle 14° north-west of Vega; orange in binoculars.
card.see: From Vega, look about 14° north-west for the four-star head of Draco. Eltanin is the brightest, at the head's southern corner, next to Rastaban. In binoculars compare the two: Eltanin is clearly orange, Rastaban yellower.
card.understand: Eltanin is a giant star, cooler than the Sun and about 50 times wider, in the later part of its life. Its real fame is historical. Because it passed almost overhead in London, James Bradley tracked it night after night. Its position shifted in a yearly pattern that only made sense if light from the star met a moving Earth, like rain slanting onto a moving car.

stops.name: g Herculis

getThere.text: From Eltanin, slide left roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Hercules.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Eltanin at about 154 light-years, g Herculis at about 384 light-years.

card.glance: A distinctly orange-red naked-eye star in northern Hercules, about 6° north-west of the Keystone.
card.see: In binoculars g Her is clearly redder than its neighbours. Over a few months its brightness drifts by about a magnitude; compare it with nearby white stars.
card.understand: It is an old giant, about 240 times wider than the Sun, whose outer layers pulse every few months and leak into space.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Take one field-widths left (about 6°); Great Hercules Globular Cluster is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Great Hercules Globular Cluster holds a record: the brightest globular cluster in the far-northern sky (globular clusters north of declination +30°). A short reminder before you look: The Milky Way band is our own galaxy: a flat disk of stars that we see edge-on because we live inside it.
stops.transitionText: From about 384 light-years to about 24,200 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 60 times farther.

card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on one side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. On the line between η and ζ Herculis, about a third of the way from η, sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star. It brightens toward the center. Binoculars won’t split it into stars; that takes a telescope. Compare it with a nearby star of similar brightness: one is a point, the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of stars that all formed together in the young Milky Way. M13 holds roughly half a million Suns’ worth of stars in a ball about 120 light-years wide. Its stars are about 12 billion years old, more than twice the Sun’s age, and they contain far less iron and other heavy elements than the Sun because they formed before many generations of stars had enriched the gas. Globulars swarm around the galaxy in a vast halo, not in the flat disk.

image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello

stops.name: Zeta Herculis

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of Great Hercules Globular Cluster, in the same view, and you have Zeta Herculis.

stops.whyHere: One gentle stop to close the loop.
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Great Hercules Globular Cluster is about 24,200 light-years away, Zeta Herculis about 35 light-years.

card.glance: The south-western corner of the Keystone of Hercules, a pale yellow star 35 light-years away.
card.see: ζ and η Herculis frame the west side of the Keystone; the globular cluster M13 lies about a third of the way from η to ζ. ζ Her itself is a simple yellowish point.
card.understand: It is a subgiant: its core hydrogen is running out and it has grown to almost three times the Sun's width. A close companion orbits it, too tight for binoculars.

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: A Ladder of Distances in Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Which of these is closest, and how do we know?
journeys.hook: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time.
journeys.story: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from 61 Cygni to Andromeda Galaxy, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Cygnus

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Look 45° up in the west. This is a big move, about 8°. Find Deneb with your eyes first, then raise the binoculars and hop to 61 Cygni.

stops.whyHere: We start here because 61 Cygni is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story.

card.glance: A faint naked-eye star in a dark sky, south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find it about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart. Compare their colour with white Deneb; then remember that the faint pair is well over a hundred times closer.
card.understand: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in a year. 61 Cygni is about 11 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours. The two stars are orange dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun, orbiting each other. They look faint not because they are far but because they give out little light; Deneb looks bright despite being enormously farther.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M39

getThere.text: Move about 11° (one and a half fields) up and to the right (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: M39 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: From about 11 light-years to about 965 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 80 times farther.

card.glance: A large, bright, loose triangle of a few dozen stars north-east of Deneb, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From Deneb, sweep about 9 degrees east-north-east. You will meet a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. Use your lowest magnification, count the members, and notice that the brightest ones are all white or blue-white.
card.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance and one motion: a true family about 1,000 light-years away. A detailed 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 400 million years, though another method gives a third of that. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already burnt out; the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Take two field-widths right, toward Cepheus; VV Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: VV Cephei holds a record: one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). A short reminder before you look: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: VV Cephei lies about 3 times farther than M39.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae
stops.class: F8pIa-0 to M3 (variable) · yellow-hypergiant · yellow-hypergiant variable

getThere.text: Take two field-widths up, toward Cassiopeia; ρ Cassiopeiae is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: ρ Cassiopeiae is one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: VV Cephei at about 3,000–3,800 light-years, ρ Cassiopeiae at about 9,170 light-years.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia. It looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most powerful stars you can see by eye.
card.see: Start at Caph, the end of the W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-southwest to a faint yellowish star: ρ Cassiopeiae. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of the cluster NGC 7789 between them. Compare ρ with nearby stars; it slowly changes.
card.understand: ρ Cas gives off more than half a million times the Sun’s light. Most bright-looking stars are nearby; this one is visible from enormous distance because of sheer power. It is in a short, unstable stage that only the heaviest stars reach: swollen, restless and losing mass in bursts. In 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up, toward Andromeda; Andromeda Galaxy is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Andromeda Galaxy is the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Andromeda Galaxy is about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 300 times farther than ρ Cassiopeiae.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Star Families of Perseus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Do stars have families?
journeys.hook: Meet star families at every age, from tight-knit newborns to scattered siblings.
journeys.story: Meet star families at every age, from tight-knit newborns to scattered siblings. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Double Cluster (h Persei) to Ain, all in the sky around Perseus. NGC 1342 is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: In the east, around Perseus

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Look 65° up in the north-east. Eyes first: locate Ruchbah, then a short binocular hop brings in Double Cluster (h Persei).

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. A short reminder before you look: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view; a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
