card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points. The western one (h) is a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white ones, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so their stars share an age. Most of what you see are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun. The handful of orange points are heavier stars that have already used up the hydrogen in their cores and swelled into red supergiants. They are living out their last chapter and will explode as supernovae.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep right about two binocular fields (about 13°).

stops.whyHere: Alpha Persei Cluster holds a record: one of the nearest young star clusters (open clusters within about 600 light-years).
stops.transitionText: From a 14-million-year-old family to one about six times older, and thirteen times closer: Alpha Persei Cluster spreads its stars across your whole field.

card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus. Dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. This is a cluster that only binoculars or the eye can take in whole. Note how similar the bright members look.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, roughly 90 million years ago. Mirfak itself is a member, a supergiant that has already left its long, steady adult life. The others are hot blue-white stars still burning hydrogen. Because the family is so close, it spreads over several Moon widths; a farther cluster just like it would shrink into a small knot.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 1342

getThere.text: Sweep right about one and a half binocular fields (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: A challenge stop: NGC 1342 is hard in binoculars. If you can't find it, the story still works. One thing first: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: NGC 1342, next to your memory of Alpha Persei Cluster.

card.glance: A small, loose cluster of faint stars in southern Perseus, between Algol and the Pleiades.
card.see: From Algol, move about six degrees south-east toward the Pleiades. Look for a handful of stars standing out from the field in a small patch.
card.understand: It is about 160 million years old; at 2,000 light-years, its stars look faint and few compared with the nearby Pleiades.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Pleiades

getThere.text: Sweep right about two binocular fields, toward Taurus.

stops.whyHere: Pleiades adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: Pleiades, a cousin of NGC 1342.

card.glance: Dozens of blue-white stars in a little dipper shape; the best cluster in the sky for binoculars.
card.see: The naked-eye dipper of six or seven stars becomes dozens of blue-white points that fill the view. Notice how alike the brightest ones are: all blue-white, all hot. Look for little chains and pairs among the fainter stars.
card.understand: These stars were born together, so they share one age. Heavy stars burn their fuel fastest and die first, like the biggest candles on a birthday cake. The Pleiades still keep their blue-white stars, so by star standards the family is young.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Ain

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down (about 11°); Ain is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Ain is first planet found around a star in an open cluster (open-cluster members (as of the 2007 discovery)).
stops.transitionText: Turn the page in a star's life, from Pleiades to Ain.

card.glance: A yellow-orange star at the northern tip of the Hyades V.
card.see: Find the Hyades V and look at the tip of its northern arm: that is ε Tauri. Compare it with Aldebaran at the other tip: both are orange-ish, but Ain is fainter and paler.
card.understand: Ain is a giant member of the Hyades. A regular 595-day wobble in its speed reveals a planet at least seven times Jupiter’s mass. Because the cluster’s age is known, so is the age of this planet’s star: a rare clock for a planetary system.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Andromeda: Light from Every Century
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar.
journeys.story: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Capella to Mirach, all in the sky around Andromeda.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Andromeda

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, about 40° up in the north-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Capella is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings.
card.see: Look for a creamy, slightly golden tint: warmer than Rigel or Sirius, not as orange as Aldebaran. No binoculars or ordinary telescope can split it; the two stars are far too close. Just south of Capella, find the small triangle of stars called the Kids.
card.understand: Capella is two giant stars, each about two and a half times the Sun’s mass, circling each other every 104 days. Timing that orbit lets astronomers weigh them directly. The weights reveal the two are at different stages: one is already burning helium in its core, the other is only now swelling into a giant.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Mirfak

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up, toward Perseus; Mirfak is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Mirfak is the brightest star of the Alpha Persei Cluster (within the cluster). Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Mirfak lies about 10 times farther than Capella.

card.glance: A bright yellow-white star in Perseus, ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains: the Alpha Persei Cluster. Mirfak itself looks a shade yellower than its siblings. This is one of the finest binocular views in the sky; it suits wide, low-power binoculars better than telescopes.
card.understand: These stars were born together and share one age. Mirfak started out heavier than most of its siblings, so it burned through its core hydrogen first and has already swollen into a yellow supergiant. Its lighter brothers and sisters are still in their long, steady adult phase, shining blue-white. One family, two stages of life, side by side.

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three binocular fields, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: From about 506 light-years to about 9,130 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 20 times farther.

card.glance: Two bright "eyes" at one end of a small, elongated swarm, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other. A faint, slightly elongated spray of stars trails away from them; with steady binoculars it becomes the outstretched wings or arms. The bright star is φ Cassiopeiae.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,000 light-years away and only some 20 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant and one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. If it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia's distances now favor membership, but the debate is not over.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), slide up roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: Andromeda Galaxy holds a record: the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Andromeda Galaxy is about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 300 times farther than Owl Cluster (ET Cluster).

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Mirach

getThere.text: Take one field-widths up and to the left (about 8°); Mirach is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: One gentle stop to close the loop.
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Andromeda Galaxy is about 2,480,000 light-years away, Mirach about 197 light-years.

card.glance: A bright orange-red star in Andromeda: the usual stepping stone to the Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies.
card.see: Binoculars show a ruddy orange point. Hop north-west through μ Andromedae to find the Andromeda Galaxy, or the other way to Triangulum.
card.understand: Mirach is a red giant: cooler than the Sun, so redder, but far larger and brighter.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Cepheus: Spot the Difference
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Polaris to Garnet Star, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north, around Cepheus

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Find Polaris by eye, about 40° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Polaris quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths up, toward Cepheus; Errai is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Errai is one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003 (history of astronomy). One thing first: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Polaris gives off about 2,210 times the Sun's light, Errai about 12 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of Cepheus’s house-shaped outline, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the “house” of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris. In binoculars it is a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen; compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the house’s other corner.
card.understand: Errai is a star a little heavier than the Sun that has finished its long hydrogen-burning life and is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 astronomers noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its velocity, a hint of a planet. Doubts about the star’s own variations left the claim in limbo until 2003, when a planet with a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed.

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: From Errai, slide left roughly one and a half fields of view (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Alfirk holds a record: the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: Alfirk is about 2,000 times more luminous than Errai, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one binocular field (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky).
stops.transitionText: Size check: VV Cephei is about 100 times larger than Alfirk.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Stay put: Garnet Star is in the same view, just left of VV Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Garnet Star is one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Two red supergiants a few degrees apart. The Garnet Star lives alone; VV Cephei has a hot partner it eclipses every 20 years, which lets astronomers measure it.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Seeing Double in Corona Borealis
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is that one star, or two, or six?
journeys.hook: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count.
journeys.story: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Nu Draconis to Alphecca, all in the sky around Corona Borealis. T Coronae Borealis is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-east, around Corona Borealis

stops.name: Nu Draconis

getThere.text: Look 30° up in the north-east. Find Rastaban by eye, then hop left to Nu Draconis.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

card.glance: Two perfectly matched white stars 62″ apart in the dragon's head: one of the finest binocular doubles.
card.see: Find the dragon's head, then the faintest of its four stars: binoculars split it into two equal white points, like a pair of eyes.
card.understand: The twins are a classic catalogued pair about 100 light-years away, both white stars a little hotter than the Sun.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: 16 & 17 Draconis
stops.class: B9.5 V + B9 V + A1 Vnn · main-sequence

getThere.text: From Nu Draconis, slide up and to the right roughly one fields of view (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: 16 & 17 Draconis shows the same idea as Nu Draconis. Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.

card.glance: A wide, nearly equal pair of white 5th-magnitude stars 90″ apart in Draco; easy in any binoculars.
card.see: Two matched white points sit 1½′ apart. A telescope would show one of them is itself a 3″ pair.
card.understand: Catalogues list a third star 3″ from one of the pair; whether all three are bound together is not settled.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: ν¹ & ν² Boötis

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the right, toward Boötes; ν¹ & ν² Boötis is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: ν¹ & ν² Boötis adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: 16 & 17 Draconis measures about 3.8 times the Sun's radius; ν¹ & ν² Boötis about 78–110 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes: one orange, one white.
card.see: In binoculars the two sit side by side, orange ν¹ and white ν², nearly equal in brightness. Defocus slightly to make the color contrast pop.
card.understand: ν¹ is an orange giant nearly 1,000 light-years away; ν² is a white star about 440 light-years away. They have nothing to do with each other and line up only from where we stand. The orange one must give out far more light to look as bright from twice as far.

stops.name: T Coronae Borealis
stops.class: M3 III + white dwarf · binary-interacting · recurrent-nova variable

getThere.text: From ν¹ & ν² Boötis, slide down and to the right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt. Quick background: A white dwarf is the leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, very dense, and slowly cooling.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: T Coronae Borealis, a cousin of ν¹ & ν² Boötis.

card.glance: Normally a faint star just south-east of the Northern Crown's bowl; during an eruption, briefly a new naked-eye star.
card.see: Find the semicircle of Corona Borealis between Arcturus and Vega, then look just under 1° south of ε CrB, the star at the eastern end of the arc. In quiet times T CrB is a 10th-magnitude speck that needs dark skies and the chart. If it has erupted, an extra star will stand out where none was, fading over about a week.
card.understand: Two stars orbit here: a bloated red giant and a white dwarf, an Earth-sized remnant. The dwarf's gravity pulls gas off the giant. Hydrogen piles up on its surface until the layer ignites in a runaway nuclear blast: a nova. The dwarf survives, and the cycle starts again.

stops.name: Alphecca
stops.class: A1 IV + G5 V · main-sequence · eclipsing-algol variable

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just above T Coronae Borealis, in the same view, and you have Alphecca.

stops.whyHere: Alphecca answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Depth check: Alphecca is about 40 times closer than T Coronae Borealis, though they share this patch of sky.

card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star of the arc; binoculars fit the whole crown in one or two fields. Use it as the reference point for the two strange variables nearby.
card.understand: Alphecca is really two stars, a white one and a Sun-like one, that eclipse each other every 17 days, but the dip is far too small to notice by eye.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Starlight Postmarked Long Ago: Corona Borealis
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when.
journeys.story: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Arcturus to Zeta Herculis, all in the sky around Corona Borealis. R Coronae Borealis is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Corona Borealis

stops.name: Arcturus

getThere.text: Find Arcturus by eye, about 50° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Arcturus quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: The brightest star of spring: a strong orange-gold light at the end of the curve you follow from the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Follow the curve of the Dipper’s handle away from the bowl; the first bright star you meet is Arcturus. In binoculars its orange-gold color is obvious. Later, carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare the two colors. Defocusing slightly makes the warm tint even richer.
card.understand: Arcturus has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 25 times the Sun’s width; that large glowing surface is why such a cool star shines so brightly. It weighs about the same as the Sun but is billions of years older and poorer in heavy elements. It also moves quickly across our line of sight, which marks it as a member of the Galaxy’s older, thicker disk passing by.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alphecca
stops.class: A1 IV + G5 V · main-sequence · eclipsing-algol variable

getThere.text: Take three field-widths down and to the left, toward Corona Borealis; Alphecca is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alphecca adds the next piece of the story. A short reminder before you look: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Alphecca lies about 2 times farther than Arcturus.

card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star of the arc; binoculars fit the whole crown in one or two fields. Use it as the reference point for the two strange variables nearby.
card.understand: Alphecca is really two stars, a white one and a Sun-like one, that eclipse each other every 17 days, but the dip is far too small to notice by eye.

stops.name: R Coronae Borealis
stops.class: G0 Iep (hydrogen-deficient carbon star) · binary-interacting · r-crb variable

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just left of Alphecca, in the same view, and you have R Coronae Borealis.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Depth check: R Coronae Borealis is about 30 times farther than Alphecca, though they share this patch of sky.

card.glance: When at normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the bowl of the Northern Crown; at other times, missing altogether.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a bit fainter than the faintest stars of the crown. If you cannot find it, the star may be in one of its fades. Either answer is a real observation; note which you saw.
card.understand: R CrB is a strange supergiant almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Every so often its outflowing gas cools enough for carbon to condense into soot grains. A cloud that forms on our side blocks the light, and the star dims by up to thousands of times. Months or years later the soot drifts away and the star returns.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 14° (two fields) left, toward Hercules.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Great Hercules Globular Cluster is the brightest globular cluster in the far-northern sky (globular clusters north of declination +30°).
stops.transitionText: From about 1,900–2,800 light-years to about 24,200 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 10 times farther.

card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on one side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. On the line between η and ζ Herculis, about a third of the way from η, sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star. It brightens toward the center. Binoculars won’t split it into stars; that takes a telescope. Compare it with a nearby star of similar brightness: one is a point, the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of stars that all formed together in the young Milky Way. M13 holds roughly half a million Suns’ worth of stars in a ball about 120 light-years wide. Its stars are about 12 billion years old, more than twice the Sun’s age, and they contain far less iron and other heavy elements than the Sun because they formed before many generations of stars had enriched the gas. Globulars swarm around the galaxy in a vast halo, not in the flat disk.

image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello

stops.name: Zeta Herculis

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Zeta Herculis is already in the field, just right of Great Hercules Globular Cluster.

stops.whyHere: One gentle stop to close the loop.
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Great Hercules Globular Cluster is about 24,200 light-years away, Zeta Herculis about 35 light-years.

card.glance: The south-western corner of the Keystone of Hercules, a pale yellow star 35 light-years away.
card.see: ζ and η Herculis frame the west side of the Keystone; the globular cluster M13 lies about a third of the way from η to ζ. ζ Her itself is a simple yellowish point.
card.understand: It is a subgiant: its core hydrogen is running out and it has grown to almost three times the Sun's width. A close companion orbits it, too tight for binoculars.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Ursa Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do these neighbors look so different?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Cor Caroli to Mizar & Alcor, all in the sky around Ursa Major.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Ursa Major

stops.name: Cor Caroli

getThere.text: Find Cor Caroli by eye, about 75° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Cor Caroli is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A white star alone under the Big Dipper’s handle; braced 10x binoculars may show a faint partner almost touching it.
card.see: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Dipper’s handle. Hold 10x binoculars very steady, or use a tripod, and look for a much fainter companion right beside it. In 7x binoculars it usually stays merged. Its white color makes a good contrast with red La Superba about seven degrees to the north.
card.understand: The brighter star is hot and white, with a strong, lopsided magnetic field. That field holds elements such as silicon and europium in large patches on its surface. As the star turns every five and a half days, the patches swing in and out of view and its light and spectrum change slightly. Astronomers named this whole class of variable star after it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Groombridge 1830

getThere.text: Sweep up about one and a half binocular fields, toward Ursa Major.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Groombridge 1830 is one of the fastest-moving stars across the sky that binoculars can show (stars brighter than about 9th magnitude). Before we go on: Globular clusters are ancient balls of stars that swarm around our galaxy in a wide halo, well away from its flat disk.
stops.transitionText: Groombridge 1830 is about 500 times less luminous than Cor Caroli, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star in a quiet corner of Ursa Major, findable in binoculars with a chart.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about 16 degrees due south of Phecda, the bowl star nearest the handle. In binoculars it is a faint yellowish point with no visible hint of its speed. Note its position against nearby stars; in a lifetime of careful sketches it would visibly creep.
card.understand: Most stars near the Sun circle the Galaxy with us in its flat disk, like cars in the same lanes. Groombridge 1830 follows a steep, looping orbit through the halo, the old, thin swarm of stars around the disk, so it cuts through our lane at high speed. It contains far less iron than the Sun, a sign it formed early, before generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy’s gas.

stops.name: La Superba

getThere.text: Sweep left about one and a half binocular fields, toward Canes Venatici.

stops.whyHere: La Superba holds a record: one of the very few carbon stars visible to the unaided eye (dark-sky naked-eye stars).
stops.transitionText: Size check: La Superba is about 800 times larger than Groombridge 1830.

card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, head about a third of the way toward Megrez, the star joining the Dipper’s handle to its bowl. Faint to the eye, it is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember. Keep looking: red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare. Then swing to white Cor Caroli for contrast.
card.understand: Late in life, a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. Carbon-rich molecules and soot block blue light, so what escapes is deep red. The star is cool, about 2,700 degrees, and it is shedding gas and dust that have piled up into a shell about three light-years across.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alkaid

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down, toward Ursa Major; Alkaid is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alkaid holds a record: the hottest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet Alkaid is about 200 times smaller than La Superba.

card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Alkaid ends the handle. In binoculars it looks crisply blue-white, a clear contrast with yellow-orange Dubhe at the other end of the Dipper. About three and a half degrees to the southwest, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 degrees, three times hotter than the Sun’s, which is why it looks blue-white. Hot stars like this are heavy and burn through their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go. It lies about 100 light-years away and travels in a different direction from the five family stars in the middle of the Dipper.

stops.name: Mizar & Alcor

getThere.text: From Alkaid, slide left roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Mizar & Alcor holds a record: the first star found to be double from its spectrum alone (Mizar A) (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: Alkaid ends the Dipper’s handle, but unlike Mizar next door it is not family: hotter, younger and heading its own way.

card.glance: Bright Mizar and fainter Alcor at the bend of the Big Dipper’s handle: a pair you can split by eye, wide apart in binoculars.
card.see: Look at the middle star of the Dipper’s handle; keen eyes see little Alcor beside it. Binoculars spread them less than half a Moon-width apart, with a fainter star nearby making a small triangle. Mizar’s own close companion needs a telescope at moderate power, so don’t expect to split it here.
card.understand: Mizar and Alcor are not a chance alignment. Both lie roughly 80–90 light-years away and drift together, and each is itself multiple: Mizar is two pairs of stars, and Alcor has a small red-dwarf companion found in 2009. That likely makes six stars in one system. They also share their motion with Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth, all born together about 400 million years ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Leo
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Regulus to Pollux, all in the sky around Leo.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the west, around Leo

stops.name: Regulus

getThere.text: Find Regulus by eye, about 55° up in the south-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Regulus is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A bright blue-white star at the foot of Leo’s ‘Sickle’; steady binoculars may show a faint companion star beside it.
card.see: Regulus is the bright dot at the bottom of the backward question mark that outlines Leo’s head. In binoculars it is crisp and blue-white. Brace the binoculars and look about a tenth of a Moon-width to the northwest for a faint point: Regulus B, a small star that travels with it. The glare makes this a test.
card.understand: Regulus is a hot, young star about three and a half times the Sun’s mass. It turns once in roughly 16 hours, so fast that its equator bulges out and glows cooler and dimmer than its poles. Why so fast? Its close partner was once the bigger star. When that star swelled, Regulus pulled away its outer gas and the spin that came with it, leaving the partner as a small, hot core.

stops.name: Algieba
stops.class: K1 III Fe−1 + G7 III · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: From Regulus, slide up and to the right roughly one fields of view (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Algieba adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: From blue-white Regulus to golden Algieba, a few steps up the Sickle: same constellation, very different surface temperatures.

card.glance: A golden star in Leo’s mane; binoculars show one star, with a fainter whitish star a third of a degree to the south.
card.see: Algieba is the brightest star of Leo’s Sickle after Regulus. Binoculars cannot split its two golden giants; they are far too close together. Instead, notice 40 Leonis, a fainter whitish star about a third of a degree south: it looks like a companion, but it is a nearer star that only happens to line up.
card.understand: Algieba is really two orange-gold giants, both past their long, steady adult lives, orbiting each other far apart. Their surfaces are around 4,500 degrees, cooler than the Sun’s, which is why they glow golden. The brighter one also has a giant planet, at least about nine times Jupiter’s mass, detected from the star’s gentle wobble.

stops.name: Ras Elased Australis

getThere.text: Move about 9° (one fields) right (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Ras Elased Australis.

card.glance: The star at the top of Leo’s Sickle, pale yellow in binoculars.
card.see: Follow the Sickle up from Regulus to its top. In binoculars this star is a soft pale yellow; compare it with blue-white Regulus at the bottom of the same curve.
card.understand: It has left its long, steady adult life and swollen to about 21 times the Sun’s width. Its surface, near 5,300 degrees, is a little cooler than the Sun’s, which gives it a slightly deeper yellow tint.

stops.name: X Cancri

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) down, toward Cancer.

stops.whyHere: Pay attention here; X Cancri upsets an easy assumption.
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet X Cancri is about 20 times larger than Ras Elased Australis.

card.glance: A vivid red-orange star a few degrees southeast of the Beehive Cluster, easy in binoculars once you know the field.
card.see: From the Beehive, move about four and a half degrees southeast. Among the faint stars there, X Cnc stands out by color, a warm red-orange that seems to deepen the longer you look. It changes brightness slowly over months, so compare it with neighboring stars rather than trusting a printed value.
card.understand: Like La Superba, X Cancri is an old giant whose core is spent; it now burns helium in thin shells. Churning currents bring freshly made carbon to the surface, and carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere soak up blue and green light, leaving mostly red. It pulses unevenly over months and is slowly shedding its outer layers into space.

image.credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO)/M. Maercker et al.

stops.name: Pollux

getThere.text: From X Cancri, slide right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Gemini.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Pollux is one of the nearest giant stars to the Sun (giant stars (luminosity class III or brighter); Arcturus is next at about 37 light-years).
stops.transitionText: X Cancri measures about 450–590 times the Sun's radius; Pollux about 8.9 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: The brighter of Gemini’s twins: a warm orange point.
card.see: Put Pollux and Castor in one field and compare: Pollux is orange, Castor white. Defocus a touch and the color difference gets vivid. The twins are not siblings at all: they lie at different distances and are at different stages of life.
card.understand: Pollux is an orange giant about 34 light-years away. It has finished burning hydrogen in its core, swollen, and cooled to about 4,850 K. Astronomers found a steady 590-day wobble in its speed toward and away from us: the tug of a planet at least twice Jupiter’s mass, a world that has outlived its star’s youth.

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Sagittarius: Our Address in the Milky Way
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far can you see beyond the Milky Way?
journeys.hook: We live inside a galaxy. Tonight you see it from within.
journeys.story: We live inside a galaxy. Tonight you see it from within. In 4 stops and about 30 minutes you go from Sagittarius Star Cloud to M14, all in the sky around Sagittarius.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Sagittarius

stops.name: Sagittarius Star Cloud

getThere.text: Look 30° up in the south. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Albaldah, aim at it, then follow the hop to Sagittarius Star Cloud.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Sagittarius Star Cloud quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: Binoculars gather much more light than your eye can, which is why crowds of extra stars pop into view.

card.glance: A bright, grainy cloud of countless faint stars, about the size of a binocular field.
card.see: Look about seven degrees north of the Teapot’s lid for a bright knot in the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye. Binoculars break it into a dense, sparkling sheet of faint stars with dark notches around its edges. Let your gaze drift: tiny knots, chains and dark blotches appear. Few views show so many stars at once.
card.understand: Toward the center of our galaxy, most of the Milky Way is hidden behind dust. Here a gap in the dust lets you look deep into the galaxy’s disk, to a crowded stretch of a spiral arm. The glow is the combined light of thousands of stars too faint to see one by one. This is what our galaxy’s disk looks like from inside: a crowded band, patchy with dust.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M25

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. M25 is already in the field, below and to the left of Sagittarius Star Cloud.

stops.whyHere: M25 adds the next piece of the story. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: A perspective trick: about 10,000–16,000 light-years to Sagittarius Star Cloud, about 2,100 light-years to M25.

card.glance: A bright, loose cluster of a few dozen stars, with a couple of yellowish members.
card.see: From μ Sagittarii, hop about four and a half degrees east-northeast. M25 is a loose group of bright stars spread over half a degree, with a central pattern and scattered outliers. U Sagittarii is one of the central stars: compare it with its neighbors on several nights and watch it change.
card.understand: U Sagittarii swells and shrinks, and its brightness rises and falls with a period of 6.7 days. For stars of this kind, a longer period means a more luminous star. Because U Sgr sits in a cluster whose distance we can measure, it helps calibrate that rule, which astronomers then use to measure distances to other galaxies.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wild Duck Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep up about two binocular fields, toward Scutum.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Wild Duck Cluster is one of the most star-rich and compact open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Wild Duck Cluster is about 7,280 light-years away, about 3 times farther than M25.

card.glance: A small, bright, grainy fan of light in Scutum, almost like a globular, with a bright star at its tip.
card.see: Follow Aquila’s tail south into little Scutum, then go about two degrees southeast of β Scuti. M11 is a compact, fan-shaped haze with a brighter star at its apex, set inside the bright Scutum star cloud. In 10×50s it looks granular; more magnification starts to break it into stars.
card.understand: Most open clusters hold a few hundred stars; M11 holds thousands. Born together a few hundred million years ago, its stars are packed tightly enough that the cluster still looks dense and rich. From over 7,000 light-years away, you see their combined light as one glowing fan.

image.credit: ESO

stops.name: M14

getThere.text: From Wild Duck Cluster, slide right roughly three fields of view, toward Ophiuchus.

stops.whyHere: The answer stop: M14 is where tonight's question comes together.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: M14 lies about 4 times farther than Wild Duck Cluster.

card.glance: A faint, round, evenly lit glow in an empty part of Ophiuchus.
card.see: From γ Ophiuchi, sweep about six and a half degrees south-southwest. Expect a faint, round, featureless glow; patient field matching helps.
card.understand: M14 holds more than five times the mass of M12, yet looks fainter because it lies nearly twice as far away.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: A Ladder of Distances in Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far away is the farthest thing you can see tonight?
journeys.hook: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time.
journeys.story: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Altair to M92, all in the sky around Cygnus. T Lyrae is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cygnus

stops.name: Altair

getThere.text: Find Altair by eye, about 50° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Altair quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: The bright white star at the southern corner of the Summer Triangle, flanked by two fainter stars like a short line of three.
card.see: Altair sits between two attendants: orange Tarazed about 2° above it and fainter Alshain below. Fit all three in one binocular field and compare their colours; Tarazed's warm tint is easy, while Altair stays crisp white.
card.understand: Altair is a normal adult star, a bit heavier and hotter than the Sun, but it spins at more than 90% of the speed that would tear it apart. Spinning flings its middle outward, so the equator bulges about a quarter wider than the poles. The poles, closer to the hot core, shine hotter; the stretched equator is cooler and dimmer.

stops.name: HD 189733

getThere.text: Move about 14° (two fields) up and to the left, toward Vulpecula.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: HD 189733 is host of the first exoplanet whose colour was measured (deep blue) (exoplanets, 2013).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: HD 189733 lies about 4 times farther than Altair.

card.glance: A 7½-magnitude star about a quarter of a degree from the Dumbbell Nebula; both fit in one binocular field.
card.see: Centre the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) in Vulpecula. HD 189733 is the brighter star just a quarter of a degree away, about half a Moon-width. When the planet passes in front, the star dims by only about 3%, far too little for the eye; there is nothing to see but a steady point.
card.understand: The planet here is a "hot Jupiter": a gas giant slightly heavier than Jupiter, orbiting so close that its year lasts just over two days. Because its orbit is edge-on to us, it crosses the star's face each orbit, and astronomers can read its atmosphere in the starlight that filters through.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, M. Kornmesser

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: Move about 9° (one and a half fields) up, toward Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Albireo holds a record: one of the most celebrated colour-contrast double stars. One thing first: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: From about 65 light-years to about 360–500 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 7 times farther.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: T Lyrae

getThere.text: From Albireo, slide up roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Lyra.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Albireo at about 360–500 light-years, T Lyrae at about 1,410 light-years.

card.glance: A faint, distinctly red dot about 2° south-west of Vega: the same binocular field holds the bluest-white and one of the reddest stars.
card.see: Put Vega at one edge of the field and look about 2° toward the south-west. T Lyrae is a faint star with a strong red tint, easiest with 10× binoculars in a dark sky. Glance at it, then at Vega, and back: the contrast is the lesson. Do not stare too long; red stars seem to brighten under a steady gaze.
card.understand: Late in life, some giants dredge carbon made in their cores up to the surface. Carbon molecules and soot in the cool atmosphere absorb blue light, so the star looks deep red, much redder than its temperature alone would make it. Its winds carry that carbon into space, where it will be built into dust, new stars and planets.

stops.name: M92

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) up, toward Hercules.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: M92 is among the oldest star clusters known in the Milky Way (Milky Way globular clusters with precise ages).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: M92 is about 27,700 light-years away, about 20 times farther than T Lyrae.

card.glance: A smaller, more concentrated glow than M13, north of the Keystone in a sparse patch of sky.
card.see: From π Herculis, the Keystone’s north-east corner, go about 6 degrees north, a little over one binocular field. M92 looks like a slightly smaller, fainter M13 with a brighter, almost starlike center. If you have just seen M13, flip back and forth and compare their size and central brightness.
card.understand: Heavy elements such as iron are made inside stars and spread when stars die, so the amount a star contains is like a family history: the less it has, the fewer generations came before it. M92’s stars hold only about 1/200 of the Sun’s share. A careful 2023 study put the cluster at about 13.8 billion years, give or take three quarters of a billion: as old as the Universe within the uncertainty.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do these neighbors look so different?
journeys.hook: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why.
journeys.story: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Deneb to Albireo, all in the sky around Cygnus. Chi Cygni is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Cygnus

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Find Deneb by eye, about 55° up in the north-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Deneb quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.

card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, at the top of the Northern Cross, set in a dense Milky Way star field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan. Sweep slowly around it in binoculars: the background fills with countless faint stars because you are looking along the Milky Way. Compare Deneb with Vega, which looks clearly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away; Deneb is roughly a hundred times farther. For Deneb to look nearly as bright from there, it must pour out vastly more light. It is a supergiant around 200 times wider than the Sun, giving off something like 200,000 Suns' worth of light. Brightness on the sky mixes two things: how much light a star makes and how far away it is.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about one binocular field (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: 61 Cygni holds a record: the first star whose distance was measured (history of astronomy (Bessel, 1838)).
stops.transitionText: Brilliant Deneb and faint 61 Cygni sit in the same constellation. The faint one is our close neighbour; the brilliant one is over a hundred times farther away.

card.glance: A faint naked-eye star in a dark sky, south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find it about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart. Compare their colour with white Deneb; then remember that the faint pair is well over a hundred times closer.
card.understand: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in a year. 61 Cygni is about 11 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours. The two stars are orange dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun, orbiting each other. They look faint not because they are far but because they give out little light; Deneb looks bright despite being enormously farther.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868)

getThere.text: From 61 Cygni, slide up and to the right roughly two fields of view (about 14°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is a star you can see in binoculars that orbits a black hole (one of the very few such systems within binocular reach). Before we go on: A star far heavier than the Sun ends in a supernova explosion that leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole.
stops.transitionText: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is about 90,000 times more luminous than 61 Cygni, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A 9th-magnitude star half a degree from η Cygni, in the swan's neck: tiny, unremarkable, unforgettable once you know.
card.see: Centre η Cygni, the star midway along the swan's neck. About 0.4° (less than the Moon's width) east-north-east, among a sprinkle of faint stars, a slightly brighter one is HDE 226868. Use the chart; there is nothing to see but a point of light. The black hole beside it is invisible at any wavelength your eye can use.
card.understand: This blue supergiant, around 40 times the Sun's mass, whips round an unseen partner every 5.6 days. From the orbit, astronomers weigh the partner at about 21 Suns, yet it gives off no starlight: it is a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star. Gas torn from the supergiant heats up as it spirals in and glows in X-rays.

stops.name: Chi Cygni

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the right of Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868), in the same view, and you have Chi Cygni.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) measures about 4.8 times the Sun's radius; Chi Cygni about 350–530 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: In the swan's neck between Albireo and η Cyg: a red star near maximum, or an empty patch of sky near minimum.
card.see: Sweep from Albireo toward η Cygni. Near maximum, χ Cyg is an obvious orange-red star; months later the same spot shows nothing in binoculars. Red stars play tricks on night vision: glance briefly when you compare it with white stars, because a long stare makes red look brighter.
card.understand: χ Cyg is a giant near the end of its life, so swollen that it would engulf the orbit of Mars. It pulses with a 408-day rhythm, and each cycle its outer layers cool and form molecules that soak up visible light. That is why the change is so dramatic. It is also shedding its outer layers into space.

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one binocular field (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Albireo is one of the most celebrated colour-contrast double stars.
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet Albireo is about 6 times smaller than Chi Cygni.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Pairs and Impostors of Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How many stars can hide in one point of light?
journeys.hook: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Sheliak to 31 Cygni, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Cygnus

stops.name: Sheliak
stops.class: B8.5 Ib-II + disk · binary-interacting · eclipsing-beta-lyrae variable

getThere.text: Look nearly overhead. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Vega, aim at it, then follow the hop to Sheliak.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Sheliak is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's parallelogram; it changes brightness every few days.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat (γ Lyr) are the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, 2° apart: an ideal comparison. Some nights the two look equal; at deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly fainter. Note which is brighter tonight and check again in a few days. Binoculars also show a 7th-magnitude companion 46″ away.
card.understand: Sheliak is two stars orbiting every 13 days, so close that one has swollen into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner. The partner is wrapped in a thick disk of that stolen gas, which hides it from view. As they circle edge-on to us, each passes in front of the other, so the light rises and falls continuously.

stops.name: Zeta Lyrae

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the left of Sheliak, in the same view, and you have Zeta Lyrae.

stops.whyHere: Zeta Lyrae adds the next piece of the story. One thing first: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: Zeta Lyrae is about 400 times less luminous than Sheliak, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A white star 2° south-east of Vega that binoculars split into a 44″ pair, one star brighter than the other.
card.see: From Vega, drop about 2° south-east: ζ Lyrae forms a small triangle with Vega and the Double-Double. Binoculars show a brighter white star with a fainter companion just to the south-east.
card.understand: The pair is easy because the gap, 44″, is wide for binoculars; compare it with the 3.5′ gap of ε Lyrae next door.

stops.name: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868)

getThere.text: Sweep down about two and a half binocular fields, toward Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is a star you can see in binoculars that orbits a black hole (one of the very few such systems within binocular reach).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Zeta Lyrae gives off about 32 times the Sun's light, Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) about 13,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A 9th-magnitude star half a degree from η Cygni, in the swan's neck: tiny, unremarkable, unforgettable once you know.
card.see: Centre η Cygni, the star midway along the swan's neck. About 0.4° (less than the Moon's width) east-north-east, among a sprinkle of faint stars, a slightly brighter one is HDE 226868. Use the chart; there is nothing to see but a point of light. The black hole beside it is invisible at any wavelength your eye can use.
card.understand: This blue supergiant, around 40 times the Sun's mass, whips round an unseen partner every 5.6 days. From the orbit, astronomers weigh the partner at about 21 Suns, yet it gives off no starlight: it is a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star. Gas torn from the supergiant heats up as it spirals in and glows in X-rays.

stops.name: 16 Cygni B

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two and a half binocular fields (about 16°).

stops.whyHere: 16 Cygni B holds a record: one of the first stars known to host a planet on a highly stretched orbit (exoplanet discoveries of the 1990s).
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) at about 13,000 times the Sun's light, 16 Cygni B at about 1.3 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: One of a matched pair of 6th-magnitude yellowish stars 40″ apart, near δ Cygni on the swan's western wing.
card.see: Use the chart from δ Cygni (Al Fawaris): about 5° north lies a pair of equal faint stars, 40″ apart, which 10× binoculars split on a steady mount. Both have the same soft yellow-white tint. 16 Cyg B is the slightly fainter one, to the south-east.
card.understand: Both stars are close copies of the Sun: similar temperature, similar mass. Studying the tiny pulsations of their surfaces, the Kepler spacecraft dated them at about 6.8 billion years, older than the Sun. Around B circles a planet heavier than Jupiter on a strongly stretched orbit, perhaps pulled into that shape by its sibling star A.

stops.name: 31 Cygni
stops.class: K4 Ib + B4 IV-V · binary-interacting · eclipsing-long-period variable

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) right (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. 31 Cygni is about 4,000 times more luminous than 16 Cygni B.

card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue companion beside it: a binocular colour trio with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter 7th-magnitude star closer in. The colours are easier than Albireo's because the gaps are wider.
card.understand: A hot blue star orbits the orange supergiant and slips behind it every 10.4 years, a slow eclipse too shallow to notice by eye.

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Cepheus: The Restless Stars
journeys.drivingQuestion: Can you catch a star in the act of changing?
journeys.hook: Catch stars that wink, breathe and hide. You'll judge their brightness yourself.
journeys.story: Catch stars that wink, breathe and hide. You'll judge their brightness yourself. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alfirk to δ Cephei, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Cepheus

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the north. Find Alderamin by eye, then hop down and to the right to Alfirk.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Alfirk is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: From Alfirk, slide up and to the left roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). One thing first: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Alfirk measures about 6.3 times the Sun's radius; VV Cephei about 779 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Caph

getThere.text: From VV Cephei, slide up and to the right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Caph shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: VV Cephei gives off about 57,000–89,000 times the Sun's light, Caph about 27 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The western end of Cassiopeia’s W: a bright white star, steady to the eye.
card.see: Binoculars show a clean white-yellow point at the end of the W. From here, ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-southwest.
card.understand: Caph swells and shrinks slightly about ten times a day, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: RW Cephei

getThere.text: Take two field-widths left, toward Cepheus; RW Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: RW Cephei holds a record: one of the largest known stars in the Milky Way (known stars in our galaxy).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet RW Cephei is about 300 times larger than Caph.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-southwest of δ Cephei. Binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so compare it with neighboring stars and note what you see; you are watching a star that can be veiled by its own dust.
card.understand: RW Cep is a cool hypergiant, a heavy star in a swollen late stage. Images from the CHARA interferometer show a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During its recent fade, one side of the disc looked darker than the other: a dust cloud, probably formed from gas the star had just thrown off, was blocking part of its light.

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: Same field of view: δ Cephei sits below and to the right of RW Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: δ Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variables (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: RW Cephei at about 900–1,800 times the Sun's radius, δ Cephei at about 28–48 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: A Ladder of Distances in Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How do astronomers measure distances no one can travel?
journeys.hook: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time.
journeys.story: Start next door and end far beyond, one measured step at a time. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from 61 Cygni to Andromeda Galaxy, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Cygnus

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Look 60° up in the west. Eyes first: locate Deneb, then a short binocular hop brings in 61 Cygni.

stops.whyHere: We start here because 61 Cygni is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story.

card.glance: A faint naked-eye star in a dark sky, south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find it about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart. Compare their colour with white Deneb; then remember that the faint pair is well over a hundred times closer.
card.understand: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in a year. 61 Cygni is about 11 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours. The two stars are orange dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun, orbiting each other. They look faint not because they are far but because they give out little light; Deneb looks bright despite being enormously farther.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M39

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one and a half binocular fields (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: M39 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: From about 11 light-years to about 965 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 80 times farther.

card.glance: A large, bright, loose triangle of a few dozen stars north-east of Deneb, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From Deneb, sweep about 9 degrees east-north-east. You will meet a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. Use your lowest magnification, count the members, and notice that the brightest ones are all white or blue-white.
card.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance and one motion: a true family about 1,000 light-years away. A detailed 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 400 million years, though another method gives a third of that. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already burnt out; the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths right, toward Cepheus; VV Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). Before we go on: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: M39 at about 965 light-years, VV Cephei at about 3,000–3,800 light-years.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae
stops.class: F8pIa-0 to M3 (variable) · yellow-hypergiant · yellow-hypergiant variable

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) up and to the right, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae holds a record: one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. Quick background: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: Next rung: ρ Cassiopeiae is about 9,170 light-years away, about 3 times farther than VV Cephei.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia. It looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most powerful stars you can see by eye.
card.see: Start at Caph, the end of the W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-southwest to a faint yellowish star: ρ Cassiopeiae. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of the cluster NGC 7789 between them. Compare ρ with nearby stars; it slowly changes.
card.understand: ρ Cas gives off more than half a million times the Sun’s light. Most bright-looking stars are nearby; this one is visible from enormous distance because of sheer power. It is in a short, unstable stage that only the heaviest stars reach: swollen, restless and losing mass in bursts. In 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From ρ Cassiopeiae, slide up and to the right roughly three fields of view, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Andromeda Galaxy is the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Andromeda Galaxy lies about 300 times farther than ρ Cassiopeiae.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Record Breakers of Andromeda
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are record-holding stars so extreme?
journeys.hook: Biggest, hottest, oldest, farthest: tonight's record holders, and why they're extreme.
journeys.story: Biggest, hottest, oldest, farthest: tonight's record holders, and why they're extreme. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Deneb to υ Andromedae, all in the sky around Andromeda.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Andromeda

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Find Deneb by eye, about 60° up in the north-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Deneb quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.

card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, at the top of the Northern Cross, set in a dense Milky Way star field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan. Sweep slowly around it in binoculars: the background fills with countless faint stars because you are looking along the Milky Way. Compare Deneb with Vega, which looks clearly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away; Deneb is roughly a hundred times farther. For Deneb to look nearly as bright from there, it must pour out vastly more light. It is a supergiant around 200 times wider than the Sun, giving off something like 200,000 Suns' worth of light. Brightness on the sky mixes two things: how much light a star makes and how far away it is.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: From Deneb, slide up and to the right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Garnet Star is one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye. A short reminder before you look: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Size up: Garnet Star is about 5 times larger than Deneb.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic.
