Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Caroline's Rose

getThere.text: Move about 18° (two and a half fields) up and to the right, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Caroline's Rose holds a record: the most massive open cluster within about 7,000 light-years in the Gaia DR3 census (Gaia DR3 open clusters in the Hunt & Reffert 2024 census, solar neighborhood).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Caroline's Rose lies about 5 times farther than Garnet Star.

card.glance: A round, even, misty glow about half the Moon's width, between Caph and ρ Cassiopeiae.
card.see: Put Caph and ρ Cassiopeiae in one field; the cluster sits a little south of the line joining them, closer to ρ. In binoculars it is a soft, uniform patch, perhaps with a faint grainy texture under a dark sky. The rose-petal pattern needs a telescope. Compare it with sparkly M52 nearby.
card.understand: NGC 7789 is roughly 1.6 billion years old. All its hot blue stars burned out long ago. The brightest members left are stars a bit heavier than the Sun that have swollen into yellow and orange giants. It is still unusually rich: Gaia counts more than 4,000 members, which is why it has survived so long.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the right, toward Andromeda; Andromeda Galaxy is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Andromeda Galaxy holds a record: the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Zoom out: Andromeda Galaxy spans about 128,000 light-years, about 4,000 times larger than Caroline's Rose.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: υ Andromedae

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down (about 10°); υ Andromedae is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: A last look that ties back to where we began.
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Andromeda Galaxy is about 2,480,000 light-years away, υ Andromedae about 44 light-years.

card.glance: A modest yellow-white star in Andromeda, a few binocular fields from the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.see: From Mirach, move about eight degrees north-east to a modest star: υ Andromedae. In binoculars it is a plain yellow-white point. Its planets are invisible; enjoy knowing they are there, then sweep west to the soft glow of the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.understand: The star’s velocity wobbles in a tangled pattern. Astronomers untangled it into three giant planets: one racing around in under five days, two more on orbits of about eight months and three and a half years. The star is a little hotter and larger than the Sun, so a planet would need to be farther out than Earth to have the same warmth.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: How Stars Die, over Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Will the Sun explode?
journeys.hook: Gentle fade or violent blast? A star's mass decides.
journeys.story: Gentle fade or violent blast? A star's mass decides. In 4 stops and about 30 minutes you go from Albireo to East Veil Nebula, all in the sky around Cygnus. East Veil Nebula is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the west, around Cygnus

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: Look 40° up in the west. Eyes first: locate Vega, then a short binocular hop brings in Albireo.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Dumbbell Nebula

getThere.text: From Albireo, slide left roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Vulpecula.

stops.whyHere: Dumbbell Nebula holds a record: the first planetary nebula ever discovered (all planetary nebulae (Messier, 1764)). A short reminder before you look: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: Albireo showed you one stage of a star's life. Dumbbell Nebula is the stage that follows.

card.glance: A small grey patch, clearly larger than any star, sometimes with a hint of a pinched “apple core” shape.
card.see: Find the little arrow of Sagitta below Albireo. From its tip star, γ Sagittae, move about 3 degrees north. M27 is a small, faint grey smudge. Brace the binoculars and use averted vision: on a dark night it looks slightly squarish or hourglass-shaped. Don’t expect the reds and greens of the photo.
card.understand: This is a planetary nebula, a name from old telescopes that showed a planet-like disk; it has nothing to do with planets. A star once like the Sun swelled into a giant and let its outer layers drift away. Its bare, extremely hot core now energizes that gas, which glows like a neon sign. Within tens of thousands of years the gas will fade into space, carrying elements made inside the star.

image.credit: ESO / I. Appenzeller, W. Seifert, O. Stahl, M. Zamani

stops.name: Sadr

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) up and to the right, toward Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Mass decides the ending. A Sun-like star finishes like Dumbbell Nebula, a puffed-off shell around a white dwarf; a star as heavy as Sadr is headed for a supernova instead.

card.glance: The star at the crossing of the Northern Cross, surrounded in binoculars by swarms of faint Milky Way stars.
card.see: Centre Sadr and simply sweep: dozens of faint stars crowd every field, with dark patches between. Drift a few degrees in any direction and the density changes. Under a dark sky the whole region glows, split by dark lanes of the Cygnus Rift: dust in the Galaxy's disk.
card.understand: When you look at Cygnus you look along the flat disk of our Galaxy, through thousands of light-years of stars, so they pile up behind one another. Sadr itself is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star roughly 1,800 light-years away, far more luminous than the Sun and only modestly hotter.

stops.name: East Veil Nebula

getThere.text: Move about 11° (one and a half fields) left (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Fast-forward. East Veil Nebula shows the stage that comes after Sadr.

card.glance: On a dark night, a faint, curved sliver of light: easier than the western arc, still a stretch for 10×50.
card.see: From ε Cygni, move about 3 degrees south-east. Under a dark, transparent sky, sweep slowly with averted vision for a faint, slightly curved arc about two full Moons long. A nebula filter helps enormously. If you saw the western arc, the empty-looking space between them is the inside of the bubble.
card.understand: This arc and the West Veil are opposite edges of one expanding shell. Where the blast wave hits denser patches of gas, it heats them until they glow; where the gas is thin, nothing shows. That is why the remnant looks like scattered threads rather than a full circle. Stars more than about eight times the Sun’s mass end like this, and the explosion seeds space with new elements.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 07:26.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Taurus Under a Bright Moon
journeys.drivingQuestion: Which wonders does moonlight leave untouched?
journeys.hook: Moonlight steals the faint stuff. Here's what it can't take.
journeys.story: Moonlight steals the faint stuff. Here's what it can't take. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Aldebaran to ζ Persei, all in the sky around Taurus.
journeys.regionLabel: In the west, around Taurus

stops.name: Aldebaran

getThere.text: Find Aldebaran by eye, about 45° up in the west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A bright orange star at one tip of the V-shaped Hyades cluster.
card.see: Frame the Hyades V so that Aldebaran sits at one tip. Its warm orange stands out against the white cluster stars, though a few of them have a faint yellow-orange tint too. Then compare it with Betelgeuse to the south-east: which looks redder to you?
card.understand: Aldebaran is an orange giant, a star that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width. It is about 67 light-years away, less than half the distance of the Hyades behind it. The two just line up from where we stand: stars that look side by side can be very far apart.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: θ Tauri

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the right of Aldebaran, in the same view, and you have θ Tauri.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: θ Tauri is θ² is the brightest true member of the Hyades (Hyades members (Aldebaran is a foreground star)).
stops.transitionText: Two stars in one V: Aldebaran is a foreground impostor at about 67 light-years, while the θ Tauri pair really belongs to the cluster, at about 150 light-years.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair in the Hyades V: one white star, one yellow-orange.
card.see: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair. Binoculars split it at a glance: almost 6 arcminutes. Compare the colors: θ² is white, θ¹ yellow-orange. Defocusing slightly makes the contrast stronger.
card.understand: Both stars were born in the Hyades about 625 million years ago, so they started out together. θ¹ has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a yellow-orange giant. θ² is still hot and white, near the end of its long, steady adult life. A small difference in their starting mass is enough to put them in different chapters.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Ain

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just right of θ Tauri, in the same view, and you have Ain.

stops.whyHere: Ain holds a record: first planet found around a star in an open cluster (open-cluster members (as of the 2007 discovery)). A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Ain is another Hyades giant like θ¹, and it has a planet.

card.glance: A yellow-orange star at the northern tip of the Hyades V.
card.see: Find the Hyades V and look at the tip of its northern arm: that is ε Tauri. Compare it with Aldebaran at the other tip: both are orange-ish, but Ain is fainter and paler.
card.understand: Ain is a giant member of the Hyades. A regular 595-day wobble in its speed reveals a planet at least seven times Jupiter’s mass. Because the cluster’s age is known, so is the age of this planet’s star: a rare clock for a planetary system.

stops.name: Alcyone

getThere.text: From Ain, slide down and to the right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Alcyone holds a record: brightest star of the Pleiades (Pleiades members). Before we go on: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Ain at about 83 times the Sun's light, Alcyone at about 1,000–1,600 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The brightest of the Pleiades, where the little dipper’s bowl meets its handle.
card.see: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle of the group. Then notice how every bright member shares its blue-white color: a family resemblance. Count how many fainter siblings binoculars add to the naked-eye six or seven.
card.understand: Alcyone is a hot B-type star of about 13,000 K, roughly a thousand times as luminous as the Sun. Like its siblings, it formed about 125 million years ago from a single cloud. The very heaviest members have already burned out; Alcyone is among the heaviest still shining, and that is exactly what dates the family.

stops.name: ζ Persei

getThere.text: Take one field-widths up and to the right, toward Perseus; ζ Persei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: A last look that ties back to where we began.
stops.transitionText: ζ Persei is what a family like Alcyone grows into: the same story, a later chapter.

card.glance: A blue-white star at the southern foot of Perseus.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its 9th-magnitude companion, 13 arcseconds away, is lost in the glare.
card.understand: ζ Per is a hot, heavy star that has begun to swell; stars like this live only tens of millions of years.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Colors and Pairs by Moonlight: Auriga
journeys.drivingQuestion: What can you still see when the Moon floods the sky?
journeys.hook: Tonight's Moon drowns faint clouds but can't touch color, doubles or bright clusters.
journeys.story: Tonight's Moon drowns faint clouds but can't touch color, doubles or bright clusters. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Capella to κ Tauri, all in the sky around Auriga.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Auriga

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, about 65° up in the north-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Capella quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Quick background: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings.
card.see: Look for a creamy, slightly golden tint: warmer than Rigel or Sirius, not as orange as Aldebaran. No binoculars or ordinary telescope can split it; the two stars are far too close. Just south of Capella, find the small triangle of stars called the Kids.
card.understand: Capella is two giant stars, each about two and a half times the Sun’s mass, circling each other every 104 days. Timing that orbit lets astronomers weigh them directly. The weights reveal the two are at different stages: one is already burning helium in its core, the other is only now swelling into a giant.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: ζ Aurigae
stops.class: K5 Ib-II + B6.5 IV-V · binary-interacting · eclipsing-long-period variable

getThere.text: Stay put: ζ Aurigae is in the same view, below and to the left of Capella.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Capella gives off about 154 times the Sun's light, ζ Aurigae about 3,300–4,300 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The western of the two lower Kids in Auriga: a 4th-magnitude, orange-tinted star.
card.see: Below ε Aurigae, the two lower Kids form a close pair; ζ is the western one. Compare its slight orange tint with whiter η Aurigae beside it. The eclipse dims it by only about a fifth, so it is subtle to the eye.
card.understand: ζ Aurigae pairs an orange supergiant with a hot blue-white star. Every 972 days the small star slips behind the giant and stays hidden for weeks. Just before and after, its light shines through the giant’s thin outer atmosphere, letting astronomers probe the layers of a star they cannot resolve.

stops.name: ε Persei

getThere.text: Move about 12° (one and a half fields) down, toward Perseus.

stops.whyHere: ε Persei adds the next piece of the story. One thing first: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: ζ Aurigae at about 110–150 times the Sun's radius, ε Persei at about 6.9 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Perseus, a handy yardstick for Algol.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point. Compare Algol with it during an eclipse.
card.understand: ε Per is a hot, heavy blue star that throbs very slightly, by about a tenth of a magnitude.

stops.name: Alcyone

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) down and to the left, toward Taurus.

stops.whyHere: Alcyone holds a record: brightest star of the Pleiades (Pleiades members).
stops.transitionText: Same life story, further along. Look for what has changed between ε Persei and Alcyone.

card.glance: The brightest of the Pleiades, where the little dipper’s bowl meets its handle.
card.see: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle of the group. Then notice how every bright member shares its blue-white color: a family resemblance. Count how many fainter siblings binoculars add to the naked-eye six or seven.
card.understand: Alcyone is a hot B-type star of about 13,000 K, roughly a thousand times as luminous as the Sun. Like its siblings, it formed about 125 million years ago from a single cloud. The very heaviest members have already burned out; Alcyone is among the heaviest still shining, and that is exactly what dates the family.

stops.name: κ Tauri

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one and a half binocular fields (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: We finish by seeing the start with new eyes.
stops.transitionText: κ Tauri is about 30 times less luminous than Alcyone, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A wide, easy pair of white stars about 6° north of the Hyades V.
card.see: Look about 6° north of the Hyades V. Binoculars split it into two white stars about 5.7 arcminutes apart. Compare their brightness: nearly equal.
card.understand: Both stars are white A-type stars, hotter than the Sun. Wide pairs like this one may be true companions drifting together, or just a chance alignment; only distances and motions can tell.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Ursa Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Dubhe to Cor Caroli, all in the sky around Ursa Major.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Ursa Major

stops.name: Dubhe

getThere.text: Find Dubhe by eye, about 50° up in the north-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Dubhe quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer.

card.glance: The bright yellow-orange pointer star at the top of the Big Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the bowl; Merak is the lower one, five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is distinctly yellow-orange and Merak white. Sweep between them a few times and compare. A faint star sits about a fifth of a Moon-width from Dubhe, but its true companion is far too close to see.
card.understand: Dubhe is a giant that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 26 times the Sun’s width, cooling to a yellow-orange glow. It lies about 120 light-years away, half again as far as Merak, and it does not share the motion of the five middle Dipper stars. So the Big Dipper is not one group: most of it is a family, and Dubhe is a passer-by seen in the same direction.

stops.name: Megrez

getThere.text: From Dubhe, slide down and to the right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Megrez is the faintest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism). Before we go on: Star families do not stay together forever; they loosen and drift apart, yet their stars keep moving in step.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: Dubhe at about 26 times the Sun's radius, Megrez at about 2.2 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: The faintest Big Dipper star, where the handle joins the bowl.
card.see: In binoculars Megrez is white. About one and a half degrees northeast lie the two faint stars of Winnecke 4 (M40); brace the binoculars to see them.
card.understand: Megrez is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass, born with Merak, Phecda, Alioth and Mizar about 400 million years ago. Interferometry shows it spins fast enough to be flattened.

stops.name: Alioth

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just below Megrez, in the same view, and you have Alioth.

stops.whyHere: Alioth holds a record: the brightest star in Ursa Major (Ursa Major).
stops.transitionText: From the bowl’s corner into the handle: Alioth shares Megrez’s birth date and its path through the Galaxy.

card.glance: The brightest Big Dipper star, first in the handle next to the bowl; plain white and steady in binoculars.
card.see: Alioth is the handle star touching the bowl. In binoculars it looks white and steady; its light changes by only about two percent as it turns, far below what eyes can notice. Sweep along the handle to Mizar and Alcor to see three family members in one short glide.
card.understand: Alioth is a hot white star born with the other stars of the Ursa Major family. Its outer layers are unusually calm, so some elements sink while others float up, and a weak magnetic field herds them into patches. As the star rotates every five days, the patches swing toward and away from us, and its light flickers very slightly.

stops.name: La Superba

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths right, toward Canes Venatici; La Superba is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: La Superba is one of the very few carbon stars visible to the unaided eye (dark-sky naked-eye stars).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet La Superba is about 100 times larger than Alioth.

card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, head about a third of the way toward Megrez, the star joining the Dipper’s handle to its bowl. Faint to the eye, it is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember. Keep looking: red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare. Then swing to white Cor Caroli for contrast.
card.understand: Late in life, a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. Carbon-rich molecules and soot block blue light, so what escapes is deep red. The star is cool, about 2,700 degrees, and it is shedding gas and dust that have piled up into a shell about three light-years across.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Cor Caroli

getThere.text: From La Superba, slide down and to the right roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Cor Caroli is the prototype after which the α² CVn class of magnetic spotted variable stars is named. One thing first: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Swing from deep-red La Superba to white Cor Caroli, a few degrees away: one of the coolest stars you can see beside one of the hotter ones. Color is a thermometer.

card.glance: A white star alone under the Big Dipper’s handle; braced 10x binoculars may show a faint partner almost touching it.
card.see: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Dipper’s handle. Hold 10x binoculars very steady, or use a tripod, and look for a much fainter companion right beside it. In 7x binoculars it usually stays merged. Its white color makes a good contrast with red La Superba about seven degrees to the north.
card.understand: The brighter star is hot and white, with a strong, lopsided magnetic field. That field holds elements such as silicon and europium in large patches on its surface. As the star turns every five and a half days, the patches swing in and out of view and its light and spectrum change slightly. Astronomers named this whole class of variable star after it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Perseus: One Star or Two?
journeys.drivingQuestion: How many stars can hide in one point of light?
journeys.hook: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Polaris to Algol, all in the sky around Perseus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Perseus

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Find Polaris by eye, about 40° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Polaris quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

stops.name: RZ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Move about 20° (three fields) left, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. Quick background: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.
stops.transitionText: Size check: RZ Cassiopeiae is about 20 times smaller than Polaris.

card.glance: A faint white star in northern Cassiopeia that fades to about a quarter of its light every 28.7 hours.
card.see: Find it with a chart near the Cassiopeia–Camelopardalis border, then check the predicted eclipse. Compare it with nearby stars of similar brightness before and during the dip.
card.understand: Two stars orbit every 1.2 days and pass in front of each other, like a miniature Algol.

stops.name: ι Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of RZ Cassiopeiae, in the same view, and you have ι Cassiopeiae.

stops.whyHere: ι Cassiopeiae shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: ι Cassiopeiae is the same type of object as RZ Cassiopeiae. Notice what makes it different.

card.glance: A white star east of Cassiopeia’s W. Binoculars show one star; a telescope shows a fine triple.
card.see: It lies about five degrees north-east of ε Cassiopeiae, the eastern end of the W. Binoculars show one white point; the triple needs a telescope.
card.understand: Three stars orbit together here, separated by only a few arcseconds.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: γ Persei

getThere.text: Sweep left about two binocular fields, toward Perseus.

stops.whyHere: γ Persei adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: ι Cassiopeiae at about 21 times the Sun's light, γ Persei at about 375 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A yellow star in the arc of Perseus, between Mirfak and Cassiopeia.
card.see: Binoculars show a yellowish point in the rich Milky Way field of Perseus. Sweep from here to Mirfak and its cluster.
card.understand: Its light combines a yellow giant and a hotter white companion; GCVS lists it as an eclipsing pair.

stops.name: Algol

getThere.text: Take two field-widths left (about 13°); Algol is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: γ Persei is an eclipsing pair whose eclipses are rare; its neighbor Algol eclipses every few days.

card.glance: A bright white star in Perseus. Every few days it fades to about a third of its light for some hours, then recovers.
card.see: Algol is one of the brightest stars of Perseus. At full light it matches Almach in Andromeda; at the bottom of an eclipse it matches ε Persei. Use the app’s predicted minimum, then look twice a few hours apart. Your eyes are enough; binoculars only make the comparison stars easier to pick out.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars plus a third, more distant companion. The pair circles every 2.87 days and we see the orbit almost edge-on. When the dim orange companion slides in front of the hot blue-white star, less light reaches us. That is an eclipsing binary: the stars do not change, our view of them does.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Perseus: Born Together, Drifting Apart
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart.
journeys.story: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) to NGC 752, all in the sky around Perseus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Perseus

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Look 60° up in the north-east. Find Ruchbah by eye, then hop up and to the right to Owl Cluster (ET Cluster).

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer.

card.glance: Two bright "eyes" at one end of a small, elongated swarm, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other. A faint, slightly elongated spray of stars trails away from them; with steady binoculars it becomes the outstretched wings or arms. The bright star is φ Cassiopeiae.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,000 light-years away and only some 20 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant and one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. If it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia's distances now favor membership, but the debate is not over.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster)

getThere.text: From Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), slide down and to the left roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Look for what time has done: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) at about 14–34 million years, Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) at about 160–460 million years.

card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north. A large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the "Muscleman". Use the widest field you have; a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster sit close together on the sky, but not in space. Stock 2 is about 1,200 light-years away; the Double Cluster is over 7,000. It is also much older, a few hundred million years, so its hottest blue stars are gone. Two clusters side by side on the sky can belong to completely different parts of the galaxy.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Double Cluster (h Persei) is already in the field, just right of Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Double Cluster (h Persei) is one of the finest binocular star clusters in the northern sky (northern sky, binocular views). Quick background: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Double Cluster (h Persei).

card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view; a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points. The western one (h) is a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white ones, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so their stars share an age. Most of what you see are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun. The handful of orange points are heavier stars that have already used up the hydrogen in their cores and swelled into red supergiants. They are living out their last chapter and will explode as supernovae.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Take two field-widths down (about 13°); Alpha Persei Cluster is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alpha Persei Cluster holds a record: one of the nearest young star clusters (open clusters within about 600 light-years).
stops.transitionText: From a 14-million-year-old family to one about six times older, and thirteen times closer: Alpha Persei Cluster spreads its stars across your whole field.

card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus. Dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. This is a cluster that only binoculars or the eye can take in whole. Note how similar the bright members look.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, roughly 90 million years ago. Mirfak itself is a member, a supergiant that has already left its long, steady adult life. The others are hot blue-white stars still burning hydrogen. Because the family is so close, it spreads over several Moon widths; a farther cluster just like it would shrink into a small knot.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 752

getThere.text: Take three field-widths up and to the right, toward Andromeda; NGC 752 is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey. One thing first: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Alpha Persei Cluster is about 80–100 million years old; NGC 752 about 1.3 billion years. Same kind of object, very different age.

card.glance: A broad, even scatter of faint stars bigger than the full Moon, next to the orange pair 56 Andromedae.
card.see: Start at the wide orange double 56 Andromedae and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. There is no bright center; let your eye relax over the whole field. Notice there are no standout blue-white stars here.
card.understand: In a young cluster the brightest stars are hot blue-white heavyweights. Here they are all gone: after more than a billion years, only stars a little heavier than the Sun remain on their long, steady adult life, and a few have swollen into giants. Its members are also drifting apart, slowly mixing into the Milky Way.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Variable Hearts of Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Can you catch a star in the act of changing?
journeys.hook: Stars are not as constant as they look. Tonight you'll see why.
journeys.story: Stars are not as constant as they look. Tonight you'll see why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Garnet Star to δ Cephei, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Cepheus

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Look nearly overhead. Eyes first: locate Alderamin, then a short binocular hop brings in Garnet Star.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Garnet Star is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Stay put: VV Cephei is in the same view, just below Garnet Star.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). Before we go on: Looks deceive: a star can seem faint only because it is far away, while its true power, its luminosity, is enormous.
stops.transitionText: Two red supergiants a few degrees apart. The Garnet Star lives alone; VV Cephei has a hot partner it eclipses every 20 years, which lets astronomers measure it.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Caph

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths right, toward Cassiopeia; Caph is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Caph shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: VV Cephei at about 57,000–89,000 times the Sun's light, Caph at about 27 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The western end of Cassiopeia’s W: a bright white star, steady to the eye.
card.see: Binoculars show a clean white-yellow point at the end of the W. From here, ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-southwest.
card.understand: Caph swells and shrinks slightly about ten times a day, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: RW Cephei

getThere.text: Sweep up about two binocular fields, toward Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: RW Cephei holds a record: one of the largest known stars in the Milky Way (known stars in our galaxy).
stops.transitionText: Size check: RW Cephei is about 300 times larger than Caph.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-southwest of δ Cephei. Binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so compare it with neighboring stars and note what you see; you are watching a star that can be veiled by its own dust.
card.understand: RW Cep is a cool hypergiant, a heavy star in a swollen late stage. Images from the CHARA interferometer show a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During its recent fade, one side of the disc looked darker than the other: a dust cloud, probably formed from gas the star had just thrown off, was blocking part of its light.

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of RW Cephei, in the same view, and you have δ Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: δ Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variables (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: RW Cephei measures about 900–1,800 times the Sun's radius; δ Cephei about 28–48 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Lyra: Spot the Difference
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Sheliak to Albireo, all in the sky around Lyra. Chi Cygni is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Lyra

stops.name: Sheliak
stops.class: B8.5 Ib-II + disk · binary-interacting · eclipsing-beta-lyrae variable

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the west. This is a big move, about 6°. Find Vega with your eyes first, then raise the binoculars and hop to Sheliak.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's parallelogram; it changes brightness every few days.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat (γ Lyr) are the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, 2° apart: an ideal comparison. Some nights the two look equal; at deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly fainter. Note which is brighter tonight and check again in a few days. Binoculars also show a 7th-magnitude companion 46″ away.
card.understand: Sheliak is two stars orbiting every 13 days, so close that one has swollen into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner. The partner is wrapped in a thick disk of that stolen gas, which hides it from view. As they circle edge-on to us, each passes in front of the other, so the light rises and falls continuously.

stops.name: Double-Double
stops.class: A4 V + F1 V (ε¹); A8 Vn + F0 Vn (ε²) · main-sequence

getThere.text: Take one field-widths right (about 6°); Double-Double is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Double-Double holds a record: the best-known "double" star. One thing first: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: The Double-Double's pairs take centuries to orbit. A few degrees south, Sheliak's two stars nearly touch and circle every 13 days.

card.glance: A pair of matching white stars just north-east of Vega; any binoculars split them easily.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two equal white stars, like headlights in the distance. Sharp-eyed observers can sometimes see them as an elongated star without optics. Do not expect binoculars to split each star again; that needs a telescope at high power.
card.understand: Each of the two stars you see is itself a pair, a couple of arcseconds apart, circling each other over centuries. The two pairs share the same distance and drift through space together, so the four stars probably form one gravitationally linked family. Pairs like these matter: timing their orbits is how astronomers weigh stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Vega

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just below Double-Double, in the same view, and you have Vega.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Vega is brightest star of the Summer Triangle (the three Summer Triangle stars).
stops.transitionText: Vega is a single star. Less than two degrees away, what looks like one faint star is a family of four.

card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings; binoculars show a white jewel in a field of faint stars.
card.see: Vega is the brightest point near the zenith. In binoculars it stays a hard white spark; notice the faint stars around it that your eyes alone miss. Look 2° east-north-east for a close pair, the Double-Double, and a little farther south for the long parallelogram of Lyra.
card.understand: Vega is in the long, steady middle of its life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, exactly as the Sun does. It is about twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight makes it burn hotter: its surface is near 9,500 K, so it looks blue-white rather than yellow. Heavier stars also spend their fuel faster, so Vega's steady phase will be much shorter than the Sun's.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Chi Cygni

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two and a half binocular fields, toward Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: A challenge stop: Chi Cygni is hard in binoculars. If you can't find it, the story still works.
stops.transitionText: Size check: Chi Cygni is about 200 times larger than Vega.

card.glance: In the swan's neck between Albireo and η Cyg: a red star near maximum, or an empty patch of sky near minimum.
card.see: Sweep from Albireo toward η Cygni. Near maximum, χ Cyg is an obvious orange-red star; months later the same spot shows nothing in binoculars. Red stars play tricks on night vision: glance briefly when you compare it with white stars, because a long stare makes red look brighter.
card.understand: χ Cyg is a giant near the end of its life, so swollen that it would engulf the orbit of Mars. It pulses with a 408-day rhythm, and each cycle its outer layers cool and form molecules that soak up visible light. That is why the change is so dramatic. It is also shedding its outer layers into space.

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: From Chi Cygni, slide down roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Albireo holds a record: one of the most celebrated colour-contrast double stars.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: Chi Cygni at about 350–530 times the Sun's radius, Albireo at about 69 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Cygnus: Near, Far, Farther
journeys.drivingQuestion: Which of these is closest, and how do we know?
journeys.hook: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last.
journeys.story: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from 61 Cygni to Andromeda Galaxy, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cygnus

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Look nearly overhead. Eyes first: locate Deneb, then a short binocular hop brings in 61 Cygni.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A faint naked-eye star in a dark sky, south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find it about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart. Compare their colour with white Deneb; then remember that the faint pair is well over a hundred times closer.
card.understand: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in a year. 61 Cygni is about 11 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours. The two stars are orange dwarfs, smaller and cooler than the Sun, orbiting each other. They look faint not because they are far but because they give out little light; Deneb looks bright despite being enormously farther.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M39

getThere.text: Move about 11° (one and a half fields) up (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: M39 lies about 80 times farther than 61 Cygni.

card.glance: A large, bright, loose triangle of a few dozen stars north-east of Deneb, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From Deneb, sweep about 9 degrees east-north-east. You will meet a loose triangle of stars about the size of the full Moon, standing out from the Milky Way. Use your lowest magnification, count the members, and notice that the brightest ones are all white or blue-white.
card.understand: Gaia shows these stars sharing one distance and one motion: a true family about 1,000 light-years away. A detailed 2024 study of their spectra fits an age of roughly 400 million years, though another method gives a third of that. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already burnt out; the brightest survivors are white stars of about three solar masses.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the right, toward Cepheus; VV Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). A short reminder before you look: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: M39 at about 965 light-years, VV Cephei at about 3,000–3,800 light-years.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae
stops.class: F8pIa-0 to M3 (variable) · yellow-hypergiant · yellow-hypergiant variable

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) right, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae holds a record: one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: Next rung: ρ Cassiopeiae is about 9,170 light-years away, about 3 times farther than VV Cephei.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia. It looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most powerful stars you can see by eye.
card.see: Start at Caph, the end of the W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-southwest to a faint yellowish star: ρ Cassiopeiae. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of the cluster NGC 7789 between them. Compare ρ with nearby stars; it slowly changes.
card.understand: ρ Cas gives off more than half a million times the Sun’s light. Most bright-looking stars are nearby; this one is visible from enormous distance because of sheer power. It is in a short, unstable stage that only the heaviest stars reach: swollen, restless and losing mass in bursts. In 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) right, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: Andromeda Galaxy holds a record: the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: From about 9,170 light-years to about 2,480,000 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 300 times farther.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 50% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 25° from it; it sets at 01:16.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Polaris to Garnet Star, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Cepheus

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Find Polaris by eye, about 50° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Polaris quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: From Polaris, slide up and to the left roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Errai holds a record: one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003 (history of astronomy). Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Errai is about 200 times less luminous than Polaris, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of Cepheus’s house-shaped outline, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the “house” of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris. In binoculars it is a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen; compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the house’s other corner.
card.understand: Errai is a star a little heavier than the Sun that has finished its long hydrogen-burning life and is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 astronomers noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its velocity, a hint of a planet. Doubts about the star’s own variations left the claim in limbo until 2003, when a planet with a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed.

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one and a half binocular fields (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Alfirk is the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Alfirk is about 2,000 times more luminous than Errai.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Take one field-widths left (about 7°); VV Cephei is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky).
stops.transitionText: Size check: VV Cephei is about 100 times larger than Alfirk.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of VV Cephei, in the same view, and you have Garnet Star.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Garnet Star is one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Two red supergiants a few degrees apart. The Garnet Star lives alone; VV Cephei has a hot partner it eclipses every 20 years, which lets astronomers measure it.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Birth, Life and Death above Taurus
journeys.drivingQuestion: What happens to a star between its birth and its death?
journeys.hook: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop.
journeys.story: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Christmas Tree Cluster to Aldebaran, all in the sky around Taurus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Taurus

stops.name: Christmas Tree Cluster

getThere.text: Look 35° up in the south-east. Eyes first: locate Betelgeuse, then a short binocular hop brings in Christmas Tree Cluster.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Christmas Tree Cluster is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

card.glance: A bright star at the base of a small triangle of fainter stars, like an upside-down Christmas tree.
card.see: Go a little under halfway from Betelgeuse to Procyon, then about three and a half degrees north. The bright star S Monocerotis marks the trunk; a narrow triangle of fainter stars points south to the tree’s tip. With north up, the tree hangs upside-down. The nebula is a photo target.
card.understand: These stars formed a few million years ago, and their birth cloud is still around them. S Monocerotis, the bright trunk star, is far hotter and heavier than the Sun, and its light eats into the surrounding gas. A dark finger of dust, the Cone Nebula, sits at the tree’s tip where gas is still collapsing into stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M35

getThere.text: From Christmas Tree Cluster, slide up roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Gemini.

stops.whyHere: M35 shows the next idea you need. Before we go on: A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: M35 is what a family like Christmas Tree Cluster grows into: the same story, a later chapter.

card.glance: A rich, glittering patch near Gemini’s feet, with many stars resolved; visible to the eye on a dark night.
card.see: Find the stars marking Gemini’s feet, η and μ Geminorum, and move about two degrees north-west. M35 is a round, grainy glow sprinkled with resolved stars, about the size of the full Moon. Then look just to its south-west for a much smaller, fainter smudge: NGC 2158.
card.understand: M35 is about as old as the Pleiades, but much farther away, so only its brightest stars come through and the rest merge into a glow. The smudge beside it is a completely different cluster, far behind M35.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Kabdhilinan

getThere.text: Move about 18° (two and a half fields) up, toward Auriga.

stops.whyHere: A surprise: Kabdhilinan breaks the pattern so far.
stops.transitionText: Fast-forward. Kabdhilinan shows the stage that comes after M35.

card.glance: The orange star at Auriga’s south-western corner.
card.see: Look at the pentagon of Auriga: its south-western corner is ι Aurigae, distinctly orange next to yellowish Capella.
card.understand: ι Aurigae is a luminous orange giant about 450 light-years away. Its surface is near 4,200 K, cooler than Capella’s stars, so it looks more orange.

stops.name: θ Tauri

getThere.text: From Kabdhilinan, slide down and to the right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Taurus.

stops.whyHere: θ Tauri holds a record: θ² is the brightest true member of the Hyades (Hyades members (Aldebaran is a foreground star)).
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Kabdhilinan at about 3,300–4,200 times the Sun's light, θ Tauri at about 70 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair in the Hyades V: one white star, one yellow-orange.
card.see: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair. Binoculars split it at a glance: almost 6 arcminutes. Compare the colors: θ² is white, θ¹ yellow-orange. Defocusing slightly makes the contrast stronger.
card.understand: Both stars were born in the Hyades about 625 million years ago, so they started out together. θ¹ has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a yellow-orange giant. θ² is still hot and white, near the end of its long, steady adult life. A small difference in their starting mass is enough to put them in different chapters.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Aldebaran

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just above θ Tauri, in the same view, and you have Aldebaran.

stops.whyHere: Aldebaran answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: θ Tauri at about 4.3–5.4 times the Sun's radius, Aldebaran at about 45 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: A bright orange star at one tip of the V-shaped Hyades cluster.
card.see: Frame the Hyades V so that Aldebaran sits at one tip. Its warm orange stands out against the white cluster stars, though a few of them have a faint yellow-orange tint too. Then compare it with Betelgeuse to the south-east: which looks redder to you?
card.understand: Aldebaran is an orange giant, a star that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width. It is about 67 light-years away, less than half the distance of the Hyades behind it. The two just line up from where we stand: stars that look side by side can be very far apart.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Star Families of Perseus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart.
journeys.story: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Double Cluster (h Persei) to θ Tauri, all in the sky around Perseus. NGC 1342 is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Perseus

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Look nearly overhead. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Ruchbah, aim at it, then follow the hop to Double Cluster (h Persei).

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Double Cluster (h Persei) quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Quick background: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view; a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia's W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points. The western one (h) is a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white ones, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so their stars share an age. Most of what you see are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun. The handful of orange points are heavier stars that have already used up the hydrogen in their cores and swelled into red supergiants. They are living out their last chapter and will explode as supernovae.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) up (about 13°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Alpha Persei Cluster is one of the nearest young star clusters (open clusters within about 600 light-years).
stops.transitionText: From a 14-million-year-old family to one about six times older, and thirteen times closer: Alpha Persei Cluster spreads its stars across your whole field.

card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus. Dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. This is a cluster that only binoculars or the eye can take in whole. Note how similar the bright members look.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, roughly 90 million years ago. Mirfak itself is a member, a supergiant that has already left its long, steady adult life. The others are hot blue-white stars still burning hydrogen. Because the family is so close, it spreads over several Moon widths; a farther cluster just like it would shrink into a small knot.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 1342

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one and a half binocular fields (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt. Before we go on: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: NGC 1342.

card.glance: A small, loose cluster of faint stars in southern Perseus, between Algol and the Pleiades.
card.see: From Algol, move about six degrees south-east toward the Pleiades. Look for a handful of stars standing out from the field in a small patch.
card.understand: It is about 160 million years old; at 2,000 light-years, its stars look faint and few compared with the nearby Pleiades.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alcyone

getThere.text: Take two field-widths down, toward Taurus; Alcyone is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alcyone holds a record: brightest star of the Pleiades (Pleiades members).
stops.transitionText: Same life story, further along. Look for what has changed between NGC 1342 and Alcyone.

card.glance: The brightest of the Pleiades, where the little dipper’s bowl meets its handle.
card.see: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle of the group. Then notice how every bright member shares its blue-white color: a family resemblance. Count how many fainter siblings binoculars add to the naked-eye six or seven.
card.understand: Alcyone is a hot B-type star of about 13,000 K, roughly a thousand times as luminous as the Sun. Like its siblings, it formed about 125 million years ago from a single cloud. The very heaviest members have already burned out; Alcyone is among the heaviest still shining, and that is exactly what dates the family.

stops.name: θ Tauri

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) down and to the left (about 13°).

stops.whyHere: θ Tauri holds a record: θ² is the brightest true member of the Hyades (Hyades members (Aldebaran is a foreground star)).
stops.transitionText: From the Pleiades, about 125 million years old, to the Hyades, about 625 million years: in the older family, the brightest stars have turned into giants.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair in the Hyades V: one white star, one yellow-orange.
card.see: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair. Binoculars split it at a glance: almost 6 arcminutes. Compare the colors: θ² is white, θ¹ yellow-orange. Defocusing slightly makes the contrast stronger.
card.understand: Both stars were born in the Hyades about 625 million years ago, so they started out together. θ¹ has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a yellow-orange giant. θ² is still hot and white, near the end of its long, steady adult life. A small difference in their starting mass is enough to put them in different chapters.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Measuring the Depths of Perseus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How do astronomers measure distances no one can travel?
journeys.hook: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last.
journeys.story: Climb a ladder of distances, each rung at least twice as far as the last. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Algol to Andromeda Galaxy, all in the sky around Perseus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Perseus

stops.name: Algol

getThere.text: Find Algol by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Algol quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A bright white star in Perseus. Every few days it fades to about a third of its light for some hours, then recovers.
card.see: Algol is one of the brightest stars of Perseus. At full light it matches Almach in Andromeda; at the bottom of an eclipse it matches ε Persei. Use the app’s predicted minimum, then look twice a few hours apart. Your eyes are enough; binoculars only make the comparison stars easier to pick out.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars plus a third, more distant companion. The pair circles every 2.87 days and we see the orbit almost edge-on. When the dim orange companion slides in front of the hot blue-white star, less light reaches us. That is an eclipsing binary: the stars do not change, our view of them does.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: From Algol, slide up roughly one fields of view (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Alpha Persei Cluster holds a record: one of the nearest young star clusters (open clusters within about 600 light-years).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Alpha Persei Cluster lies about 6 times farther than Algol.

card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus. Dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains, too big for most telescopes to frame. This is a cluster that only binoculars or the eye can take in whole. Note how similar the bright members look.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, roughly 90 million years ago. Mirfak itself is a member, a supergiant that has already left its long, steady adult life. The others are hot blue-white stars still burning hydrogen. Because the family is so close, it spreads over several Moon widths; a farther cluster just like it would shrink into a small knot.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep right about two binocular fields, toward Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) is about 1,210 light-years away, about 2 times farther than Alpha Persei Cluster.

card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north. A large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the "Muscleman". Use the widest field you have; a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Stock 2 and the Double Cluster sit close together on the sky, but not in space. Stock 2 is about 1,200 light-years away; the Double Cluster is over 7,000. It is also much older, a few hundred million years, so its hottest blue stars are gone. Two clusters side by side on the sky can belong to completely different parts of the galaxy.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae
stops.class: F8pIa-0 to M3 (variable) · yellow-hypergiant · yellow-hypergiant variable

getThere.text: Sweep down about two and a half binocular fields (about 18°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: ρ Cassiopeiae is one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: From about 1,210 light-years to about 9,170 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 8 times farther.
