card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia. It looks ordinary, yet it is one of the most powerful stars you can see by eye.
card.see: Start at Caph, the end of the W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-southwest to a faint yellowish star: ρ Cassiopeiae. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of the cluster NGC 7789 between them. Compare ρ with nearby stars; it slowly changes.
card.understand: ρ Cas gives off more than half a million times the Sun’s light. Most bright-looking stars are nearby; this one is visible from enormous distance because of sheer power. It is in a short, unstable stage that only the heaviest stars reach: swollen, restless and losing mass in bursts. In 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Move about 18° (two and a half fields) left, toward Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: Andromeda Galaxy holds a record: the farthest object most people can see with the unaided eye (naked-eye objects from a dark site; M33 is slightly farther but needs exceptional skies).
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: ρ Cassiopeiae at about 9,170 light-years, Andromeda Galaxy at about 2,480,000 light-years.

card.glance: An elongated grey glow with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, climb two faint stars north and the glow appears. The bright oval core is obvious; with averted vision the haze stretches across most of a 7° field. Look for a fuzzy "star" just south of the core: that is M32. Do not expect spiral arms or color.
card.understand: Every bit of that glow is starlight: hundreds of billions of suns, too far away to see one by one. Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our own Milky Way, and we see it tilted almost edge-on. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a pulsing star in it whose true brightness he knew, and its faintness proved the "nebula" lay far outside our galaxy. The universe suddenly became much bigger.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 05:30.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Time Machine over Draco
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar.
journeys.story: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Psi Draconis to Zeta Herculis, all in the sky around Draco.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Draco

stops.name: Psi Draconis

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the north-east. Find Kochab by eye, then hop down and to the right to Psi Draconis.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Psi Draconis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

card.glance: A 30″ pair of yellow-white stars high in the north, circumpolar from mid-northern latitudes.
card.see: At 10× the pair splits cleanly: a brighter primary with a fainter companion just north of it.
card.understand: Two Sun-like stars, slightly warmer than the Sun, about 74 light-years away.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: 39 Draconis

getThere.text: From Psi Draconis, slide down and to the right roughly two fields of view (about 14°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: From about 74 light-years to about 184 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 2 times farther.

card.glance: A 5th-magnitude white star with an 8th-magnitude companion 89″ away; binoculars show the wide pair.
card.see: Look for the faint companion about 1½′ to the north-north-east of the white primary.
card.understand: The primary also has a close companion 3.7″ away, visible only in a telescope: three stars in all.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Rastaban

getThere.text: From 39 Draconis, slide up and to the right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: Rastaban adds the next piece of the story. A short reminder before you look: Stars come in wildly different sizes, and a star that is cool but still very bright has to be enormous.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: 39 Draconis at about 184 light-years, Rastaban at about 380 light-years.

card.glance: The fainter of the two bright stars in the dragon's head, 4° west of orange Eltanin; it looks yellow.
card.see: Compare Rastaban with Eltanin in one sweep: yellow versus orange.
card.understand: Rastaban is a bright giant, a little cooler than the Sun yet about 40 times wider, which is why it shines so strongly from 380 light-years away.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Take three field-widths right, toward Hercules; Great Hercules Globular Cluster is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Great Hercules Globular Cluster is the brightest globular cluster in the far-northern sky (globular clusters north of declination +30°).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Great Hercules Globular Cluster is about 24,200 light-years away, about 60 times farther than Rastaban.

card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on one side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. On the line between η and ζ Herculis, about a third of the way from η, sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star. It brightens toward the center. Binoculars won’t split it into stars; that takes a telescope. Compare it with a nearby star of similar brightness: one is a point, the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of stars that all formed together in the young Milky Way. M13 holds roughly half a million Suns’ worth of stars in a ball about 120 light-years wide. Its stars are about 12 billion years old, more than twice the Sun’s age, and they contain far less iron and other heavy elements than the Sun because they formed before many generations of stars had enriched the gas. Globulars swarm around the galaxy in a vast halo, not in the flat disk.

image.credit: Giuseppe Donatiello

stops.name: Zeta Herculis

getThere.text: Stay put: Zeta Herculis is in the same view, just right of Great Hercules Globular Cluster.

stops.whyHere: We finish by seeing the start with new eyes.
stops.transitionText: A perspective trick: about 24,200 light-years to Great Hercules Globular Cluster, about 35 light-years to Zeta Herculis.

card.glance: The south-western corner of the Keystone of Hercules, a pale yellow star 35 light-years away.
card.see: ζ and η Herculis frame the west side of the Keystone; the globular cluster M13 lies about a third of the way from η to ζ. ζ Her itself is a simple yellowish point.
card.understand: It is a subgiant: its core hydrogen is running out and it has grown to almost three times the Sun's width. A close companion orbits it, too tight for binoculars.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Ursa Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do these neighbors look so different?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Cor Caroli to Mizar & Alcor, all in the sky around Ursa Major.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Ursa Major

stops.name: Cor Caroli

getThere.text: Find Cor Caroli by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Cor Caroli quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A white star alone under the Big Dipper’s handle; braced 10x binoculars may show a faint partner almost touching it.
card.see: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Dipper’s handle. Hold 10x binoculars very steady, or use a tripod, and look for a much fainter companion right beside it. In 7x binoculars it usually stays merged. Its white color makes a good contrast with red La Superba about seven degrees to the north.
card.understand: The brighter star is hot and white, with a strong, lopsided magnetic field. That field holds elements such as silicon and europium in large patches on its surface. As the star turns every five and a half days, the patches swing in and out of view and its light and spectrum change slightly. Astronomers named this whole class of variable star after it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Groombridge 1830

getThere.text: Sweep right about two binocular fields, toward Ursa Major.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Groombridge 1830 is one of the fastest-moving stars across the sky that binoculars can show (stars brighter than about 9th magnitude). A short reminder before you look: Globular clusters are ancient balls of stars that swarm around our galaxy in a wide halo, well away from its flat disk.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Cor Caroli at about 117 times the Sun's light, Groombridge 1830 at about 0.22 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A faint yellowish star in a quiet corner of Ursa Major, findable in binoculars with a chart.
card.see: Use a chart: it lies about 16 degrees due south of Phecda, the bowl star nearest the handle. In binoculars it is a faint yellowish point with no visible hint of its speed. Note its position against nearby stars; in a lifetime of careful sketches it would visibly creep.
card.understand: Most stars near the Sun circle the Galaxy with us in its flat disk, like cars in the same lanes. Groombridge 1830 follows a steep, looping orbit through the halo, the old, thin swarm of stars around the disk, so it cuts through our lane at high speed. It contains far less iron than the Sun, a sign it formed early, before generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy’s gas.

stops.name: La Superba

getThere.text: From Groombridge 1830, slide up roughly two fields of view, toward Canes Venatici.

stops.whyHere: La Superba holds a record: one of the very few carbon stars visible to the unaided eye (dark-sky naked-eye stars).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet La Superba is about 800 times larger than Groombridge 1830.

card.glance: A modest star that turns out to be one of the deepest orange-red points in the sky, between Cor Caroli and the Dipper’s bowl.
card.see: From Cor Caroli, head about a third of the way toward Megrez, the star joining the Dipper’s handle to its bowl. Faint to the eye, it is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember. Keep looking: red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare. Then swing to white Cor Caroli for contrast.
card.understand: Late in life, a giant like this burns helium in thin shells around its core, and churning currents carry freshly made carbon up to the surface. Carbon-rich molecules and soot block blue light, so what escapes is deep red. The star is cool, about 2,700 degrees, and it is shedding gas and dust that have piled up into a shell about three light-years across.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alkaid

getThere.text: From La Superba, slide up and to the left roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Ursa Major.

stops.whyHere: Alkaid holds a record: the hottest of the seven Big Dipper stars (Big Dipper asterism).
stops.transitionText: La Superba measures about 370–570 times the Sun's radius; Alkaid about 2.9 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: The bright blue-white star at the very end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Alkaid ends the handle. In binoculars it looks crisply blue-white, a clear contrast with yellow-orange Dubhe at the other end of the Dipper. About three and a half degrees to the southwest, under dark skies, the Whirlpool Galaxy is a faint smudge for patient eyes.
card.understand: Alkaid’s surface is about 17,900 degrees, three times hotter than the Sun’s, which is why it looks blue-white. Hot stars like this are heavy and burn through their fuel quickly, so Alkaid is young as stars go. It lies about 100 light-years away and travels in a different direction from the five family stars in the middle of the Dipper.

stops.name: Mizar & Alcor

getThere.text: Move about 7° (one fields) up and to the left (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Mizar & Alcor is the first star found to be double from its spectrum alone (Mizar A) (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: Alkaid ends the Dipper’s handle, but unlike Mizar next door it is not family: hotter, younger and heading its own way.

card.glance: Bright Mizar and fainter Alcor at the bend of the Big Dipper’s handle: a pair you can split by eye, wide apart in binoculars.
card.see: Look at the middle star of the Dipper’s handle; keen eyes see little Alcor beside it. Binoculars spread them less than half a Moon-width apart, with a fainter star nearby making a small triangle. Mizar’s own close companion needs a telescope at moderate power, so don’t expect to split it here.
card.understand: Mizar and Alcor are not a chance alignment. Both lie roughly 80–90 light-years away and drift together, and each is itself multiple: Mizar is two pairs of stars, and Alcor has a small red-dwarf companion found in 2009. That likely makes six stars in one system. They also share their motion with Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth, all born together about 400 million years ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Seeing Double in Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Are double stars real partners or chance alignments?
journeys.hook: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count.
journeys.story: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Psi Draconis to VV Cephei, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Cepheus

stops.name: Psi Draconis

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the north-east. Find Kochab by eye, then hop down and to the right to Psi Draconis.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Psi Draconis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Quick background: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

card.glance: A 30″ pair of yellow-white stars high in the north, circumpolar from mid-northern latitudes.
card.see: At 10× the pair splits cleanly: a brighter primary with a fainter companion just north of it.
card.understand: Two Sun-like stars, slightly warmer than the Sun, about 74 light-years away.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Sweep left about three binocular fields, toward Ursa Minor.

stops.whyHere: Polaris holds a record: the nearest Cepheid variable, the kind of pulsating star used as a cosmic yardstick (all known classical Cepheids). One thing first: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Psi Draconis at about 6 times the Sun's light, Polaris at about 2,210 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: Take two field-widths down and to the right, toward Cepheus; Errai is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Errai is one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003 (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Errai is about 200 times less luminous than Polaris.

card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of Cepheus’s house-shaped outline, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the “house” of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris. In binoculars it is a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen; compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the house’s other corner.
card.understand: Errai is a star a little heavier than the Sun that has finished its long hydrogen-burning life and is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 astronomers noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its velocity, a hint of a planet. Doubts about the star’s own variations left the claim in limbo until 2003, when a planet with a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed.

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: From Errai, slide right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Alfirk holds a record: the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Errai gives off about 12 times the Sun's light, Alfirk about 17,000–22,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: From Alfirk, slide down roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: VV Cephei holds a record: one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky).
stops.transitionText: Alfirk measures about 6.3 times the Sun's radius; VV Cephei about 779 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Seeing Double in Boötes
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is that one star, or two, or six?
journeys.hook: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Nu Draconis to Alphecca, all in the sky around Boötes.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Boötes

stops.name: Nu Draconis

getThere.text: Look 50° up in the north-east. This is a big move, about 3°. Find Rastaban with your eyes first, then raise the binoculars and hop to Nu Draconis.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Nu Draconis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

card.glance: Two perfectly matched white stars 62″ apart in the dragon's head: one of the finest binocular doubles.
card.see: Find the dragon's head, then the faintest of its four stars: binoculars split it into two equal white points, like a pair of eyes.
card.understand: The twins are a classic catalogued pair about 100 light-years away, both white stars a little hotter than the Sun.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: 16 & 17 Draconis
stops.class: B9.5 V + B9 V + A1 Vnn · main-sequence

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths up and to the right (about 9°); 16 & 17 Draconis is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: 16 & 17 Draconis adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: 16 & 17 Draconis shows the same idea as Nu Draconis. Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.

card.glance: A wide, nearly equal pair of white 5th-magnitude stars 90″ apart in Draco; easy in any binoculars.
card.see: Two matched white points sit 1½′ apart. A telescope would show one of them is itself a 3″ pair.
card.understand: Catalogues list a third star 3″ from one of the pair; whether all three are bound together is not settled.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: ν¹ & ν² Boötis

getThere.text: From 16 & 17 Draconis, slide up and to the right roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Boötes.

stops.whyHere: ν¹ & ν² Boötis shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet ν¹ & ν² Boötis is about 20 times larger than 16 & 17 Draconis.

card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes: one orange, one white.
card.see: In binoculars the two sit side by side, orange ν¹ and white ν², nearly equal in brightness. Defocus slightly to make the color contrast pop.
card.understand: ν¹ is an orange giant nearly 1,000 light-years away; ν² is a white star about 440 light-years away. They have nothing to do with each other and line up only from where we stand. The orange one must give out far more light to look as bright from twice as far.

stops.name: Alkalurops

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just right of ν¹ & ν² Boötis, in the same view, and you have Alkalurops.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: ν¹ & ν² Boötis is a real triple whose stars travel together. A few degrees north, the two stars of ν Boötis look like a matched pair, but one lies more than twice as far as the other.

card.glance: A white star in Boötes with a faint companion binoculars can split; the companion is itself double.
card.see: In 10x binoculars a much fainter star sits just south of μ Boo, about a sixteenth of a Moon-width away. Hold steady to separate it from the glare. Its own two stars need a telescope.
card.understand: The bright star is a white star about twice the Sun’s mass. The companion is a pair of Sun-like stars orbiting each other closely, and all three share the same motion through space.

stops.name: Alphecca
stops.class: A1 IV + G5 V · main-sequence · eclipsing-algol variable

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about one and a half binocular fields, toward Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: Alphecca answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Alphecca.

card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star of the arc; binoculars fit the whole crown in one or two fields. Use it as the reference point for the two strange variables nearby.
card.understand: Alphecca is really two stars, a white one and a Sun-like one, that eclipse each other every 17 days, but the dip is far too small to notice by eye.

conditions.message: The Moon is 47% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 24° from it; it sets at 15:22.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Cepheus: The Restless Stars
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do some stars brighten and fade?
journeys.hook: Catch stars that wink, breathe and hide. You'll judge their brightness yourself.
journeys.story: Catch stars that wink, breathe and hide. You'll judge their brightness yourself. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from P Cygni to δ Cephei, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cepheus

stops.name: P Cygni

getThere.text: Look 75° up in the south-west. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Sadr, aim at it, then follow the hop to P Cygni.

stops.whyHere: We start here because P Cygni is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A modest 5th-magnitude star about 2° south-west of Sadr, at the heart of the Northern Cross.
card.see: From Sadr, slide about 2½° south-west, toward Albireo. P Cygni is a plain white point against the Milky Way, easy in binoculars. Nothing about the view hints at its power; the story is in the distance.
card.understand: P Cygni is a luminous blue variable, one of the heaviest kinds of star. It is so bright that the push of its own light almost overcomes gravity, so it sheds mass in a strong wind and sometimes in eruptions. Stars like this are only a short step from the end of their lives.

stops.name: 31 Cygni
stops.class: K4 Ib + B4 IV-V · binary-interacting · eclipsing-long-period variable

getThere.text: From P Cygni, slide up and to the right roughly one fields of view (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. Quick background: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: 31 Cygni is the same type of object as P Cygni. Notice what makes it different.

card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue companion beside it: a binocular colour trio with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter 7th-magnitude star closer in. The colours are easier than Albireo's because the gaps are wider.
card.understand: A hot blue star orbits the orange supergiant and slips behind it every 10.4 years, a slow eclipse too shallow to notice by eye.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the right, toward Cepheus; Garnet Star is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Garnet Star holds a record: one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: Garnet Star, a cousin of 31 Cygni.

card.glance: A deep orange-red point in Cepheus, on the edge of the Milky Way. One of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: It sits about halfway between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, at the base of Cepheus’s “house”. In binoculars the color leaps out against white neighbors. Nudge the focus slightly off sharp to spread the light into a small disc; the orange deepens. Its brightness drifts over months, so compare it with nearby stars.
card.understand: This is a red supergiant: a heavy star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface is only about 3,700 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows like a dull stove ring rather than white-hot metal. Yet it pours out light, so it must be gigantic. Dust between us and the star makes it look redder still.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: RW Cephei

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) right (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: RW Cephei is one of the largest known stars in the Milky Way (known stars in our galaxy).
stops.transitionText: Garnet Star and RW Cephei look like neighbors, but RW Cephei is about 8 times farther than Garnet Star.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-southwest of δ Cephei. Binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so compare it with neighboring stars and note what you see; you are watching a star that can be veiled by its own dust.
card.understand: RW Cep is a cool hypergiant, a heavy star in a swollen late stage. Images from the CHARA interferometer show a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During its recent fade, one side of the disc looked darker than the other: a dust cloud, probably formed from gas the star had just thrown off, was blocking part of its light.

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. δ Cephei is already in the field, below and to the left of RW Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: δ Cephei is the prototype of the Cepheid variables (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: RW Cephei measures about 900–1,800 times the Sun's radius; δ Cephei about 28–48 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: A Thermometer in Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Albireo to 10 Lacertae, all in the sky around Cygnus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Cygnus

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: Look 60° up in the south-west. Eyes first: locate Vega, then a short binocular hop brings in Albireo.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. A short reminder before you look: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Al Fawaris

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two and a half binocular fields (about 17°).

stops.whyHere: Al Fawaris shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Al Fawaris shows the same idea as Albireo. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: The white star at the end of the Northern Cross's western arm, 8° north-west of Sadr.
card.see: A bright white point; from here, the 16 Cygni pair lies about 5° to the north.
card.understand: A hot white star about 165 light-years away, a little past the start of its long steady phase.

stops.name: Aljanah

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) left (about 16°).

stops.whyHere: Aljanah adds the next piece of the story. Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Aljanah shows the same idea as Al Fawaris. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: The orange star at the tip of the swan's eastern wing, about 8° south-east of Sadr; the Veil Nebula lies just beyond.
card.see: A clear orange-yellow point. From here the faint arcs of the Veil lie about 3° to the south-east; you need dark skies and ideally a nebula filter.
card.understand: ε Cyg is a giant about 11 times wider than the Sun, 73 light-years away.

stops.name: W Cygni

getThere.text: Sweep up about two binocular fields (about 15°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: W Cygni shows the same idea as Aljanah. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: A reddish 5th–7th-magnitude star less than half a degree south-east of ρ Cygni.
card.see: Centre ρ Cygni; W Cyg is the reddish star just to its south-east. Compare it with ρ Cyg each week over a season.
card.understand: A cool red giant late in life, swelling and shrinking roughly every 130 days and shedding gas as it does.

stops.name: 10 Lacertae

getThere.text: Sweep left about two binocular fields, toward Lacerta.

stops.whyHere: 10 Lacertae holds a record: a defining reference star for its class (O9 V) (spectral classification).
stops.transitionText: Opposite ends of the thermometer, one short swing apart: W Cygni near 3,400 K, 10 Lacertae near 34,600 K.

card.glance: A plain-looking blue-white star in little Lacerta, and one of the hottest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Lacerta’s faint zigzag lies between Cygnus and Andromeda; 10 Lacertae is at its southern end. In binoculars it is an unremarkable white point with, at best, a hint of blue. The drama here is in the numbers, not the view.
card.understand: 10 Lac has about 22 times the Sun’s mass and a surface near 35,000 K, six times hotter than the Sun’s. It pours out about 70,000 times the Sun’s light. Heavy stars burn their fuel ferociously, so although this one is only a few million years old, its whole life will last millions of years, not billions.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Splitting Stars over Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How many stars can hide in one point of light?
journeys.hook: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count.
journeys.story: One point of light can hide a whole family. Let's count. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from δ Cephei to Polaris, all in the sky around Cepheus.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cepheus

stops.name: δ Cephei

getThere.text: Look nearly overhead. Eyes first: locate Alderamin, then a short binocular hop brings in δ Cephei.

stops.whyHere: We start here because δ Cephei is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Quick background: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a fainter blue-white companion. Over five days it brightens and fades with clockwork regularity.
card.see: Binoculars show a fainter blue-white companion just beside it; steady 10× binoculars help. To catch the change, compare it on several nights with ζ Cephei, its match at brightest, and ε Cephei, its match at faintest. It brightens quickly and fades slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant whose outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days, and its light follows. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that stars like this with longer periods are truly more powerful. Time the beat and you know the star’s real output; compare that with how bright it looks and you have its distance. Stars you can use this way are called standard candles.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: VV Cephei

getThere.text: Sweep left about one binocular field (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: VV Cephei is one of the largest stars within binocular reach (stars brighter than 6th magnitude, northern sky). One thing first: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: VV Cephei is about 40 times more luminous than δ Cephei, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus. Nothing in the view betrays that it is two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees from the Garnet Star; sweep between the two and compare. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery. Its slow changes are too small to judge reliably by eye, so enjoy it for what it hides rather than what it shows.
card.understand: The visible star is a red supergiant hundreds of times wider than the Sun. A hot blue star circles it every 20.3 years. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so once per orbit the giant passes in front of its partner and blocks its light for months. Timing how long that takes measures the giant’s size, a rare direct check on how big such stars are.

stops.name: Alfirk

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one binocular field (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Alfirk holds a record: the star that gives its name to the β Cephei class of pulsating hot stars (class prototype).
stops.transitionText: Size check: Alfirk is about 100 times smaller than VV Cephei.

card.glance: A blue-white star in Cepheus that pulses every four and a half hours, too gently for your eyes.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point; its faint companion, 13.5 arcseconds away, is a hard test even in steady 10× binoculars.
card.understand: β Cep is a hot, heavy star whose surface rings like a bell every 4.57 hours, changing its light by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: Move about 11° (one and a half fields) down and to the right (about 11°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Errai is one of the first planet signals ever reported (1988), confirmed in 2003 (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Alfirk gives off about 17,000–22,000 times the Sun's light, Errai about 12 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of Cepheus’s house-shaped outline, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the “house” of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris. In binoculars it is a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen; compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the house’s other corner.
card.understand: Errai is a star a little heavier than the Sun that has finished its long hydrogen-burning life and is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 astronomers noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its velocity, a hint of a planet. Doubts about the star’s own variations left the claim in limbo until 2003, when a planet with a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed.

stops.name: Polaris

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down and to the left, toward Ursa Minor; Polaris is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Polaris is the nearest Cepheid variable, the kind of pulsating star used as a cosmic yardstick (all known classical Cepheids).
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Errai at about 12 times the Sun's light, Polaris at about 2,210 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole; binoculars show it on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Extend the line through the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl to reach Polaris. In binoculars it sits on a little loop of fainter stars nicknamed the Engagement Ring, with Polaris as the diamond. Its color is a soft yellow-white. Its brightness changes are far too small to notice by eye.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant about five times the Sun’s mass that swells and shrinks every four days. Stars like it, called Cepheids, pulse at a rate tied to how much light they really give out, so timing the beat tells astronomers their true power and therefore their distance. Polaris also has a close partner whose orbit lets astronomers weigh it directly, a rare check on a Cepheid.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Lyra
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do these neighbors look so different?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Sheliak to Albireo, all in the sky around Lyra. Chi Cygni is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Lyra

stops.name: Sheliak
stops.class: B8.5 Ib-II + disk · binary-interacting · eclipsing-beta-lyrae variable

getThere.text: Look 60° up in the west. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Vega, aim at it, then follow the hop to Sheliak.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: The western of the two stars at the bottom of Lyra's parallelogram; it changes brightness every few days.
card.see: Sheliak and Sulafat (γ Lyr) are the two stars at the bottom of Lyra, 2° apart: an ideal comparison. Some nights the two look equal; at deepest eclipse Sheliak is clearly fainter. Note which is brighter tonight and check again in a few days. Binoculars also show a 7th-magnitude companion 46″ away.
card.understand: Sheliak is two stars orbiting every 13 days, so close that one has swollen into a teardrop and spills gas onto its partner. The partner is wrapped in a thick disk of that stolen gas, which hides it from view. As they circle edge-on to us, each passes in front of the other, so the light rises and falls continuously.

stops.name: Double-Double
stops.class: A4 V + F1 V (ε¹); A8 Vn + F0 Vn (ε²) · main-sequence

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one binocular field (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Double-Double is the best-known "double" star. One thing first: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: The Double-Double's pairs take centuries to orbit. A few degrees south, Sheliak's two stars nearly touch and circle every 13 days.

card.glance: A pair of matching white stars just north-east of Vega; any binoculars split them easily.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two equal white stars, like headlights in the distance. Sharp-eyed observers can sometimes see them as an elongated star without optics. Do not expect binoculars to split each star again; that needs a telescope at high power.
card.understand: Each of the two stars you see is itself a pair, a couple of arcseconds apart, circling each other over centuries. The two pairs share the same distance and drift through space together, so the four stars probably form one gravitationally linked family. Pairs like these matter: timing their orbits is how astronomers weigh stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Vega

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just below Double-Double, in the same view, and you have Vega.

stops.whyHere: Vega holds a record: brightest star of the Summer Triangle (the three Summer Triangle stars).
stops.transitionText: Vega is a single star. Less than two degrees away, what looks like one faint star is a family of four.

card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings; binoculars show a white jewel in a field of faint stars.
card.see: Vega is the brightest point near the zenith. In binoculars it stays a hard white spark; notice the faint stars around it that your eyes alone miss. Look 2° east-north-east for a close pair, the Double-Double, and a little farther south for the long parallelogram of Lyra.
card.understand: Vega is in the long, steady middle of its life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, exactly as the Sun does. It is about twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight makes it burn hotter: its surface is near 9,500 K, so it looks blue-white rather than yellow. Heavier stars also spend their fuel faster, so Vega's steady phase will be much shorter than the Sun's.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Chi Cygni

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the left, toward Cygnus; Chi Cygni is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: A challenge stop: Chi Cygni is hard in binoculars. If you can't find it, the story still works.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: Vega at about 2.7 times the Sun's radius, Chi Cygni at about 350–530 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: In the swan's neck between Albireo and η Cyg: a red star near maximum, or an empty patch of sky near minimum.
card.see: Sweep from Albireo toward η Cygni. Near maximum, χ Cyg is an obvious orange-red star; months later the same spot shows nothing in binoculars. Red stars play tricks on night vision: glance briefly when you compare it with white stars, because a long stare makes red look brighter.
card.understand: χ Cyg is a giant near the end of its life, so swollen that it would engulf the orbit of Mars. It pulses with a 408-day rhythm, and each cycle its outer layers cool and form molecules that soak up visible light. That is why the change is so dramatic. It is also shedding its outer layers into space.

stops.name: Albireo
stops.class: K3 II + B9.5 V (A + B) · red-giant-branch

getThere.text: Sweep down about one binocular field (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Albireo holds a record: one of the most celebrated colour-contrast double stars.
stops.transitionText: Chi Cygni measures about 350–530 times the Sun's radius; Albireo about 69 times the Sun's radius. To your eye both are points of light.

card.glance: The swan's head star; steady binoculars split it into a close gold star and a fainter blue one, 34″ apart.
card.see: Brace the binoculars on something solid; at 10× the pair is tight but splittable. The brighter star is golden-orange, its companion blue-white. If the split is hard, let the image drift and look for the blue spark beside the gold. Expect two points, not two discs.
card.understand: The gold star is a cool giant, its surface near 4,400 K, about three-quarters of the Sun's temperature. The blue star's surface is around 13,000 K, more than twice the Sun's. Hot things glow blue-white, cooler things glow orange, just as a stove ring shifts colour as it heats. Your eyes are reading two thermometers at once.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Centaurus: Light from Every Century
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far back in time can your binoculars see?
journeys.hook: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when.
journeys.story: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alpha Centauri to Omega Centauri, all in the sky around Centaurus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-west, around Centaurus

stops.name: Alpha Centauri

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, about 65° up in the south, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Alpha Centauri quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Quick background: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross: one dazzling yellow-white point.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show a single brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars are too close together to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm yellow tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Alpha Centauri is two stars circling each other every 80 years. The brighter one is nearly a twin of our Sun, a little heavier and a little wider; its partner is a smaller, cooler orange star. Their light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. A third member, the faint red dwarf Proxima, is invisible in binoculars but is the nearest single star of all.

stops.name: Hadar

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just right of Alpha Centauri, in the same view, and you have Hadar.

stops.whyHere: Hadar shows the next idea you need. Before we go on: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: The two Pointers look like a matched pair, but Hadar is about 80 times farther away; it only looks similar because it is far more powerful.

card.glance: The Pointer nearer the Southern Cross: a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Swing between the two Pointers. Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. They look like a matched pair, but only our line of sight links them. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point: its three stars sit far too close together to split.
card.understand: Hadar is a hot, young triple. Two stars, about 12 and 11 times the Sun’s mass, circle each other almost exactly once a year, with a third star farther out. Heavy stars like these shine with enormous power, which is how a star 360 light-years away can rival one only 4.4 light-years away.

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: From Hadar, slide down and to the right roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Crux.

stops.whyHere: Jewel Box adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Next rung: Jewel Box is about 6,450 light-years away, about 20 times farther than Hadar.

card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, the bright star on the Cross’s eastern arm, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon. Most stars are blue-white; look near the middle for one distinctly orange star. Defocus slightly to bring the colors out. A telescope shows the full jewel box.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, roughly 16 million years ago. The heaviest burned their fuel fastest: one has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a red supergiant, cooler and therefore orange-red. Its blue-white siblings are lighter and still in their long, steady adult life. Same age, different mass, different stage.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just right of Jewel Box, in the same view, and you have Gacrux.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Gacrux is by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars (Crux).
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Jewel Box is about 6,450 light-years away, Gacrux about 89 light-years.

card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross: the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out. Look for a faint white star just to the northeast: a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant: a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. At about 89 light-years it is nearly four times closer than the hot blue stars around it.

stops.name: Omega Centauri

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two binocular fields, toward Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: Omega Centauri holds a record: the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way (Milky Way globular clusters).
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Gacrux at about 89 light-years, Omega Centauri at about 17,700 light-years.

card.glance: A big round glow nearly half the width of the full Moon, brightening toward the middle; to the eye, a fuzzy star.
card.see: To the eye it looks like a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow that brightens steadily toward the center, like a snowball. Under a dark sky, with the binoculars braced, the outer edge can look grainy. Individual stars are a telescope job.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of very old stars orbiting far above and below the galaxy’s disk. This one packs millions of Suns’ worth of stars into a ball under 200 light-years wide. Unlike ordinary globulars, its stars formed in several batches with different chemistry, a clue that it may be the leftover core of a small galaxy torn apart by ours long ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Reading Star Colors over Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: Read the temperature of stars from their color, ember-orange to blue-white, by eye.
journeys.story: Read the temperature of stars from their color, ember-orange to blue-white, by eye. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Antares to ζ Ophiuchi, all in the sky around Scorpius.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Scorpius

stops.name: Antares

getThere.text: Find Antares by eye, about 65° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster just beside it.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and its orange deepens; nudge the focus slightly off and the color gets easier. About two Moon-widths west, look for M4, a soft round grey glow. Antares' close blue companion needs a telescope, so binoculars show a single point.
card.understand: Antares was born with its Scorpius neighbors about 11 million years ago. Starting out perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, it used up the hydrogen in its core quickly and swelled into a supergiant. Its surface is only about 3,700 degrees, far cooler than the Sun's 5,800, so it glows orange-red. Yet it pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun's light. Cool and bright can only mean one thing: it is enormous.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Fang

getThere.text: From Antares, slide up and to the left roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Fang shows the next idea you need. One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: Same family, different spot: Fang shares a birth cloud with Antares.

card.glance: The lowest of the three stars in Scorpius' head; a blue-white point.
card.see: π is the bottom star of the short arc formed with δ and β. Use it, with β, as a brightness yardstick for δ, whose brightness wanders.
card.understand: π Sco is a close pair of hot young stars, too tight for any telescope to split, and part of the 11-million-year-old Upper Scorpius group.

stops.name: Dschubba

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Dschubba is already in the field, just left of Fang.

stops.whyHere: Dschubba adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: π Scorpii, the bottom of the head arc, is another Upper Scorpius sibling and a good comparison star for δ.

card.glance: The middle star of the arc at Scorpius' head; a bright white point whose brightness has wandered since 2000.
card.see: δ is the middle of the three stars in the short vertical arc that forms Scorpius' head. Compare it with β above and π below. Is δ clearly the brightest of the three, or about equal? Your answer is a real measurement: the disk has made it vary for two decades.
card.understand: δ Sco is a hot, heavy star spinning so fast that gas at its equator is barely held on. When its companion swept in close in 2000, the star began to build a flat disk of gas around its waist. That disk glows and adds light, so the star brightened. Hot stars with such disks are called Be stars; the 'e' stands for the glow of the disk gas.

stops.name: τ Scorpii

getThere.text: From Dschubba, slide right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: τ Scorpii is a sister to Dschubba. Their stars came from one cloud.

card.glance: A plain blue-white point just south-east of Antares; the color contrast with its neighbor is the show.
card.see: Put Antares at one edge of a wide field and sweep about two degrees south-east, toward the tail. Swing back and forth: deep orange against crisp blue-white. Defocus both slightly and judge the colors as disks; the difference is unmistakable.
card.understand: τ's surface is about 31,000 degrees, five times hotter than the Sun's and eight times hotter than Antares'. Yet the two stars formed from the same cloud at about the same time. What differs is mass. Antares started heavier, burned its fuel faster, and has already ballooned and cooled into a giant. τ is still in its long, steady adult life, so it stays small, hot and blue-white.

stops.name: ζ Ophiuchi

getThere.text: Move about 18° (two and a half fields) left, toward Ophiuchus.

stops.whyHere: ζ Ophiuchi answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Massive stars rarely live alone, and partners change their lives: τ may be two stars merged into one, while ζ Oph was flung away when its partner exploded.

card.glance: A lone blue-white star in southern Ophiuchus; plain in binoculars, but its story is one of the best in the sky.
card.see: Look about 16 degrees north of Antares for a lone bright star with no obvious neighbors. In binoculars it is a clean blue-white point in a fairly empty field. Notice that emptiness: no cluster, no family around it. The glowing arc in the photo is visible only in infrared light.
card.understand: About 20 times heavier than the Sun, ζ Oph was once half of a close pair in the Scorpius–Centaurus family. When its even heavier partner exploded, the pair came apart and ζ Oph flew off like a stone from a sling. Today it ploughs through thin interstellar dust, and its fierce wind piles that dust into a glowing arc ahead of it, like a ship's bow wave.

image.credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/Dublin Inst. Advanced Studies/S. Green et al.; Infrared: NASA/JPL/Spitzer

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from NGC 6397 to Antares, all in the sky around Scorpius. M4 is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Scorpius

stops.name: NGC 6397

getThere.text: Look 55° up in the south-east. Eyes first: locate β Arae, then a short binocular hop brings in NGC 6397.

stops.whyHere: We start here because NGC 6397 is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: The Milky Way band is our own galaxy: a flat disk of stars that we see edge-on because we live inside it.

card.glance: A bright, slightly irregular glow low in Ara, larger than most globulars in binoculars; best from southern latitudes.
card.see: From β Arae, sweep about three degrees northeast. NGC 6397 is a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo that looks almost grainy in steady 10×50s. From mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon; from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
card.understand: Like M4, this is an ancient swarm of stars. Its heavier stars have already died, leaving white dwarfs: Earth-sized embers that cool and fade at a predictable rate, like coals after a fire. By finding the faintest white dwarfs with Hubble, astronomers read off how long they have been cooling, and so how old the cluster is.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Ptolemy’s Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 19° (three fields) left, toward Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Ptolemy’s Cluster is one of the earliest deep-sky objects on record, noted by Ptolemy around 130 CE. Before we go on: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: One young, one old: about 11 billion years for NGC 6397, about 110–330 million years for Ptolemy’s Cluster.

card.glance: A big, bright spray of stars, easy to the naked eye, that overfills much of a binocular field.
card.see: From Shaula, go about five degrees northeast; M7 lies a few degrees southeast of M6. It is a bright patch to the naked eye; binoculars turn it into dozens of stars spread over more than a degree, on a rich Milky Way background. Look for chains and pairs, and for the yellowish star near the middle. Low power frames it best.
card.understand: M7 is about three times older than M6 and much nearer. Its heaviest stars have had time to finish their lives, so its brightest survivors are a little less massive, and one has become a yellow giant. Sweep M6 and M7 together and you are comparing two family photos taken at different ages.

image.credit: ESO

stops.name: Butterfly Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the left of Ptolemy’s Cluster, in the same view, and you have Butterfly Cluster.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Butterfly Cluster.

card.glance: A bright, scattered cluster shaped like a butterfly with open wings, with one orange star on a wingtip.
card.see: From Shaula, the stinger star, go about five degrees north. M6 fills a modest part of a 7° field: two loose wings of stars spreading from a central body. At one wingtip sits BM Scorpii, clearly orange beside the blue-white members. Defocus slightly to make its color pop.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, so the orange one is a sibling of the blue-white ones. It is simply heavier. Heavier stars run out of hydrogen in their cores first and swell into cool, luminous giants. In a family this age, only the most massive members have reached that stage, so that single orange star is a timestamp.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M4

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two and a half binocular fields (about 18°).

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Butterfly Cluster is about 30–91 million years old; M4 about 12 billion years. Same kind of object, very different age.

card.glance: A large, soft, round glow just west of bright orange Antares; both fit in one binocular field.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and look just over a degree west. M4 is a pale, round patch, larger but dimmer-looking than you might expect, with little central brightening. From a dark site it is obvious; under suburban skies use averted vision and keep Antares just out of view to cut its glare.
card.understand: Antares and M4 look like neighbors, but M4 is about ten times farther away. Antares is a young star from a nearby group; M4 is an ancient swarm orbiting through the galaxy’s halo. Its brightest stars died long ago and became white dwarfs, cooling stellar cores that Hubble has seen directly. How faint the coolest have become is a clock for the cluster’s age.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Antares

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Antares is already in the field, above and to the left of M4.

stops.whyHere: Antares holds a record: one of the largest stars you can see with the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: Compare ages: Antares is about 1,000 times younger than M4.

card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster just beside it.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and its orange deepens; nudge the focus slightly off and the color gets easier. About two Moon-widths west, look for M4, a soft round grey glow. Antares' close blue companion needs a telescope, so binoculars show a single point.
card.understand: Antares was born with its Scorpius neighbors about 11 million years ago. Starting out perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, it used up the hydrogen in its core quickly and swelled into a supergiant. Its surface is only about 3,700 degrees, far cooler than the Sun's 5,800, so it glows orange-red. Yet it pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun's light. Cool and bright can only mean one thing: it is enormous.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Scorpius: A Star's Whole Life
journeys.drivingQuestion: Could you watch a star's whole life in one patch of sky?
journeys.hook: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop.
journeys.story: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Eagle Nebula to Antares, all in the sky around Scorpius.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Scorpius

stops.name: Eagle Nebula

getThere.text: Look 40° up in the east. Find Kaus Borealis by eye, then hop left to Eagle Nebula.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Eagle Nebula is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A small, bright scatter of stars wrapped in a faint haze, north of the Sagittarius star cloud.
card.see: Sweep north from the Sagittarius star cloud past M17. M16 shows as a tight scatter of a dozen or so stars in a soft glow. Under a dark sky, averted vision brings out a dim haze around the cluster, brighter on one side. The famous pillars are far too small and faint for binoculars.
card.understand: The cluster is only a few million years old. Its hottest stars flood the surrounding cloud with ultraviolet light, making the gas glow and slowly boiling it away. Dense knots resist longest and are left standing as dark columns, like sandcastle towers as the tide washes the beach flat. Those columns are the Pillars of Creation, and stars are still forming inside them.

image.credit: ESO

stops.name: M25

getThere.text: Take one field-widths right, toward Sagittarius; M25 is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: M25 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Turn the page in a star's life, from Eagle Nebula to M25.

card.glance: A bright, loose cluster of a few dozen stars, with a couple of yellowish members.
card.see: From μ Sagittarii, hop about four and a half degrees east-northeast. M25 is a loose group of bright stars spread over half a degree, with a central pattern and scattered outliers. U Sagittarii is one of the central stars: compare it with its neighbors on several nights and watch it change.
card.understand: U Sagittarii swells and shrinks, and its brightness rises and falls with a period of 6.7 days. For stars of this kind, a longer period means a more luminous star. Because U Sgr sits in a cluster whose distance we can measure, it helps calibrate that rule, which astronomers then use to measure distances to other galaxies.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alnasl

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two binocular fields (about 13°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. Quick background: Binoculars gather much more light than your eye can, which is why crowds of extra stars pop into view.
stops.transitionText: Same life story, further along. Look for what has changed between M25 and Alnasl.

card.glance: The orange-tinted tip of the Teapot's spout; the Milky Way's brightest star clouds rise just above it.
card.see: Find the Teapot in Sagittarius and center its spout tip, Alnasl, a yellow-orange point. Now sweep slowly west and north: the background thickens into rich star clouds broken by dark lanes. The Galaxy's center lies behind those clouds about four and a half degrees west-north-west of Alnasl, hidden by dust.
card.understand: Alnasl is a nearby orange giant, about 97 light-years away: a foreground lamp. Behind it, the Milky Way is a flat disk of stars and we sit inside it. Looking toward the center, you look along the thickest part of the disk. The center itself is tens of thousands of light-years away, and dust blocks its light; what you see are nearer star clouds in front of it.

stops.name: ε Scorpii

getThere.text: Sweep up about two and a half binocular fields, toward Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: Pay attention here; ε Scorpii upsets an easy assumption.
stops.transitionText: ε Scorpii is the same type of object as Alnasl. Notice what makes it different.

card.glance: The bright orange-yellow star where the tail of Scorpius starts to curve, south-south-east of Antares.
card.see: Drop about nine degrees south-south-east from Antares to the first bright star of the tail. Put each in your binoculars in turn: ε is paler, more yellow-orange, while Antares is a deeper orange. Notice how similar they are in brightness.
card.understand: ε Sco is about 64 light-years away; Antares is roughly 550, nearly nine times farther. Distance alone would make Antares look about 75 times fainter if both stars made the same light. Antares actually looks brighter, so it must give out hundreds of times more light than ε. How bright a star looks mixes two things: how much light it makes and how far away it is.

stops.name: Antares

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one and a half binocular fields (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Antares is one of the largest stars you can see with the naked eye.
stops.transitionText: ε Sco and Antares look similar in brightness, yet Antares is nearly nine times farther: it must make far more light.

card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster just beside it.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and its orange deepens; nudge the focus slightly off and the color gets easier. About two Moon-widths west, look for M4, a soft round grey glow. Antares' close blue companion needs a telescope, so binoculars show a single point.
card.understand: Antares was born with its Scorpius neighbors about 11 million years ago. Starting out perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, it used up the hydrogen in its core quickly and swelled into a supergiant. Its surface is only about 3,700 degrees, far cooler than the Sun's 5,800, so it glows orange-red. Yet it pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun's light. Cool and bright can only mean one thing: it is enormous.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 50% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 25° from it; it sets at 02:11. Only “Same Sky, Different Stories” stories fit this part of the sky right now; other themes may open up later in the night.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Piscis Austrinus: Spot the Difference
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why.
journeys.story: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Fomalhaut to Epsilon Indi, all in the sky around Piscis Austrinus.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Piscis Austrinus

stops.name: Fomalhaut

getThere.text: Find Fomalhaut by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Many stars have planets of their own, called exoplanets, found from the tiny tug or dimming they cause.

card.glance: A lone bright white star low in the south on autumn evenings, with nothing as bright for a long way around.
card.see: Follow the western side of the Great Square of Pegasus, Scheat to Markab, and keep going about 45 degrees south. Fomalhaut is the only bright star there. In binoculars it is white; from northern sites it hangs low, so our air may make it twinkle and flash colors. Its dust ring is invisible in any backyard instrument.
card.understand: Fomalhaut has about twice the Sun’s mass, shines about 16 times brighter and is only about 440 million years old, a tenth of the Sun’s age. A wide ring of dust and ice circles it roughly 140 times farther out than Earth is from the Sun. The ring’s sharp edges hint at unseen planets shaping it, and Webb found more belts closer in.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alnair

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about three binocular fields, toward Grus.

stops.whyHere: Alnair shows the next idea you need. One thing first: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Fomalhaut gives off about 17 times the Sun's light, Alnair about 353 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The brightest star of the Crane: blue-white, six degrees from orange-red Tiaki.
card.see: Center Alnair, then Tiaki. One is blue-white, the other orange-red. Defocusing both slightly makes the colors richer.
card.understand: Alnair is a hot young star with a surface several times hotter than the Sun’s, so it shines blue-white.

stops.name: Lacaille 8760

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one and a half binocular fields, toward Microscopium.

stops.whyHere: Lacaille 8760 holds a record: the brightest red dwarf in the night sky.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Alnair at about 353 times the Sun's light, Lacaille 8760 at about 0.12 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A dim orange point low in the southern sky: the brightest red dwarf there is, and still just below naked-eye view.
card.see: Look about twenty degrees west of Fomalhaut, a little lower. From mid-northern sites it stays low, so it is a southern-sky treat. In binoculars it is a faint, faintly orange point among other faint stars; use the chart to be sure which one it is.
card.understand: A red dwarf is a small, cool star, smaller and far dimmer than the Sun. Red dwarfs sip their fuel so slowly that they will outlive the Sun many times over. This one is also a flare star: magnetic outbursts on its surface can briefly brighten it.

stops.name: Peacock

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about three binocular fields, toward Pavo.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Peacock is the same type of object as Lacaille 8760. Notice what makes it different.

card.glance: A blue-white star alone in Pavo.
card.see: The Peacock is the bright blue-white star of Pavo. Binoculars show a sharp point with a few faint field stars around it.
card.understand: It is a hot young star much heavier than the Sun, orbited by a close companion seen only in its spectrum.

stops.name: Epsilon Indi

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) up and to the left, toward Indus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Epsilon Indi is one of the closest stars with a directly photographed planet (as of 2024).
stops.transitionText: Epsilon Indi is about 8,000 times less luminous than Peacock, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A modest orange star in faint Indus; easy in binoculars, dim to the naked eye.
card.see: Ten degrees from brilliant Alnair, Epsilon Indi looks like an unremarkable faint star. In binoculars notice its soft orange tint, warmer than Alnair’s blue-white. That contrast hides a surprise: the faint one is the near one.
card.understand: Epsilon Indi is an orange dwarf, smaller, cooler and fainter than the Sun, only about 12 light-years away. It looks dim only because it gives out little light. Alnair looks brighter because it is far more powerful, even though it is about eight times farther away. Brightness in the sky mixes power and distance.

image.credit: ESA/Webb, NASA, CSA, STScI, E. Matthews (Max Planck Institute for Astronomy)

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Pegasus
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why.
journeys.story: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why. In 4 stops and about 30 minutes you go from TX Piscium to 51 Pegasi, all in the sky around Pegasus.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north, around Pegasus

stops.name: TX Piscium

getThere.text: Look 45° up in the north-east. Eyes first: locate Algenib, then a short binocular hop brings in TX Piscium.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find TX Piscium quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A strongly orange-red star just east of the Circlet in Pisces; one of the reddest stars visible to the naked eye.
