card.see: Find the faint ring of stars called the Circlet, below the Great Square of Pegasus. TX Piscium is the ruddy star just east of it. In binoculars its color is striking beside white field stars. Look away and back: red stars seem to grow brighter the longer you stare.
card.understand: TX Psc is a giant near the end of its life. Deep inside, it fuses helium into carbon in pulses, and churning currents carry that new carbon up to the surface. There the carbon forms molecules and sooty grains that soak up blue light, leaving a deep red glow. Its surface is only about 3,100 K, roughly half the Sun’s temperature.

stops.name: Algenib

getThere.text: Sweep down about two binocular fields, toward Pegasus.

stops.whyHere: Algenib shows the next idea you need. Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet Algenib is about 50 times smaller than TX Piscium.

card.glance: The south-east corner of the Great Square of Pegasus: a blue-white star, a little fainter than the others.
card.see: Binoculars show a blue-white point. It is the faintest corner of the Square, partly because it is by far the most distant of the four.
card.understand: Algenib is a hot B-type star that throbs gently about every 3.6 hours, far too slightly for the eye.

stops.name: Markab

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the left (about 17°); Markab is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Markab adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Algenib at about 4,700–6,100 times the Sun's light, Markab at about 183 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The south-west corner of the Great Square of Pegasus: a blue-white star.
card.see: Binoculars show a crisp blue-white point. Compare it with Scheat directly north: white versus orange.
card.understand: Markab is a hot white star just beginning to leave its steady adult phase.

stops.name: 51 Pegasi

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) down and to the left (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: 51 Pegasi is the first planet found around a Sun-like star (history of astronomy).
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Markab gives off about 183 times the Sun's light, 51 Pegasi about 1.4 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A faint yellow star beside the Great Square of Pegasus: a near-twin of the Sun that changed astronomy in 1995.
card.see: 51 Pegasi lies about one and a half degrees west of the midpoint between Scheat and Markab, the western side of the Great Square. In binoculars it is a modest yellowish point. You cannot see the planet; what you see is its sun.
card.understand: Astronomers found the planet by measuring a tiny back-and-forth wobble of the star as the planet tugged on it. The surprise was the planet: a giant like Jupiter circling closer to its star than Mercury is to ours, once every 4.2 days. Nobody expected such “hot Jupiters”, and they forced a rethink of how planetary systems form and migrate.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Twins and Opposites in Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 4 stops and about 30 minutes you go from μ¹ Scorpii to NGC 6397, all in the sky around Scorpius.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-west, around Scorpius

stops.name: μ¹ Scorpii

getThere.text: Look 30° up in the south-west. Eyes first: locate ε Scorpii, then a short binocular hop brings in μ¹ Scorpii.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. A short reminder before you look: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair of blue-white stars in the curl of Scorpius' tail; the brighter one quietly dips every day and a half.
card.see: Follow the tail down from Antares to where it starts to curl. μ¹ and μ² sit about a fifth of a Moon-width apart, a naked-eye pair that binoculars widen into two clear blue-white points. Use μ² as your yardstick: on some nights μ¹ looks clearly brighter, on others almost equal.
card.understand: μ¹ is really two hot stars whirling around each other every 35 hours. They are so close that one has swollen to fill its share of space and spills gas onto its partner. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so each star passes in front of the other once per lap and the light dips by about a fifth.

stops.name: ζ¹ Scorpii

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just left of μ¹ Scorpii, in the same view, and you have ζ¹ Scorpii.

stops.whyHere: ζ¹ Scorpii holds a record: one of the most luminous stars visible to the naked eye. Quick background: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: Two naked-eye pairs in the tail: μ¹ and μ² are neighbors in space, but ζ¹ and ζ² are a perspective trick, one forty times farther than the other.

card.glance: The fainter, blue-white star of a naked-eye pair low in Scorpius' tail, with a sparkling cluster just to its north.
card.see: Where the tail bends south, two stars sit side by side, about a fifth of a Moon-width apart: orange ζ² and the fainter, blue-white ζ¹. Now look half a degree north: a tight knot of stars, the cluster NGC 6231. From mid-northern sites this scene hugs the horizon, so it needs a clear southern view.
card.understand: The orange star is a nearby giant, about 135 light-years away. The blue-white one is roughly forty times farther, around 5,500 light-years, and belongs to NGC 6231. To look almost as bright from that far, ζ¹ must give off nearly a million times the Sun's light. It is a hypergiant: an unstable, swollen stage that only the heaviest stars reach.

image.credit: ESO/S. Brunier

stops.name: β Arae

getThere.text: Take two field-widths up and to the left, toward Ara; β Arae is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: β Arae shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: ζ¹ Scorpii gives off about 850,000–1,300,000 times the Sun's light, β Arae about 4,200–7,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: An orange star low in the far south, in Ara below Scorpius' tail.
card.see: Look below the tail of Scorpius, near the southern horizon. β Ara is a distinctly orange point; α Arae, about six degrees north, is blue-white. The bright globular NGC 6397 lies about three degrees to the north-east.
card.understand: β Ara is a supergiant, a star several times heavier than the Sun that has swollen and cooled late in its life.

stops.name: NGC 6397

getThere.text: Stay put: NGC 6397 is in the same view, just right of β Arae.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: NGC 6397 is the second-nearest globular cluster to the Sun, after M4 (all catalogued Milky Way globular clusters (Baumgardt catalogue)).
stops.transitionText: From a heavy star living fast to one of the oldest and nearest globular clusters, three degrees away.

card.glance: A bright, slightly irregular glow low in Ara, larger than most globulars in binoculars; best from southern latitudes.
card.see: From β Arae, sweep about three degrees northeast. NGC 6397 is a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo that looks almost grainy in steady 10×50s. From mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon; from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
card.understand: Like M4, this is an ancient swarm of stars. Its heavier stars have already died, leaving white dwarfs: Earth-sized embers that cool and fade at a predictable rate, like coals after a fire. By finding the faintest white dwarfs with Hubble, astronomers read off how long they have been cooling, and so how old the cluster is.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Tucana
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Tiaki to 47 Tucanae, all in the sky around Tucana.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Tucana

stops.name: Tiaki

getThere.text: Find Tiaki by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Tiaki quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. A short reminder before you look: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: The orange-red star of the Crane, six degrees from blue-white Alnair: a ready-made color contrast.
card.see: Put Tiaki and Alnair in turn at the center of your binoculars. Tiaki is a deep orange-red, Alnair a clean blue-white. Defocus slightly and the colors strengthen. Over weeks, compare Tiaki with Alnair: its brightness wanders a little.
card.understand: Tiaki is a red giant near the end of its life, swollen to about 150 times the Sun’s width. Its surface is only about 3,500 K, cooler than the Sun’s 5,800 K, so it glows orange-red. Red here means cool, not hot: in stars the everyday color code runs backwards.

stops.name: Alnair

getThere.text: Take one field-widths up and to the right (about 6°); Alnair is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alnair shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: From Tiaki to Alnair, the colors swap from icy to ember. Red here means cool.

card.glance: The brightest star of the Crane: blue-white, six degrees from orange-red Tiaki.
card.see: Center Alnair, then Tiaki. One is blue-white, the other orange-red. Defocusing both slightly makes the colors richer.
card.understand: Alnair is a hot young star with a surface several times hotter than the Sun’s, so it shines blue-white.

stops.name: Alpha Tucanae

getThere.text: Take two field-widths down, toward Tucana; Alpha Tucanae is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alpha Tucanae adds the next piece of the story. Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Picture them side by side: Alnair at about 3.4 times the Sun's radius, Alpha Tucanae at about 38 times the Sun's radius.

card.glance: An orange star in Tucana, between Grus and the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.see: Alpha Tucanae is a soft orange point in binoculars, alone in a quiet field.
card.understand: It is a giant about 38 times the Sun’s width, with a cool surface near 4,200 K.

stops.name: Beta Hydri

getThere.text: Move about 20° (three fields) down, toward Hydrus.

stops.whyHere: A surprise: Beta Hydri breaks the pattern so far.
stops.transitionText: Beta Hydri is about 100 times less luminous than Alpha Tucanae, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A modest yellowish star near the south celestial pole, close to the Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.see: Beta Hydri sits near the south celestial pole, roughly between the Small Magellanic Cloud and the pole. Binoculars show a soft yellow star, the same tint as the Sun would show at night. Sweep about 5° to the Small Cloud’s misty glow for a sense of scale.
card.understand: Beta Hydri is a near-twin of the Sun, a bit heavier, and about 6.5 billion years old. It has finished burning hydrogen in its core and is now slowly swelling. It is already almost twice the Sun’s width and over three times as bright. Our Sun will reach this stage in a few billion years.

stops.name: 47 Tucanae

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. 47 Tucanae is already in the field, above and to the left of Beta Hydri.

stops.whyHere: 47 Tucanae holds a record: the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky, after Omega Centauri.
stops.transitionText: Beta Hydri is older than the Sun at about 6.5 billion years; 47 Tucanae is nearly twice as old again, among the oldest things in the Galaxy.

card.glance: A bright, compact glow with a blazing core, right at the edge of the faint Small Magellanic Cloud.
card.see: To the eye it is a fuzzy star at the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Binoculars show a round glow that brightens sharply to an intense, almost starlike core, quite different from the softer look of Omega Centauri. Wide binoculars can hold the cluster and the edge of the Cloud in one view.
card.understand: This is a ball of hundreds of thousands of old stars held together by their own gravity. Globulars like it orbit in a vast halo around our galaxy and are among the oldest things we can date, close to 12 billion years. It is richer in heavy elements than most globulars, so it formed from gas already seeded by earlier generations of stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 06:28.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: The Family Album of Carina
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: The Sun lost its siblings long ago. Tonight, meet stars that still have theirs.
journeys.story: The Sun lost its siblings long ago. Tonight, meet stars that still have theirs. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from NGC 2451 to Wishing Well Cluster, all in the sky around Carina.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Carina

stops.name: NGC 2451

getThere.text: Find NGC 2451 by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because NGC 2451 is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story.

card.glance: A bright, scattered group of stars around the orange giant c Puppis, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Under dark skies it shows to the naked eye. Binoculars reveal a bold scatter of bright stars around the orange giant c Puppis; nothing marks the two clusters apart, because their stars mingle in the view. Then find the misty glow of NGC 2477 about one and a half degrees to the east-south-east: a third family, much farther still.
card.understand: Only measurements of motion and distance can untangle this field. Gaia shows one group, NGC 2451A, about 620 light-years away, and a second, NGC 2451B, about 1,200 light-years away. Both are a few tens of millions of years old, but they are separate families that happen to lie in the same direction. The sky is a flat screen hiding depth behind it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 2547

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about two binocular fields, toward Vela.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. One thing first: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: Similar in age, a few tens of millions of years, but NGC 2547 is about twice as far as the nearer NGC 2451 group.

card.glance: A neat little cluster of a few dozen stars, about two degrees south of Gamma Velorum.
card.see: Start at Gamma Velorum, the bright star in Vela’s sail, and drop about two degrees south. Binoculars show a compact group of perhaps two dozen stars, a few bright ones over a fainter scatter, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.understand: These stars are about 35 million years old. Astronomers dated them two ways: from the brighter stars just settling into their adult life, and from the faintest red dwarfs, which slowly destroy the fragile element lithium. Both clocks agree, which tells us our picture of how young stars grow up is working.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Omicron Velorum Cluster

getThere.text: From NGC 2547, slide down roughly one fields of view (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Omicron Velorum Cluster holds a record: one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: Omicron Velorum Cluster, a cousin of NGC 2547.

card.glance: A loose naked-eye scatter of bright stars around Omicron Velorum, bigger than the full Moon.
card.see: It lies less than two degrees north of Delta Velorum, a corner of the False Cross. To the eye it is a small knot of five or six stars around Omicron Velorum. Binoculars show a loose, sparkling group of a few dozen bright stars; low-power, wide binoculars frame it best.
card.understand: Like the Southern Pleiades, this is a young family about 50 million years old, born together from one cloud. Because it is only about 490 light-years away, even its modest stars look bright, and the group spreads wider than the Moon. Nearby young clusters like this let astronomers watch how small stars grow up.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Pleiades

getThere.text: Take three field-widths down, toward Carina; Southern Pleiades is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Southern Pleiades is one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.
stops.transitionText: Same distance, nearly the same age, different spot in the sky: a second young family to compare with the first.

card.glance: A naked-eye spray of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye counts five or six; binoculars show two or three dozen, mostly blue-white, spread across about a third of the field. If you know the Pleiades, the resemblance is striking: similar look, similar distance.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, so they share an age and a birthplace. Their blue-white color shows that the brightest members are hot, heavy stars still in their long, steady adult life. Astronomers dated the family from its faintest, coolest members, which slowly destroy a fragile element, lithium: the point where lithium still survives works like a clock.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: Take one field-widths left (about 6°); Wishing Well Cluster is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Wishing Well Cluster holds a record: one of the richest open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters). Quick background: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Southern Pleiades is about 41–52 million years old; Wishing Well Cluster about 300 million years. Same kind of object, very different age.

card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between. Look for a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones; defocusing slightly makes them easier to pick out.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already died, so its brightest survivors are white, and a few have swollen into orange giants. Compare it with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula: the same kind of family, but this one has lived through many more chapters of its life.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Carina
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Delta Velorum to Wishing Well Cluster, all in the sky around Carina.
journeys.regionLabel: In the south, around Carina

stops.name: Delta Velorum

getThere.text: Find Delta Velorum by eye, about 60° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Delta Velorum quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: One corner of the False Cross: a bright white star that dims for about a day every few weeks.
card.see: Find the False Cross, a larger, fainter look-alike of the Southern Cross. Delta Velorum is one of its four corners. Compare it with Kappa Velorum and Aspidiske: on most nights it is clearly brighter, but during an eclipse it drops to about their level for roughly a day.
card.understand: Delta Velorum is two white stars orbiting each other every 45 days. Our view runs almost along their orbit, so once per orbit one star passes in front of the other and blocks part of its light. The stars themselves do not change; only our view of them does.

stops.name: Theta Carinae

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths down, toward Carina; Theta Carinae is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. One thing first: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: True power against looks: Delta Velorum gives off about 85 times the Sun's light, Theta Carinae about 19,300 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The brightest star of the Southern Pleiades, a scatter of blue-white stars that fills a binocular view.
card.see: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group fills about half your view, with dozens of fainter members. About 5° north lies the glowing Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae.
card.understand: The Southern Pleiades (IC 2602) is a family of stars born together tens of millions of years ago, about 490 light-years away. Theta Carinae is its brightest and hottest star. From here, Eta Carinae looks fainter, yet it is more than 15 times farther away and far more powerful.

stops.name: Eta Carinae

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Eta Carinae is already in the field, just left of Theta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: Eta Carinae holds a record: briefly the second-brightest star in the night sky during its 1840s Great Eruption (historical (1840s)).
stops.transitionText: Five degrees apart, these two stars swap roles: the bright one is the near one, the dimmer one the monster.

card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula; its brightness changes over the years.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbours. That is Eta Carinae. It looks like an ordinary star; the drama is in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years. The heavier one may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived. That gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus, which dims and reddens the star we see.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, N. Smith (University of Arizona, Tucson), and J. Morse (BoldlyGo Institute, New York)

stops.name: Gem Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just above Eta Carinae, in the same view, and you have Gem Cluster.

stops.whyHere: Gem Cluster shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Same family, different spot: Gem Cluster shares a birth cloud with Eta Carinae.

card.glance: A small, bright knot of stars about two degrees north-west of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula, move about two degrees north-west. Binoculars show a compact, bright clump much smaller than the Moon, with a few stars resolved around a hazy center. Higher magnification or a telescope shows many more.
card.understand: This family was born in the same great cloud complex as the Carina Nebula’s clusters, but several million years earlier. Its hottest stars have already blown most of their birth gas away. Look from the glowing nebula to this clean cluster and you see the before and after of star birth.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just below Gem Cluster, in the same view, and you have Wishing Well Cluster.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Wishing Well Cluster is one of the richest open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters).
stops.transitionText: Gem Cluster is about 9.7–23 million years old; Wishing Well Cluster about 300 million years. Same kind of object, very different age.

card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between. Look for a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones; defocusing slightly makes them easier to pick out.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already died, so its brightest survivors are white, and a few have swollen into orange giants. Compare it with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula: the same kind of family, but this one has lived through many more chapters of its life.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Orion in Living Color
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: Your eyes are a thermometer tonight. All you need is a slight defocus.
journeys.story: Your eyes are a thermometer tonight. All you need is a slight defocus. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from W Orionis to θ¹ Orionis C, all in the sky around Orion.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Orion

stops.name: W Orionis

getThere.text: Look 50° up in the north-west. Eyes first: locate Orion’s Belt, then a short binocular hop brings in W Orionis.

stops.whyHere: We start here because W Orionis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A 6th-magnitude orange-red star in western Orion, easy in binoculars.
card.see: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix. Among white field stars it stands out as orange-red; defocus slightly to boost the color.
card.understand: W Orionis is an old giant that has dredged up carbon from its core. That carbon forms molecules in its cool atmosphere that soak up blue light, so it glows warm red. It slowly varies in brightness over about seven months.

stops.name: Alnilam

getThere.text: Take one field-widths up and to the right (about 8°); Alnilam is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alnilam adds the next piece of the story. One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: From W Orionis at about 2,700 K to Alnilam at about 25,000 K. Defocus slightly and the colors jump out.

card.glance: The middle star of Orion’s Belt, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. Notice the curving string of fainter stars winding through the Belt; many were born in the same burst. Alnilam shares the same icy blue-white as its two neighbours.
card.understand: Alnilam is a blue supergiant of about 28 Suns, roughly 1,250 light-years away. ESO’s Very Large Telescope interferometer recently measured it: about 28 times the Sun’s width, a surface near 25,000 K, and spinning so fast it is close to flinging gas off its equator. A star this heavy lives only a few million years.

stops.name: Mintaka

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of Alnilam, in the same view, and you have Mintaka.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Alnilam and Mintaka, the Belt’s middle and western stars, were born in the same wave of star formation.

card.glance: The western (right-hand) star of Orion’s Belt, with an easy companion to its north.
card.see: Center Mintaka, the Belt star nearest Rigel’s side. Look about 50 arcseconds due north for a 7th-magnitude companion: binoculars split it with steady hands.
card.understand: Mintaka is a group of hot, heavy stars. Its inner pair eclipses every 5.7 days, dimming it slightly. Careful modelling suggests it lies about twice as far as early satellite measurements implied, near the young σ Orionis cluster.

stops.name: σ Orionis

getThere.text: Same field of view: σ Orionis sits above and to the left of Mintaka.

stops.whyHere: σ Orionis shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Careful modelling puts σ Orionis near the distance of Mintaka: neighbours in Orion’s young family.

card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the eastern Belt star.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; brace the binoculars and look for a second, closer one due east. A small, faint triangle of stars sits a few arcminutes away. A telescope splits the scene into many more.
card.understand: The bright point is really at least five stars. The central pair, far too close for any ordinary telescope, holds about 17 and 13 times the Sun’s mass. Interferometers tracked their orbit, and that orbit also gave a very precise distance, about 1,260 light-years, for the young cluster around them.

stops.name: θ¹ Orionis C

getThere.text: Stay put: θ¹ Orionis C is in the same view, just left of σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: Both σ Orionis and θ¹ Orionis C hide pairs of very heavy stars whose orbits, tracked with interferometers, let astronomers weigh them.

card.glance: One bright point inside the glowing heart of the Orion Nebula.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula and look at the bright knot in its core. At binocular power the four Trapezium stars merge into one point, and θ¹ Orionis C is the brightest of them. Just south-east, θ² Orionis adds an easier pair of points.
card.understand: θ¹ Orionis C is a young pair of very heavy stars, together about 44 times the Sun’s mass. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot and flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light. That light energizes the hydrogen gas around them, and the gas glows, much like the gas in a neon sign. Without this one system, most of the nebula would be dark.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Moonlight Can't Hide These: Carina
journeys.drivingQuestion: Which wonders does moonlight leave untouched?
journeys.hook: A bright Moon? Perfect for star colors and double stars.
journeys.story: A bright Moon? Perfect for star colors and double stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Canopus to Southern Pleiades, all in the sky around Carina.
journeys.regionLabel: In the south, around Carina

stops.name: Canopus

getThere.text: Find Canopus by eye, about 70° up in the south, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Canopus is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.

card.glance: The second-brightest star of the night: a dazzling white point well south of Sirius.
card.see: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers through colors as our air splits its light; higher up it is a steady white. Then sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer.
card.understand: Canopus is a giant (a star swollen past its long, steady adult life) of roughly nine or ten Suns’ mass and 73 times the Sun’s width. It now burns helium in its core. A star that big and that hot gives out about 16,000 times the Sun’s light, enough to look dazzling from 310 light-years.

stops.name: Tau Puppis

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the left of Canopus, in the same view, and you have Tau Puppis.

stops.whyHere: Tau Puppis shows the next idea you need. Before we go on: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Tau Puppis is about 60 times less luminous than Canopus.

card.glance: A yellow-orange star in southern Puppis, between Canopus and the Milky Way.
card.see: In binoculars Tau Puppis is a soft yellow-orange point. Compare it with brilliant white Canopus about 5° to the west-southwest.
card.understand: Tau Puppis is a giant about 25 times the Sun’s width, with a cooler surface near 4,600 K.

stops.name: Avior

getThere.text: From Tau Puppis, slide down and to the left roughly two and a half fields of view, toward Carina.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Tau Puppis at about 261 times the Sun's light, Avior at about 8,100–11,000 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: The orange corner of the False Cross.
card.see: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Delta Velorum and Aspidiske.
card.understand: Avior’s light comes from two stars too close to split: a cool orange giant and a hotter blue companion.

stops.name: Eta Carinae

getThere.text: From Avior, slide down and to the left roughly two and a half fields of view (about 18°).

stops.whyHere: Eta Carinae holds a record: briefly the second-brightest star in the night sky during its 1840s Great Eruption (historical (1840s)).
stops.transitionText: Eta Carinae is what a family like Avior grows into: the same story, a later chapter.

card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula; its brightness changes over the years.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbours. That is Eta Carinae. It looks like an ordinary star; the drama is in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years. The heavier one may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived. That gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus, which dims and reddens the star we see.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, N. Smith (University of Arizona, Tucson), and J. Morse (BoldlyGo Institute, New York)

stops.name: Southern Pleiades

getThere.text: Stay put: Southern Pleiades is in the same view, just right of Eta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Southern Pleiades is one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.
stops.transitionText: Eta Carinae and Southern Pleiades look like neighbors, but Southern Pleiades is about 20 times closer than Eta Carinae.

card.glance: A naked-eye spray of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye counts five or six; binoculars show two or three dozen, mostly blue-white, spread across about a third of the field. If you know the Pleiades, the resemblance is striking: similar look, similar distance.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, so they share an age and a birthplace. Their blue-white color shows that the brightest members are hot, heavy stars still in their long, steady adult life. Astronomers dated the family from its faintest, coolest members, which slowly destroy a fragile element, lithium: the point where lithium still survives works like a clock.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 52% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 26° from it; it sets at 13:14.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Measuring the Depths of Triangulum Australe
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far away is the farthest thing you can see tonight?
journeys.hook: Which star is nearest? Which is farthest? Looks will mislead you.
journeys.story: Which star is nearest? Which is farthest? Looks will mislead you. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alpha Centauri to NGC 6397, all in the sky around Triangulum Australe.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Triangulum Australe

stops.name: Alpha Centauri

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, about 60° up in the south-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Quick background: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross: one dazzling yellow-white point.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show a single brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars are too close together to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm yellow tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Alpha Centauri is two stars circling each other every 80 years. The brighter one is nearly a twin of our Sun, a little heavier and a little wider; its partner is a smaller, cooler orange star. Their light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. A third member, the faint red dwarf Proxima, is invisible in binoculars but is the nearest single star of all.

stops.name: Gamma Trianguli Australis

getThere.text: Move about 9° (one fields) down and to the left, toward Triangulum Australe.

stops.whyHere: Gamma Trianguli Australis adds the next piece of the story. Before we go on: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Alpha Centauri and Gamma Trianguli Australis look like neighbors, but Gamma Trianguli Australis is about 40 times farther than Alpha Centauri.

card.glance: A white corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.see: Compare the three corners of the Southern Triangle: orange Atria, creamy Beta and white Gamma.
card.understand: Gamma Trianguli Australis is a hot white star about 190 light-years away.

stops.name: Atria

getThere.text: Sweep left about one binocular field (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: The Southern Triangle looks flat, but its corners lie at about 40, 190 and 390 light-years.

card.glance: The bright orange corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.see: Atria is a vivid orange point; defocus slightly to enhance the color, then compare with the white corners of the triangle.
card.understand: Atria is a giant about 120 times the Sun’s width and nearly 4,000 times its light, with a cool surface near 4,300 K.

stops.name: NGC 6087

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one and a half binocular fields, toward Norma.

stops.whyHere: NGC 6087 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Atria at about 391 light-years, NGC 6087 at about 3,060 light-years.

card.glance: A modest cluster gathered around a bright yellowish star in the rich Norma Milky Way.
card.see: From η Arae, sweep about four degrees west into Norma. NGC 6087 shows a dozen or more stars around S Normae, the brightest one, slightly yellow. Over a week or two, compare S Nor with its neighbors: it changes by nearly a factor of two.
card.understand: S Normae swells and shrinks with a period of nearly ten days. Its fellow cluster members tell us its distance and age, so S Nor is a test of how such stars work: a Cepheid’s period predicts its true brightness, and comparing that with how bright it looks gives its distance.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 6397

getThere.text: From NGC 6087, slide up and to the left roughly one and a half fields of view, toward Ara.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: NGC 6397 is the second-nearest globular cluster to the Sun, after M4 (all catalogued Milky Way globular clusters (Baumgardt catalogue)).
stops.transitionText: Next rung: NGC 6397 is about 8,090 light-years away, about 3 times farther than NGC 6087.

card.glance: A bright, slightly irregular glow low in Ara, larger than most globulars in binoculars; best from southern latitudes.
card.see: From β Arae, sweep about three degrees northeast. NGC 6397 is a bright, irregular glow with a concentrated core and a ragged halo that looks almost grainy in steady 10×50s. From mid-northern latitudes it barely clears the horizon; from the southern hemisphere it is a highlight.
card.understand: Like M4, this is an ancient swarm of stars. Its heavier stars have already died, leaving white dwarfs: Earth-sized embers that cool and fade at a predictable rate, like coals after a fire. By finding the faintest white dwarfs with Hubble, astronomers read off how long they have been cooling, and so how old the cluster is.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Starlight Postmarked Long Ago: Centaurus
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight set out?
journeys.hook: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar.
journeys.story: Every stop shows light from a different moment in history. Read it like a calendar. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alpha Centauri to Omega Centauri, all in the sky around Centaurus.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Centaurus

stops.name: Alpha Centauri

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, about 60° up in the south-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Quick background: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross: one dazzling yellow-white point.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show a single brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars are too close together to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm yellow tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Alpha Centauri is two stars circling each other every 80 years. The brighter one is nearly a twin of our Sun, a little heavier and a little wider; its partner is a smaller, cooler orange star. Their light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. A third member, the faint red dwarf Proxima, is invisible in binoculars but is the nearest single star of all.

stops.name: Hadar

getThere.text: Same field of view: Hadar sits below and to the right of Alpha Centauri.

stops.whyHere: Hadar adds the next piece of the story. Before we go on: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: The two Pointers look like a matched pair, but Hadar is about 80 times farther away; it only looks similar because it is far more powerful.

card.glance: The Pointer nearer the Southern Cross: a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Swing between the two Pointers. Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. They look like a matched pair, but only our line of sight links them. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point: its three stars sit far too close together to split.
card.understand: Hadar is a hot, young triple. Two stars, about 12 and 11 times the Sun’s mass, circle each other almost exactly once a year, with a third star farther out. Heavy stars like these shine with enormous power, which is how a star 360 light-years away can rival one only 4.4 light-years away.

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: From Hadar, slide down roughly one fields of view, toward Crux.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Hadar at about 361 light-years, Jewel Box at about 6,450 light-years.

card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, the bright star on the Cross’s eastern arm, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon. Most stars are blue-white; look near the middle for one distinctly orange star. Defocus slightly to bring the colors out. A telescope shows the full jewel box.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, roughly 16 million years ago. The heaviest burned their fuel fastest: one has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a red supergiant, cooler and therefore orange-red. Its blue-white siblings are lighter and still in their long, steady adult life. Same age, different mass, different stage.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: Stay put: Gacrux is in the same view, below and to the right of Jewel Box.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Gacrux is by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars (Crux).
stops.transitionText: Jewel Box and Gacrux look like neighbors, but Gacrux is about 70 times closer than Jewel Box.

card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross: the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out. Look for a faint white star just to the northeast: a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant: a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. At about 89 light-years it is nearly four times closer than the hot blue stars around it.

stops.name: Omega Centauri

getThere.text: Move about 13° (two fields) up and to the right, toward Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: Omega Centauri holds a record: the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way (Milky Way globular clusters).
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Omega Centauri lies about 200 times farther than Gacrux.

card.glance: A big round glow nearly half the width of the full Moon, brightening toward the middle; to the eye, a fuzzy star.
card.see: To the eye it looks like a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow that brightens steadily toward the center, like a snowball. Under a dark sky, with the binoculars braced, the outer edge can look grainy. Individual stars are a telescope job.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of very old stars orbiting far above and below the galaxy’s disk. This one packs millions of Suns’ worth of stars into a ball under 200 light-years wide. Unlike ordinary globulars, its stars formed in several batches with different chemistry, a clue that it may be the leftover core of a small galaxy torn apart by ours long ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Reading Star Colors over Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are stars different colors, and what does that tell us?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Antares to Shaula, all in the sky around Scorpius.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Scorpius

stops.name: Antares

getThere.text: Find Antares by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster just beside it.
card.see: Put Antares near the edge of the field and its orange deepens; nudge the focus slightly off and the color gets easier. About two Moon-widths west, look for M4, a soft round grey glow. Antares' close blue companion needs a telescope, so binoculars show a single point.
card.understand: Antares was born with its Scorpius neighbors about 11 million years ago. Starting out perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, it used up the hydrogen in its core quickly and swelled into a supergiant. Its surface is only about 3,700 degrees, far cooler than the Sun's 5,800, so it glows orange-red. Yet it pours out tens of thousands of times the Sun's light. Cool and bright can only mean one thing: it is enormous.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alniyat

getThere.text: Stay put: Alniyat is in the same view, just left of Antares.

stops.whyHere: Alniyat adds the next piece of the story. One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: σ and Antares were born in the same Upper Scorpius family. One is still blue-white, the other has already turned red: heavier stars age faster.

card.glance: A blue-white star two degrees west-north-west of Antares; M4 sits between them.
card.see: Put Antares at the edge of the field and look two degrees west-north-west for σ. M4's soft glow lies about a degree south-east of σ, between the two stars. A faint companion 20 arcseconds away needs a steady, mounted view.
card.understand: σ Sco is a hot giant of the Upper Scorpius family. Hot, heavy stars like this one gently pulse in and out several times a day, changing brightness by only a few hundredths, far too little for the eye.

stops.name: Fang

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just left of Alniyat, in the same view, and you have Fang.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Fang is a sister to Alniyat. Their stars came from one cloud.

card.glance: The lowest of the three stars in Scorpius' head; a blue-white point.
card.see: π is the bottom star of the short arc formed with δ and β. Use it, with β, as a brightness yardstick for δ, whose brightness wanders.
card.understand: π Sco is a close pair of hot young stars, too tight for any telescope to split, and part of the 11-million-year-old Upper Scorpius group.

stops.name: μ¹ Scorpii

getThere.text: Move about 16° (two and a half fields) up (about 16°).

stops.whyHere: μ¹ Scorpii shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Fang and μ¹ Scorpii are siblings: born from the same cloud at about the same time.

card.glance: A naked-eye pair of blue-white stars in the curl of Scorpius' tail; the brighter one quietly dips every day and a half.
card.see: Follow the tail down from Antares to where it starts to curl. μ¹ and μ² sit about a fifth of a Moon-width apart, a naked-eye pair that binoculars widen into two clear blue-white points. Use μ² as your yardstick: on some nights μ¹ looks clearly brighter, on others almost equal.
card.understand: μ¹ is really two hot stars whirling around each other every 35 hours. They are so close that one has swollen to fill its share of space and spills gas onto its partner. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so each star passes in front of the other once per lap and the light dips by about a fifth.

stops.name: Shaula

getThere.text: From μ¹ Scorpii, slide left roughly one fields of view (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: μ¹ and Shaula are both tight families of hot stars; their orbits are how astronomers weigh them.

card.glance: The bright blue-white stinger at the tip of Scorpius' tail, with fainter Lesath just beside it.
card.see: Follow the tail to its hook: the bright stinger is Shaula, with fainter Lesath just over half a degree to the west-south-west. Both look blue-white. Keep them in view and sweep about five degrees north-east to the big, bright cluster M7, then north to M6.
card.understand: Shaula looks like one star but is at least three. Two hot stars, about ten and eight times the Sun's mass, circle each other every few years, and a small third star whips around the brightest every six days. Measuring those orbits weighs the stars directly, the most reliable way to learn a star's mass.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: The Family Album of Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: The Sun lost its siblings long ago. Tonight, meet stars that still have theirs.
journeys.story: The Sun lost its siblings long ago. Tonight, meet stars that still have theirs. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Butterfly Cluster to NGC 6633, all in the sky around Scorpius. Wild Duck Cluster is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Scorpius

stops.name: Butterfly Cluster

getThere.text: Look 75° up in the east. Eyes first: locate Shaula, then a short binocular hop brings in Butterfly Cluster.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Butterfly Cluster is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.

card.glance: A bright, scattered cluster shaped like a butterfly with open wings, with one orange star on a wingtip.
card.see: From Shaula, the stinger star, go about five degrees north. M6 fills a modest part of a 7° field: two loose wings of stars spreading from a central body. At one wingtip sits BM Scorpii, clearly orange beside the blue-white members. Defocus slightly to make its color pop.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, so the orange one is a sibling of the blue-white ones. It is simply heavier. Heavier stars run out of hydrogen in their cores first and swell into cool, luminous giants. In a family this age, only the most massive members have reached that stage, so that single orange star is a timestamp.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Ptolemy’s Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: look just right of Butterfly Cluster, in the same view, and you have Ptolemy’s Cluster.

stops.whyHere: Ptolemy’s Cluster holds a record: one of the earliest deep-sky objects on record, noted by Ptolemy around 130 CE. A short reminder before you look: A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: Two clusters in one sweep, two ages: Butterfly Cluster is the younger family, Ptolemy’s Cluster the older one.

card.glance: A big, bright spray of stars, easy to the naked eye, that overfills much of a binocular field.
card.see: From Shaula, go about five degrees northeast; M7 lies a few degrees southeast of M6. It is a bright patch to the naked eye; binoculars turn it into dozens of stars spread over more than a degree, on a rich Milky Way background. Look for chains and pairs, and for the yellowish star near the middle. Low power frames it best.
card.understand: M7 is about three times older than M6 and much nearer. Its heaviest stars have had time to finish their lives, so its brightest survivors are a little less massive, and one has become a yellow giant. Sweep M6 and M7 together and you are comparing two family photos taken at different ages.

image.credit: ESO

stops.name: M25

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths down and to the left, toward Sagittarius; M25 is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: M25 adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: M25, a cousin of Ptolemy’s Cluster.

card.glance: A bright, loose cluster of a few dozen stars, with a couple of yellowish members.
card.see: From μ Sagittarii, hop about four and a half degrees east-northeast. M25 is a loose group of bright stars spread over half a degree, with a central pattern and scattered outliers. U Sagittarii is one of the central stars: compare it with its neighbors on several nights and watch it change.
card.understand: U Sagittarii swells and shrinks, and its brightness rises and falls with a period of 6.7 days. For stars of this kind, a longer period means a more luminous star. Because U Sgr sits in a cluster whose distance we can measure, it helps calibrate that rule, which astronomers then use to measure distances to other galaxies.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wild Duck Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 14° (two fields) down and to the left, toward Scutum.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Wild Duck Cluster is the same type of object as M25. Notice what makes it different.

card.glance: A small, bright, grainy fan of light in Scutum, almost like a globular, with a bright star at its tip.
card.see: Follow Aquila’s tail south into little Scutum, then go about two degrees southeast of β Scuti. M11 is a compact, fan-shaped haze with a brighter star at its apex, set inside the bright Scutum star cloud. In 10×50s it looks granular; more magnification starts to break it into stars.
card.understand: Most open clusters hold a few hundred stars; M11 holds thousands. Born together a few hundred million years ago, its stars are packed tightly enough that the cluster still looks dense and rich. From over 7,000 light-years away, you see their combined light as one glowing fan.

image.credit: ESO

stops.name: NGC 6633

getThere.text: Move about 14° (two fields) left, toward Ophiuchus.

stops.whyHere: NGC 6633 answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: NGC 6633, next to your memory of Wild Duck Cluster.

card.glance: A long, loose spray of stars in a rich Milky Way field, easy in any binoculars.
card.see: From IC 4665, sweep about 10 degrees due east, roughly a field and a half. Look for an elongated scatter of stars about the width of the full Moon, set against a dense star background. Pick out its brightest members first, then compare the overall feel with IC 4665: similar size, similar distance, different age.
card.understand: You can read a star family’s age from its brightest stars. Heavy, hot, blue stars burn out first. In NGC 6633 the hottest ones are long gone; its brightest members are white stars and a few yellow-orange giants that have begun to swell. Its Sun-like stars also hold lithium in nearly the same pattern as the Hyades, a cluster of similar age.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Time Machine over Crux
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far back in time can your binoculars see?
journeys.hook: Old news from space: each stop's light is older than the last.
journeys.story: Old news from space: each stop's light is older than the last. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alpha Centauri to Omega Centauri, all in the sky around Crux.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Crux

stops.name: Alpha Centauri

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, about 35° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. One thing first: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

stops.name: Mimosa

getThere.text: Sweep up about two binocular fields, toward Crux.

stops.whyHere: Mimosa shows the next idea you need. A short reminder before you look: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: Climb again: Mimosa lies about 60 times farther than Alpha Centauri.

card.glance: The left-hand star of the Southern Cross: blue-white, and your signpost to the Jewel Box.
card.see: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the Cross’s eastern arm. Place it at the edge of your view and look about 1° to the southeast: a tight, glittering knot of stars appears. That is the Jewel Box. Its brightest stars share Mimosa’s icy color.
card.understand: Mimosa is a heavy, hot star that swells and shrinks very slightly several times a day, too little for your eye to notice. It probably belongs to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. The Jewel Box is a family of about the same age, but more than twenty times farther away.

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: Same field of view: Jewel Box sits just right of Mimosa.

stops.whyHere: Jewel Box adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Same age, different distance: Jewel Box is the same kind of young family as Mimosa’s, seen from far away.

card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, the bright star on the Cross’s eastern arm, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon. Most stars are blue-white; look near the middle for one distinctly orange star. Defocus slightly to bring the colors out. A telescope shows the full jewel box.

The heaviest burned their fuel fastest: one has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a red supergiant, cooler and therefore orange-red. Its blue-white siblings are lighter and still in their long, steady adult life. Same age, different mass, different stage.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Gacrux is already in the field, just above Jewel Box.

stops.whyHere: Gacrux holds a record: by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars (Crux).
stops.transitionText: On the sky they are close; in space they are not. Jewel Box is about 6,450 light-years away, Gacrux about 89 light-years.

card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross: the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out. Look for a faint white star just to the northeast: a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant: a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. At about 89 light-years it is nearly four times closer than the hot blue stars around it.

stops.name: Omega Centauri

getThere.text: From Gacrux, slide left roughly two fields of view, toward Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Omega Centauri is the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way (Milky Way globular clusters).
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Gacrux at about 89 light-years, Omega Centauri at about 17,700 light-years.

card.glance: A big round glow nearly half the width of the full Moon, brightening toward the middle; to the eye, a fuzzy star.
card.see: To the eye it looks like a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow that brightens steadily toward the center, like a snowball. Under a dark sky, with the binoculars braced, the outer edge can look grainy. Individual stars are a telescope job.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of very old stars orbiting far above and below the galaxy’s disk. This one packs millions of Suns’ worth of stars into a ball under 200 light-years wide. Unlike ordinary globulars, its stars formed in several batches with different chemistry, a clue that it may be the leftover core of a small galaxy torn apart by ours long ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Star Families of Carina
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart.
journeys.story: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from NGC 2451 to Wishing Well Cluster, all in the sky around Carina.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-west, around Carina

stops.name: NGC 2451

getThere.text: Find NGC 2451 by eye, about 65° up in the west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A bright, scattered group of stars around the orange giant c Puppis, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Under dark skies it shows to the naked eye. Binoculars reveal a bold scatter of bright stars around the orange giant c Puppis; nothing marks the two clusters apart, because their stars mingle in the view. Then find the misty glow of NGC 2477 about one and a half degrees to the east-south-east: a third family, much farther still.
card.understand: Only measurements of motion and distance can untangle this field. Gaia shows one group, NGC 2451A, about 620 light-years away, and a second, NGC 2451B, about 1,200 light-years away. Both are a few tens of millions of years old, but they are separate families that happen to lie in the same direction. The sky is a flat screen hiding depth behind it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Omicron Velorum Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half binocular fields, toward Vela.

stops.whyHere: Omicron Velorum Cluster holds a record: one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun. Before we go on: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: Omicron Velorum Cluster, next to your memory of NGC 2451.

card.glance: A loose naked-eye scatter of bright stars around Omicron Velorum, bigger than the full Moon.
card.see: It lies less than two degrees north of Delta Velorum, a corner of the False Cross. To the eye it is a small knot of five or six stars around Omicron Velorum. Binoculars show a loose, sparkling group of a few dozen bright stars; low-power, wide binoculars frame it best.
card.understand: Like the Southern Pleiades, this is a young family about 50 million years old, born together from one cloud. Because it is only about 490 light-years away, even its modest stars look bright, and the group spreads wider than the Moon. Nearby young clusters like this let astronomers watch how small stars grow up.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Beehive

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down, toward Carina; Southern Beehive is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Southern Beehive adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: From a 50-million-year-old family to one more than twice as old, and three times farther away.

card.glance: A rich, naked-eye cluster about three degrees west of Avior, in the False Cross.
card.see: To the naked eye it is a small hazy spot. Binoculars resolve dozens of stars in a patch about the width of the full Moon, with a few brighter ones in a rough box and a fainter haze of members behind them under a dark sky. Defocus slightly and check whether any look warmer in color than the rest.
card.understand: These stars formed together about 125 million years ago, roughly when the Pleiades did. The hottest, heaviest members are already gone, but many blue-white stars remain, so it still looks young. Because it sits about three times farther away than the Pleiades, the family looks smaller and fainter: how big and bright something looks depends on its distance.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Pleiades

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half binocular fields (about 19°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Southern Pleiades is one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.
stops.transitionText: Another of the same kind: Southern Pleiades, a cousin of Southern Beehive.

card.glance: A naked-eye spray of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye counts five or six; binoculars show two or three dozen, mostly blue-white, spread across about a third of the field. If you know the Pleiades, the resemblance is striking: similar look, similar distance.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, so they share an age and a birthplace. Their blue-white color shows that the brightest members are hot, heavy stars still in their long, steady adult life. Astronomers dated the family from its faintest, coolest members, which slowly destroy a fragile element, lithium: the point where lithium still survives works like a clock.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one binocular field (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Wishing Well Cluster is one of the richest open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters). A short reminder before you look: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Compare ages: Wishing Well Cluster is about 7 times older than Southern Pleiades.

card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between. Look for a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones; defocusing slightly makes them easier to pick out.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already died, so its brightest survivors are white, and a few have swollen into orange giants. Compare it with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula: the same kind of family, but this one has lived through many more chapters of its life.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Carina: Spot the Difference
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why.
journeys.story: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Delta Velorum to Wishing Well Cluster, all in the sky around Carina. Gem Cluster is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-west, around Carina

stops.name: Delta Velorum

getThere.text: Find Delta Velorum by eye, about 65° up in the south, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. One thing first: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: One corner of the False Cross: a bright white star that dims for about a day every few weeks.
card.see: Find the False Cross, a larger, fainter look-alike of the Southern Cross. Delta Velorum is one of its four corners. Compare it with Kappa Velorum and Aspidiske: on most nights it is clearly brighter, but during an eclipse it drops to about their level for roughly a day.
card.understand: Delta Velorum is two white stars orbiting each other every 45 days. Our view runs almost along their orbit, so once per orbit one star passes in front of the other and blocks part of its light. The stars themselves do not change; only our view of them does.

stops.name: Theta Carinae

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half binocular fields, toward Carina.

stops.whyHere: Theta Carinae adds the next piece of the story. A short reminder before you look: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: Theta Carinae is about 200 times more luminous than Delta Velorum, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: The brightest star of the Southern Pleiades, a scatter of blue-white stars that fills a binocular view.
card.see: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group fills about half your view, with dozens of fainter members. About 5° north lies the glowing Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae.
card.understand: The Southern Pleiades (IC 2602) is a family of stars born together tens of millions of years ago, about 490 light-years away. Theta Carinae is its brightest and hottest star. From here, Eta Carinae looks fainter, yet it is more than 15 times farther away and far more powerful.

stops.name: Eta Carinae

getThere.text: Same field of view: Eta Carinae sits just above Theta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: Eta Carinae holds a record: briefly the second-brightest star in the night sky during its 1840s Great Eruption (historical (1840s)).
stops.transitionText: Five degrees apart, these two stars swap roles: the bright one is the near one, the dimmer one the monster.

card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula; its brightness changes over the years.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbours. That is Eta Carinae. It looks like an ordinary star; the drama is in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years. The heavier one may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived. That gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus, which dims and reddens the star we see.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, N. Smith (University of Arizona, Tucson), and J. Morse (BoldlyGo Institute, New York)

stops.name: Gem Cluster

getThere.text: Stay put: Gem Cluster is in the same view, above and to the right of Eta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: A challenge stop: Gem Cluster is hard in binoculars. If you can't find it, the story still works.
stops.transitionText: Gem Cluster is a sister to Eta Carinae. Their stars came from one cloud.

card.glance: A small, bright knot of stars about two degrees north-west of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula, move about two degrees north-west. Binoculars show a compact, bright clump much smaller than the Moon, with a few stars resolved around a hazy center. Higher magnification or a telescope shows many more.
card.understand: This family was born in the same great cloud complex as the Carina Nebula’s clusters, but several million years earlier. Its hottest stars have already blown most of their birth gas away. Look from the glowing nebula to this clean cluster and you see the before and after of star birth.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of Gem Cluster, in the same view, and you have Wishing Well Cluster.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Wishing Well Cluster is one of the richest open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters).
stops.transitionText: One young, one old: about 9.7–23 million years for Gem Cluster, about 300 million years for Wishing Well Cluster.

card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between. Look for a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones; defocusing slightly makes them easier to pick out.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already died, so its brightest survivors are white, and a few have swollen into orange giants. Compare it with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula: the same kind of family, but this one has lived through many more chapters of its life.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Puppis in Living Color
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are stars different colors, and what does that tell us?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from L² Puppis to Wezen, all in the sky around Puppis.
journeys.regionLabel: In the west, around Puppis

stops.name: L² Puppis

getThere.text: Find L² Puppis by eye, about 60° up in the south-west, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A reddish variable star in Puppis that can be easy or faint depending on the year.
card.see: Find L² Puppis about 7.5° south of Pi Puppis; it forms a wide pair with its blue-white neighbour L¹ Puppis. In binoculars compare their colors: L² is clearly redder. Check its brightness against L¹ on different nights.
card.understand: L² Puppis has about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass and is shedding its outer layers in a slow, dusty wind. It pulses in and out every 140 days or so, and dust it sheds can dim it for years. In the far future the Sun will go through this same stage, before leaving a small, hot core behind.

image.credit: ESO/P. Kervella

stops.name: Naos

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths up (about 10°); Naos is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Naos is one of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye. Quick background: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: L² Puppis burns at about 3,500 K; Naos at about 40,000 K. That temperature gap is the color difference you see.
