card.glance: A steely blue-white star in a rich Milky Way field in Puppis.
card.see: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Then swing about 10° west to Pi Puppis, a deep yellow-orange star. You are reading both ends of the temperature scale in neighbouring fields.
card.understand: Naos is a supergiant of the hottest common type. With about 25 times the Sun’s mass, it pours out roughly 450,000 times the Sun’s light, most of it ultraviolet your eyes cannot see. Hot gas glows blue-white, like metal heated far past red. It also spins very fast and races through space, probably thrown out of its birth cluster.

stops.name: Pi Puppis

getThere.text: From Naos, slide down roughly one and a half fields of view (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: A surprise: Pi Puppis breaks the pattern so far.
stops.transitionText: Ten degrees apart, these two read opposite ends of the thermometer: about 40,000 K for Naos and about 3,900 K for Pi Puppis.

card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange. Look for a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant about 230 times the Sun’s width, its surface near 3,900 K, about 11,000 times more luminous than the Sun.

stops.name: Adhara

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths down and to the right, toward Canis Major; Adhara is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: From Pi Puppis at about 3,900 K to Adhara at about 22,200 K. Defocus slightly and the colors jump out.

card.glance: A bright blue-white star in the hindquarters of Canis Major.
card.see: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius’s white.
card.understand: Adhara is about 400 light-years away, nearly fifty times farther than Sirius, yet it is one of the brightest stars in the sky. It must give out close to a thousand times more light than Sirius to manage that.

stops.name: Wezen

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Wezen is already in the field, just right of Adhara.

stops.whyHere: A last look that ties back to where we began.
stops.transitionText: Wezen shows the same idea as Adhara. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: A creamy-yellow star in Canis Major’s hindquarters.
card.see: In Canis Major’s triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara and Aludra nearby: a temperature ladder in one sweep.
card.understand: Wezen is a supergiant tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun. Swollen and cooled, it shines yellow-white; heavy stars like it end as supernovae.

conditions.message: The Moon is 53% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 26° from it; it sets at 01:00.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Monoceros: A Star's Whole Life
journeys.drivingQuestion: Could you watch a star's whole life in one patch of sky?
journeys.hook: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop.
journeys.story: Nursery, family, giant, wreck: a star's life story, told stop by stop. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Christmas Tree Cluster to Aludra, all in the sky around Monoceros. M50 is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Monoceros

stops.name: Christmas Tree Cluster

getThere.text: Look 45° up in the north. Eyes first: locate Betelgeuse, then a short binocular hop brings in Christmas Tree Cluster.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Christmas Tree Cluster is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

card.glance: A bright star at the base of a small triangle of fainter stars, like an upside-down Christmas tree.
card.see: Go a little under halfway from Betelgeuse to Procyon, then about three and a half degrees north. The bright star S Monocerotis marks the trunk; a narrow triangle of fainter stars points south to the tree’s tip. With north up, the tree hangs upside-down. The nebula is a photo target.
card.understand: These stars formed a few million years ago, and their birth cloud is still around them. S Monocerotis, the bright trunk star, is far hotter and heavier than the Sun, and its light eats into the surrounding gas. A dark finger of dust, the Cone Nebula, sits at the tree’s tip where gas is still collapsing into stars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: NGC 2232

getThere.text: Sweep up about two and a half binocular fields (about 15°).

stops.whyHere: NGC 2232 shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Twenty million years on, the cloud is gone, and what is left is a loose family with dusty planet-building rubble.

card.glance: A loose, bright scatter of stars around a 5th-magnitude star in western Monoceros.
card.see: From γ Monocerotis move about three and a half degrees north-east to the star 10 Monocerotis. A loose group of white stars spreads around it, filling half a degree. No glow, no haze: the gas is gone.
card.understand: At about 25 million years this family has cleared its birth cloud. Infrared telescopes found warm dust rings around many of its stars, the rubble left from building icy planets.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: M50

getThere.text: From NGC 2232, slide right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 10°).

stops.whyHere: A challenge stop: M50 is hard in binoculars. If you can't find it, the story still works. One thing first: A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: Another step on the clock: about 140 million years, the Pleiades’ age.

card.glance: A compact, grainy glow with a few stars resolved, in a busy Milky Way field.
card.see: From Sirius, move about nine degrees north-north-east (θ Canis Majoris is a stepping stone). M50 is a small, round glow with a few sparkles; the field around it is thick with faint Milky Way stars.
card.understand: M50 formed about 140 million years ago. Like the Pleiades it still has blue-white stars at the top, but at its distance they blur into a soft patch in binoculars.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Mirzam

getThere.text: From M50, slide up and to the left roughly two fields of view, toward Canis Major.

stops.whyHere: A surprise: Mirzam breaks the pattern so far.
stops.transitionText: Same life story, further along. Look for what has changed between M50 and Mirzam.

card.glance: A blue-white star just west of Sirius: ‘the announcer’ that rises first.
card.see: Look about 5° west of Sirius for a blue-white star: Mirzam. Then compare: Sirius looks dazzling, Mirzam modest.
card.understand: Mirzam is about 490 light-years away, nearly sixty times farther than Sirius, yet still easy to see. It is a hot star that gently pulses every six hours, far too slightly for the eye.

stops.name: Aludra

getThere.text: Move about 18° (three fields) up and to the right (about 18°).

stops.whyHere: Aludra answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Turn the page in a star's life, from Mirzam to Aludra.

card.glance: The blue-white star at the tip of Canis Major’s tail.
card.see: Find the tail of Canis Major, east of Wezen. Aludra is the blue-white star at its tip; compare it with yellow Wezen.
card.understand: Aludra is a blue supergiant, tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun. Its distance is uncertain, around 2,000 light-years, so its true power is uncertain too.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Same Sky, Different Stories: Puppis
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another.
journeys.story: Every stop has a partner that shares one trait and flips another. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from L² Puppis to Canopus, all in the sky around Puppis.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Puppis

stops.name: L² Puppis

getThere.text: Find L² Puppis by eye, about 70° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because L² Puppis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A reddish variable star in Puppis that can be easy or faint depending on the year.
card.see: Find L² Puppis about 7.5° south of Pi Puppis; it forms a wide pair with its blue-white neighbour L¹ Puppis. In binoculars compare their colors: L² is clearly redder. Check its brightness against L¹ on different nights.
card.understand: L² Puppis has about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass and is shedding its outer layers in a slow, dusty wind. It pulses in and out every 140 days or so, and dust it sheds can dim it for years. In the far future the Sun will go through this same stage, before leaving a small, hot core behind.

image.credit: ESO/P. Kervella

stops.name: Pi Puppis

getThere.text: Move about 8° (one fields) up and to the left (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Pi Puppis shows the next idea you need. Quick background: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Both glow orange-red, but L² Puppis is a star of about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, while Pi Puppis is a supergiant destined for a far more violent end.

card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange. Look for a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant about 230 times the Sun’s width, its surface near 3,900 K, about 11,000 times more luminous than the Sun.

stops.name: Mu Columbae

getThere.text: From Pi Puppis, slide up roughly three fields of view, toward Columba.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Mu Columbae is one of the two classic runaway stars flung out of the Orion Nebula’s cluster (known runaway stars).
stops.transitionText: Both are stars, both are points of light, yet Mu Columbae is about 40 times smaller than Pi Puppis.

card.glance: A faint bluish star about 2° from Phact in Columba; easy in binoculars, hard to pick out by eye.
card.see: Find Phact, the brightest star of the Dove, and nudge about 2° toward the east-northeast. Mu Columbae is the faint bluish-white star there. Nothing about it looks special; its story is in its motion, not its appearance.
card.understand: About 2.5 million years ago, two pairs of stars came too close inside the young cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula. In the gravitational tangle, two stars were flung out in opposite directions: Mu Columbae one way, AE Aurigae the other. Each now moves at more than 100 km/s.

stops.name: Beta Pictoris

getThere.text: Sweep left about three binocular fields, toward Pictor.

stops.whyHere: Beta Pictoris holds a record: the first star around which a dusty planet-forming disk was photographed (1984) (historical, all stars).
stops.transitionText: Beta Pictoris is about 5,000 times less luminous than Mu Columbae, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A modest white star in faint Pictor, about 6° west of brilliant Canopus.
card.see: Start at Canopus and sweep about 6° west to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. That is Beta Pictoris. Nothing in binoculars hints at its planets; the wonder is knowing what is there. Compare its faintness with Canopus, a star five times farther away.
card.understand: Beta Pictoris is only about 23 million years old, a toddler among stars. Around it swirls a flat disk of dust and rock, like a young version of our own Kuiper belt. Two giant planets, each several times Jupiter’s mass, have been photographed orbiting inside it. We are seeing a planetary system in the making.

image.credit: ESO/A.-M. Lagrange

stops.name: Canopus

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) left, toward Carina.

stops.whyHere: Canopus holds a record: the second-brightest star in the night sky, after Sirius (whole night sky).
stops.transitionText: From the second-brightest star in the sky to a modest one six degrees away that is actually much nearer.

card.glance: The second-brightest star of the night: a dazzling white point well south of Sirius.
card.see: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers through colors as our air splits its light; higher up it is a steady white. Then sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer.
card.understand: Canopus is a giant (a star swollen past its long, steady adult life) of roughly nine or ten Suns’ mass and 73 times the Sun’s width. It now burns helium in its core. A star that big and that hot gives out about 16,000 times the Sun’s light, enough to look dazzling from 310 light-years.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Orion in Living Color
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are stars different colors, and what does that tell us?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Betelgeuse to θ¹ Orionis C, all in the sky around Orion.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Orion

stops.name: Betelgeuse

getThere.text: Find Betelgeuse by eye, about 50° up in the north, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. A short reminder before you look: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

card.glance: A bright orange-red point at Orion’s shoulder; nudge the focus slightly and the color jumps out.
card.see: Center Betelgeuse, then turn the focus a little off sharp so the point spreads into a small disk; the orange-red gets much easier to see. Swing to blue-white Rigel at Orion’s opposite corner and back. Don’t judge its brightness from memory: it varies.
card.understand: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant, a star of roughly 18 Suns that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its surface has cooled to about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, which is why it glows orange. A star this cool that still shines this brightly must be gigantic.

image.credit: ESO/M. Montargès et al.

stops.name: Alnilam

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths up and to the left (about 10°); Alnilam is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alnilam shows the next idea you need. One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: Swing from Betelgeuse to Alnilam and compare colors. About 3,600 K against 25,000 K: your eyes are reading a thermometer.

card.glance: The middle star of Orion’s Belt, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. Notice the curving string of fainter stars winding through the Belt; many were born in the same burst. Alnilam shares the same icy blue-white as its two neighbours.
card.understand: Alnilam is a blue supergiant of about 28 Suns, roughly 1,250 light-years away. ESO’s Very Large Telescope interferometer recently measured it: about 28 times the Sun’s width, a surface near 25,000 K, and spinning so fast it is close to flinging gas off its equator. A star this heavy lives only a few million years.

stops.name: Mintaka

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of Alnilam, in the same view, and you have Mintaka.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Alnilam and Mintaka, the Belt’s middle and western stars, were born in the same wave of star formation.

card.glance: The western (right-hand) star of Orion’s Belt, with an easy companion to its north.
card.see: Center Mintaka, the Belt star nearest Rigel’s side. Look about 50 arcseconds due north for a 7th-magnitude companion: binoculars split it with steady hands.
card.understand: Mintaka is a group of hot, heavy stars. Its inner pair eclipses every 5.7 days, dimming it slightly. Careful modelling suggests it lies about twice as far as early satellite measurements implied, near the young σ Orionis cluster.

stops.name: σ Orionis

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the left of Mintaka, in the same view, and you have σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: σ Orionis adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: Careful modelling puts σ Orionis near the distance of Mintaka: neighbours in Orion’s young family.

card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the eastern Belt star.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; brace the binoculars and look for a second, closer one due east. A small, faint triangle of stars sits a few arcminutes away. A telescope splits the scene into many more.
card.understand: The bright point is really at least five stars. The central pair, far too close for any ordinary telescope, holds about 17 and 13 times the Sun’s mass. Interferometers tracked their orbit, and that orbit also gave a very precise distance, about 1,260 light-years, for the young cluster around them.

stops.name: θ¹ Orionis C

getThere.text: Stay put: θ¹ Orionis C is in the same view, above and to the left of σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: Both σ Orionis and θ¹ Orionis C hide pairs of very heavy stars whose orbits, tracked with interferometers, let astronomers weigh them.

card.glance: One bright point inside the glowing heart of the Orion Nebula.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula and look at the bright knot in its core. At binocular power the four Trapezium stars merge into one point, and θ¹ Orionis C is the brightest of them. Just south-east, θ² Orionis adds an easier pair of points.
card.understand: θ¹ Orionis C is a young pair of very heavy stars, together about 44 times the Sun’s mass. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot and flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light. That light energizes the hydrogen gas around them, and the gas glows, much like the gas in a neon sign. Without this one system, most of the nebula would be dark.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Siblings Scattered over Carina
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
journeys.hook: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart.
journeys.story: Stars are born in families. Watch those families grow up and drift apart. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from NGC 2451 to Wishing Well Cluster, all in the sky around Carina.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Carina

stops.name: NGC 2451

getThere.text: Find NGC 2451 by eye, about 70° up in the east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A bright, scattered group of stars around the orange giant c Puppis, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Under dark skies it shows to the naked eye. Binoculars reveal a bold scatter of bright stars around the orange giant c Puppis; nothing marks the two clusters apart, because their stars mingle in the view. Then find the misty glow of NGC 2477 about one and a half degrees to the east-south-east: a third family, much farther still.
card.understand: Only measurements of motion and distance can untangle this field. Gaia shows one group, NGC 2451A, about 620 light-years away, and a second, NGC 2451B, about 1,200 light-years away. Both are a few tens of millions of years old, but they are separate families that happen to lie in the same direction. The sky is a flat screen hiding depth behind it.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Omicron Velorum Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 18° (two and a half fields) down and to the right, toward Vela.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Omicron Velorum Cluster is one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun. Before we go on: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.
stops.transitionText: Same species, different individual: Omicron Velorum Cluster.

card.glance: A loose naked-eye scatter of bright stars around Omicron Velorum, bigger than the full Moon.
card.see: It lies less than two degrees north of Delta Velorum, a corner of the False Cross. To the eye it is a small knot of five or six stars around Omicron Velorum. Binoculars show a loose, sparkling group of a few dozen bright stars; low-power, wide binoculars frame it best.
card.understand: Like the Southern Pleiades, this is a young family about 50 million years old, born together from one cloud. Because it is only about 490 light-years away, even its modest stars look bright, and the group spreads wider than the Moon. Nearby young clusters like this let astronomers watch how small stars grow up.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Beehive

getThere.text: Take one and a half field-widths right, toward Carina; Southern Beehive is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Southern Beehive shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: From a 50-million-year-old family to one more than twice as old, and three times farther away.

card.glance: A rich, naked-eye cluster about three degrees west of Avior, in the False Cross.
card.see: To the naked eye it is a small hazy spot. Binoculars resolve dozens of stars in a patch about the width of the full Moon, with a few brighter ones in a rough box and a fainter haze of members behind them under a dark sky. Defocus slightly and check whether any look warmer in color than the rest.
card.understand: These stars formed together about 125 million years ago, roughly when the Pleiades did. The hottest, heaviest members are already gone, but many blue-white stars remain, so it still looks young. Because it sits about three times farther away than the Pleiades, the family looks smaller and fainter: how big and bright something looks depends on its distance.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Pleiades

getThere.text: Move about 19° (three fields) down (about 19°).

stops.whyHere: Southern Pleiades holds a record: one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.
stops.transitionText: One more example so you can compare: Southern Pleiades, next to your memory of Southern Beehive.

card.glance: A naked-eye spray of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye counts five or six; binoculars show two or three dozen, mostly blue-white, spread across about a third of the field. If you know the Pleiades, the resemblance is striking: similar look, similar distance.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, so they share an age and a birthplace. Their blue-white color shows that the brightest members are hot, heavy stars still in their long, steady adult life. Astronomers dated the family from its faintest, coolest members, which slowly destroy a fragile element, lithium: the point where lithium still survives works like a clock.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) left (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Wishing Well Cluster holds a record: one of the richest open clusters known (Milky Way open clusters). One thing first: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.
stops.transitionText: Southern Pleiades is about 41–52 million years old; Wishing Well Cluster about 300 million years. Same kind of object, very different age.

card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between. Look for a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones; defocusing slightly makes them easier to pick out.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old. Its heaviest, bluest stars have already died, so its brightest survivors are white, and a few have swollen into orange giants. Compare it with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula: the same kind of family, but this one has lived through many more chapters of its life.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 07:46.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Crux in Living Color
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: Your eyes are a thermometer tonight. All you need is a slight defocus.
journeys.story: Your eyes are a thermometer tonight. All you need is a slight defocus. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Atria to Delta Centauri, all in the sky around Crux.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Crux

stops.name: Atria

getThere.text: Find Atria by eye, about 55° up in the south, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because Atria is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: The bright orange corner of the Southern Triangle.
card.see: Atria is a vivid orange point; defocus slightly to enhance the color, then compare with the white corners of the triangle.
card.understand: Atria is a giant about 120 times the Sun’s width and nearly 4,000 times its light, with a cool surface near 4,300 K.

stops.name: Hadar

getThere.text: Take two and a half field-widths up and to the right, toward Centaurus; Hadar is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. A short reminder before you look: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: Opposite ends of the thermometer, one short swing apart: Atria near 4,300 K, Hadar near 25,000 K.

card.glance: The Pointer nearer the Southern Cross: a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Swing between the two Pointers. Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. They look like a matched pair, but only our line of sight links them. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point: its three stars sit far too close together to split.
card.understand: Hadar is a hot, young triple. Two stars, about 12 and 11 times the Sun’s mass, circle each other almost exactly once a year, with a third star farther out. Heavy stars like these shine with enormous power, which is how a star 360 light-years away can rival one only 4.4 light-years away.

stops.name: Acrux

getThere.text: Move about 12° (one and a half fields) down, toward Crux.

stops.whyHere: Acrux holds a record: the brightest star of the Southern Cross (Crux).
stops.transitionText: Hadar may belong to the same scattered family of young stars as the Southern Cross’s blue stars; astronomers still debate it.

card.glance: The foot of the Southern Cross: a dazzling blue-white point with a fainter star beside it.
card.see: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross. In binoculars look just beside it for a much fainter star, an easy companion that may or may not belong to it. The two brilliant stars that make up Acrux itself sit too close for binoculars; a small telescope splits them.
card.understand: Acrux is a knot of hot, heavy stars, so hot that they shine blue-white. Delta Crucis, and probably Mimosa, belong to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. Acrux may be part of it too, though its motion keeps astronomers debating.

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: From Acrux, slide right roughly one fields of view (about 6°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Gacrux is by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars (Crux).
stops.transitionText: Same constellation, different neighbourhoods: from Acrux at about 320 light-years to Gacrux at about 89.

card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross: the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out. Look for a faint white star just to the northeast: a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant: a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. At about 89 light-years it is nearly four times closer than the hot blue stars around it.

stops.name: Delta Centauri

getThere.text: Move about 7° (one fields) down and to the right, toward Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: The answer stop: Delta Centauri is where tonight's question comes together.
stops.transitionText: Color is temperature. Delta Centauri is about 6 times hotter than Gacrux, and the color difference shows it.

card.glance: A blue-white star west of the Southern Cross, with two fainter stars nearby in binoculars.
card.see: In binoculars Delta Centauri forms a wide group with two fainter stars close beside it. Its brightness drifts slightly over months as its gas disk grows and fades.
card.understand: Delta Centauri spins so fast that gas leaks from its equator into a thin disk, which adds light and makes its brightness wander.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Libra
journeys.drivingQuestion: Birth or death: how can two glowing clouds mean opposite things?
journeys.hook: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences.
journeys.story: Twins that aren't, neighbors that aren't: tonight is about differences. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Dschubba to Zubenelgenubi, all in the sky around Libra. HD 140283 is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Libra

stops.name: Dschubba

getThere.text: Find Dschubba by eye, nearly overhead, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question. Before we go on: Some stars spin so fast that they flatten into squashed balls, hotter at their poles than around their waists.

card.glance: The middle star of the arc at Scorpius' head; a bright white point whose brightness has wandered since 2000.
card.see: δ is the middle of the three stars in the short vertical arc that forms Scorpius' head. Compare it with β above and π below. Is δ clearly the brightest of the three, or about equal? Your answer is a real measurement: the disk has made it vary for two decades.
card.understand: δ Sco is a hot, heavy star spinning so fast that gas at its equator is barely held on. When its companion swept in close in 2000, the star began to build a flat disk of gas around its waist. That disk glows and adds light, so the star brightened. Hot stars with such disks are called Be stars; the 'e' stands for the glow of the disk gas.

stops.name: 18 Scorpii

getThere.text: From Dschubba, slide down roughly two fields of view (about 15°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: 18 Scorpii is one of the closest known matches to the Sun (stars visible in binoculars). Quick background: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.
stops.transitionText: 18 Scorpii is about 30,000 times less luminous than Dschubba, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A faint yellow-white point south of the 'Yed' pair in Ophiuchus. It looks ordinary because it is almost a copy of our Sun.
card.see: Start at δ and ε Ophiuchi, the close naked-eye pair called Yed, and sweep about five degrees south. 18 Sco is the brightest star in a modest field, a soft yellow-white point. Under dark skies it is just visible to the naked eye. Compare its tint with blue-white ζ Ophiuchi about six degrees to the east.
card.understand: Measurements of its width, its mass and the way its surface quivers give almost exactly the Sun's numbers. Like the Sun, it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium deep inside, steadily, for billions of years: a nuclear furnace, not a fire. Twins like this let astronomers ask whether the Sun is typical, and what our own star looks like from far away.

stops.name: HD 140283

getThere.text: From 18 Scorpii, slide up and to the left roughly one fields of view, toward Libra.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Two Sun-like stars, two eras: HD 140283 formed when the Galaxy was nearly free of heavy elements; 18 Sco, like the Sun, formed billions of years later from enriched gas.

card.glance: A faint, unremarkable point in western Libra that needs a careful hop. It is one of the oldest stars you will ever see.
card.see: Hop about six and a half degrees east of Zubeneschamali (β Librae) and use the chart to pick out a faint, slightly yellow point among similar field stars. There is nothing special to see; the wonder is in knowing what it is. Once you have it, let your eyes rest on it a moment.
card.understand: Its atoms reveal its age. It holds only about a 250th of the Sun's share of elements heavier than helium, so it formed before many generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy's gas. It also moves fast on a long, tilted orbit through the Galaxy's halo, a hint that it was born in a small galaxy the Milky Way later swallowed.

stops.name: Zubeneschamali

getThere.text: From HD 140283, slide left roughly one fields of view (about 7°).

stops.whyHere: Zubeneschamali holds a record: often called the only naked-eye green star, though most observers see it blue-white (observing folklore).
stops.transitionText: HD 140283 is about 12 billion years old; Zubeneschamali, the hop-off star a few degrees west, about 80 million years. Two stars side by side in the sky, born more than ten billion years apart.

card.glance: Libra's northern claw: a blue-white star that some observers insist looks green. Defocus it and decide.
card.see: Center Zubeneschamali, then defocus slightly so it becomes a small disk. Compare it with white Zubenelgenubi nine degrees to the south-west and, if it is up, orange Antares low in the south-east. Do you see a green tinge, pale blue, or plain white? Decide before reading on.
card.understand: Its surface is about 12,000 degrees, twice as hot as the Sun's, so its light leans toward blue and it should look blue-white. No star can look truly green: even a star whose light peaked in green would pour out red and blue as well, and the mix looks white. Green reports probably come from contrast with nearby colors and from how our eyes handle color in dim light.

stops.name: Zubenelgenubi

getThere.text: From Zubeneschamali, slide left roughly one and a half fields of view (about 9°).

stops.whyHere: This is the high point of the journey.
stops.transitionText: The two claws of Libra look almost equally bright, but β is more than twice as far away as α, so it must shine several times more strongly.

card.glance: Libra's southern claw: a bright white star with a fainter companion clearly separate in any binoculars.
card.see: Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west of it: a fainter star stands clearly apart, about an eighth of a Moon-width away. It is easy even at 7×, and sharp-eyed observers can split it without optics. Compare the tints: the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
card.understand: Unlike many doubles, these two really belong together. Both are about 76 light-years away and they drift across the sky side by side. They are so far apart that, if they orbit at all, one lap would take well over a hundred thousand years. The brighter star is itself a tight pair that only spectra reveal.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Old Light in Crux
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far back in time can your binoculars see?
journeys.hook: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when.
journeys.story: Tonight's starlight left home in different centuries. Find out when. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Alpha Centauri to Omega Centauri, all in the sky around Crux.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-west, around Crux

stops.name: Alpha Centauri

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, about 60° up in the south, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Alpha Centauri quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross: one dazzling yellow-white point.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show a single brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars are too close together to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm yellow tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Alpha Centauri is two stars circling each other every 80 years. The brighter one is nearly a twin of our Sun, a little heavier and a little wider; its partner is a smaller, cooler orange star. Their light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. A third member, the faint red dwarf Proxima, is invisible in binoculars but is the nearest single star of all.

stops.name: Mimosa

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about two binocular fields, toward Crux.

stops.whyHere: Mimosa adds the next piece of the story. Before we go on: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: Keep counting: Alpha Centauri at about 4.4 light-years, Mimosa at about 279 light-years.

card.glance: The left-hand star of the Southern Cross: blue-white, and your signpost to the Jewel Box.
card.see: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the Cross’s eastern arm. Place it at the edge of your view and look about 1° to the southeast: a tight, glittering knot of stars appears. That is the Jewel Box. Its brightest stars share Mimosa’s icy color.
card.understand: Mimosa is a heavy, hot star that swells and shrinks very slightly several times a day, too little for your eye to notice. It probably belongs to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. The Jewel Box is a family of about the same age, but more than twenty times farther away.

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: No hop needed: look below and to the left of Mimosa, in the same view, and you have Jewel Box.

stops.whyHere: Jewel Box shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Same age, different distance: Jewel Box is the same kind of young family as Mimosa’s, seen from far away.

card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, the bright star on the Cross’s eastern arm, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon. Most stars are blue-white; look near the middle for one distinctly orange star. Defocus slightly to bring the colors out. A telescope shows the full jewel box.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, roughly 16 million years ago. The heaviest burned their fuel fastest: one has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a red supergiant, cooler and therefore orange-red. Its blue-white siblings are lighter and still in their long, steady adult life. Same age, different mass, different stage.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Gacrux is already in the field, below and to the right of Jewel Box.

stops.whyHere: Gacrux holds a record: by far the closest of the Southern Cross’s bright stars (Crux).
stops.transitionText: Depth check: Gacrux is about 70 times closer than Jewel Box, though they share this patch of sky.

card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross: the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out. Look for a faint white star just to the northeast: a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant: a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. At about 89 light-years it is nearly four times closer than the hot blue stars around it.

stops.name: Omega Centauri

getThere.text: From Gacrux, slide up and to the right roughly two fields of view, toward Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Omega Centauri is the most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way (Milky Way globular clusters).
stops.transitionText: From about 89 light-years to about 17,700 light-years: your binoculars just reached about 200 times farther.

card.glance: A big round glow nearly half the width of the full Moon, brightening toward the middle; to the eye, a fuzzy star.
card.see: To the eye it looks like a fuzzy star in Centaurus that never sharpens. Binoculars turn it into a large, round glow that brightens steadily toward the center, like a snowball. Under a dark sky, with the binoculars braced, the outer edge can look grainy. Individual stars are a telescope job.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of very old stars orbiting far above and below the galaxy’s disk. This one packs millions of Suns’ worth of stars into a ball under 200 light-years wide. Unlike ordinary globulars, its stars formed in several batches with different chemistry, a clue that it may be the leftover core of a small galaxy torn apart by ours long ago.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Pairs and Impostors of Scorpius
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is that one star, or two, or six?
journeys.hook: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Split stars that your eyes think are single, then ask which pairs are real partners. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from δ Librae to Dschubba, all in the sky around Scorpius.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Scorpius

stops.name: δ Librae

getThere.text: Look 65° up in the north-west. Put the binoculars down for a moment. Spot Zubeneschamali, aim at it, then follow the hop to δ Librae.

stops.whyHere: We start here because δ Librae is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. Before we go on: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

card.glance: A modest white star in Libra that loses more than half its light for part of a night every 2.3 days.
card.see: δ Lib sits about eight degrees north-north-east of Zubenelgenubi. Compare it with neighboring stars of similar brightness, ideally on two different nights. Usually it holds steady; during an eclipse it fades enough to look clearly fainter than its neighbors. The app's eclipse list tells you whether tonight is a good night.
card.understand: δ Lib is two stars orbiting each other every 2 days and 8 hours, far too close for any telescope to split. Their orbit is tilted nearly edge-on to us, so once per lap the dimmer star slides in front of the brighter one and blocks much of its light. They are so close that gas streams from one star onto the other.

stops.name: Acrab

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two and a half binocular fields, toward Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further. A short reminder before you look: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: Acrab is about 200 times more luminous than δ Librae, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: Top star of Scorpius' head. Hand-held you see one point; a steady 10× or more may show a close companion.
card.see: Brace your binoculars on something solid, or use a tripod. At 10× or more, look for a fainter star hugging β on its north-north-east side, separated by about a third of Jupiter's width. Hand-held, most people see only one star, and that is normal. Then look for ν and ω, its two neighboring doubles.
card.understand: The two stars you may split are true partners: they lie at the same distance and drift through space together. Each one is itself a tight pair that only special telescope techniques reveal. Heavy stars are usually born in multiples like this, and watching partners orbit is how astronomers weigh stars.

stops.name: ω¹ Scorpii

getThere.text: No hop needed: look above and to the left of Acrab, in the same view, and you have ω¹ Scorpii.

stops.whyHere: ω¹ Scorpii adds the next piece of the story.
stops.transitionText: β's two stars truly travel together. ω's two stars, one degree south, only look like a pair: they lie at very different distances.

card.glance: Two similar stars a quarter-degree apart just south of β Scorpii; easy in any binoculars, with a gentle color contrast.
card.see: From β, drop about one degree south. Two stars of similar brightness sit side by side, about half a Moon-width apart: easy even at 7×, and sharp-eyed observers split them without optics. Compare colors: the north-western one is blue-white, its partner faintly yellow.
card.understand: The blue-white star, ω¹, is a hot young member of the Scorpius family about 460 light-years away. The yellow one, ω², is an older giant only about 290 light-years away, and it drifts across the sky in a different direction. They are not partners, just two stars that happen to line up from where we stand. Distance and motion are how astronomers tell real pairs from chance pairs.

stops.name: Jabbah

getThere.text: Same field of view: Jabbah sits below and to the left of ω¹ Scorpii.

stops.whyHere: Jabbah shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: ν's faint companion truly belongs to it; ω's two stars, two degrees away, only line up by chance.

card.glance: A modest star east of β Scorpii; a steady 10× view can tease out a faint companion.
card.see: From β, nudge about one and a half degrees east-north-east to ν. On a tripod at 10× or more, a much fainter star sits just north-north-west of it, roughly one Jupiter-width away. Hand-held, the companion usually drowns in ν's glare; that makes this the hardest of the three doubles here.
card.understand: The pair you can split is only the top layer. Telescopes show that each of those two stars is itself a close pair, and the brightest of them is a tighter pair still. That is at least five suns in one system, all born with the rest of Scorpius' blue-white stars about eleven million years ago.

stops.name: Dschubba

getThere.text: Stay put: Dschubba is in the same view, above and to the left of Jabbah.

stops.whyHere: The answer stop: Dschubba is where tonight's question comes together.
stops.transitionText: Don't judge a star by how bright it looks. Dschubba is about 80 times more luminous than Jabbah.

card.glance: The middle star of the arc at Scorpius' head; a bright white point whose brightness has wandered since 2000.
card.see: δ is the middle of the three stars in the short vertical arc that forms Scorpius' head. Compare it with β above and π below. Is δ clearly the brightest of the three, or about equal? Your answer is a real measurement: the disk has made it vary for two decades.
card.understand: δ Sco is a hot, heavy star spinning so fast that gas at its equator is barely held on. When its companion swept in close in 2000, the star began to build a flat disk of gas around its waist. That disk glows and adds light, so the star brightened. Hot stars with such disks are called Be stars; the 'e' stands for the glow of the disk gas.

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.label: A
journeys.title: Reading Star Colors over Orion
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are stars different colors, and what does that tell us?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Aldebaran to Nihal, all in the sky around Orion.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-east, around Orion

stops.name: Aldebaran

getThere.text: Find Aldebaran by eye, about 30° up in the north-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The opening stop: easy to find, striking, and it sets up tonight's question.

card.glance: A bright orange star at one tip of the V-shaped Hyades cluster.
card.see: Frame the Hyades V so that Aldebaran sits at one tip. Its warm orange stands out against the white cluster stars, though a few of them have a faint yellow-orange tint too. Then compare it with Betelgeuse to the south-east: which looks redder to you?
card.understand: Aldebaran is an orange giant, a star that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width. It is about 67 light-years away, less than half the distance of the Hyades behind it. The two just line up from where we stand: stars that look side by side can be very far apart.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Bellatrix

getThere.text: Sweep right about two and a half binocular fields, toward Orion.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Opposite ends of the thermometer, one short swing apart: Aldebaran near 3,900 K, Bellatrix near 21,900 K.

card.glance: Orion’s western shoulder: a blue-white star opposite orange Betelgeuse.
card.see: Put Bellatrix in the field, then swing across to Betelgeuse: blue-white versus orange. Both look similar in brightness, yet they are very different stars at different distances.
card.understand: Bellatrix is a hot blue-white star about 250 light-years away, roughly half as far as Betelgeuse and much closer than the Belt stars. Orion’s figure mixes stars at very different distances; only from Earth do they line up into a hunter.

stops.name: Rigel

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two and a half binocular fields (about 15°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Rigel is usually the brightest star in Orion (Orion (Betelgeuse varies and occasionally rivals it)). Before we go on: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.
stops.transitionText: Rigel shows the same idea as Bellatrix. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: A brilliant blue-white star at Orion’s lower-right foot.
card.see: Center Rigel and compare its icy blue-white with Betelgeuse’s orange across Orion. Then glance down at Sirius: Rigel looks a little fainter. Keep that in mind. A faint companion sits very close, but it is lost in Rigel’s glare at binocular power.
card.understand: Rigel is a blue supergiant whose surface is about 12,000 K, twice as hot as the Sun’s, so it glows blue-white the way metal does when it gets very hot. It lies roughly a hundred times farther away than Sirius, yet it looks almost as bright. Only a star giving out tens of thousands of times the Sun’s light can do that.

stops.name: Saiph

getThere.text: Move about 8° (one and a half fields) down and to the right (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Saiph answers the question we started with.
stops.transitionText: Orion’s two feet: Saiph is the hotter star, yet Rigel looks brighter. Much of a very hot star’s light is ultraviolet that our eyes cannot see.

card.glance: Orion’s lower-left foot: a blue-white star, a bit fainter than Rigel.
card.see: Compare Saiph with Rigel at the opposite foot. Rigel looks brighter, but Saiph is the hotter star.
card.understand: Saiph’s surface is more than twice as hot as Rigel’s. Much of its energy comes out as ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see, so in visible light it looks fainter than it really is.

stops.name: Nihal

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two binocular fields, toward Lepus.

stops.whyHere: A last look that ties back to where we began. One thing first: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: Saiph burns at about 26,500 K; Nihal at about 5,200 K. That temperature gap is the color difference you see.

card.glance: A yellowish 3rd-magnitude star in Lepus, just south-west of Arneb.
card.see: Put Nihal and Arneb in the same field: Arneb is slightly brighter and whiter, Nihal yellowish.
card.understand: Nihal is a yellow giant about 160 light-years away. Arneb, beside it, is more than ten times farther, yet it looks a bit brighter: a supergiant outshining a nearby giant.

journeys.label: B
journeys.title: Reading Star Colors over Canis Major
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why are stars different colors, and what does that tell us?
journeys.hook: Read the temperature of stars from their color, ember-orange to blue-white, by eye.
journeys.story: Read the temperature of stars from their color, ember-orange to blue-white, by eye. In 4 stops and about 30 minutes you go from L² Puppis to τ Canis Majoris, all in the sky around Canis Major.
journeys.regionLabel: In the south-east, around Canis Major

stops.name: L² Puppis

getThere.text: Find L² Puppis by eye, about 35° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: We start here because L² Puppis is bright, beautiful and at the heart of the story. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A reddish variable star in Puppis that can be easy or faint depending on the year.
card.see: Find L² Puppis about 7.5° south of Pi Puppis; it forms a wide pair with its blue-white neighbour L¹ Puppis. In binoculars compare their colors: L² is clearly redder. Check its brightness against L¹ on different nights.
card.understand: L² Puppis has about two-thirds of the Sun’s mass and is shedding its outer layers in a slow, dusty wind. It pulses in and out every 140 days or so, and dust it sheds can dim it for years. In the far future the Sun will go through this same stage, before leaving a small, hot core behind.

image.credit: ESO/P. Kervella

stops.name: Adhara

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half binocular fields, toward Canis Major.

stops.whyHere: Adhara adds the next piece of the story. A short reminder before you look: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.
stops.transitionText: Opposite ends of the thermometer, one short swing apart: L² Puppis near 3,500 K, Adhara near 22,200 K.

card.glance: A bright blue-white star in the hindquarters of Canis Major.
card.see: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius’s white.
card.understand: Adhara is about 400 light-years away, nearly fifty times farther than Sirius, yet it is one of the brightest stars in the sky. It must give out close to a thousand times more light than Sirius to manage that.

stops.name: Wezen

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. Wezen is already in the field, below and to the left of Adhara.

stops.whyHere: Wezen shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Wezen shows the same idea as Adhara. A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.

card.glance: A creamy-yellow star in Canis Major’s hindquarters.
card.see: In Canis Major’s triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara and Aludra nearby: a temperature ladder in one sweep.
card.understand: Wezen is a supergiant tens of thousands of times as luminous as the Sun. Swollen and cooled, it shines yellow-white; heavy stars like it end as supernovae.

stops.name: τ Canis Majoris

getThere.text: Stay put: τ Canis Majoris is in the same view, below and to the left of Wezen.

stops.whyHere: Record holder: τ Canis Majoris is brightest star of the cluster NGC 2362 (NGC 2362 members).
stops.transitionText: Swing from Wezen to τ Canis Majoris and compare colors. About 6,200 K against 32,800 K: your eyes are reading a thermometer.

card.glance: A 4th-magnitude star sitting inside a tiny, sparkling cluster in Canis Major.
card.see: Find τ Canis Majoris about 2½° north-east of Wezen. In 10× binoculars a halo of faint stars surrounds it; at 7× the cluster may look like a soft glow around one bright star. Steady the view and use averted vision to count members.
card.understand: τ CMa is a small group of very hot, very heavy stars, including a pair that eclipses every 1.3 days. NGC 2362 is only about five to seven million years old, young enough that its heaviest stars are still shining. They give out so much light that from about 4,000 light-years away τ CMa still reaches naked-eye brightness.

journeys.label: C
journeys.title: Pictor: Spot the Difference
journeys.drivingQuestion: What makes look-alikes live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why.
journeys.story: Pairs that look alike but live opposite lives. Spot the difference, then learn why. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from Pi Puppis to Canopus, all in the sky around Pictor. Kapteyn’s Star is the one challenge: give it a minute, and skip it without guilt if it does not show.
journeys.regionLabel: In the south-east, around Pictor

stops.name: Pi Puppis

getThere.text: Find Pi Puppis by eye, about 30° up in the south-east, then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find Pi Puppis quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. Before we go on: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look grey and show best when you look a little to one side.

card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange. Look for a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant about 230 times the Sun’s width, its surface near 3,900 K, about 11,000 times more luminous than the Sun.

stops.name: Mu Columbae

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three binocular fields, toward Columba.

stops.whyHere: Mu Columbae holds a record: one of the two classic runaway stars flung out of the Orion Nebula’s cluster (known runaway stars). One thing first: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: Size check: Mu Columbae is about 40 times smaller than Pi Puppis.

card.glance: A faint bluish star about 2° from Phact in Columba; easy in binoculars, hard to pick out by eye.
card.see: Find Phact, the brightest star of the Dove, and nudge about 2° toward the east-northeast. Mu Columbae is the faint bluish-white star there. Nothing about it looks special; its story is in its motion, not its appearance.
card.understand: About 2.5 million years ago, two pairs of stars came too close inside the young cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula. In the gravitational tangle, two stars were flung out in opposite directions: Mu Columbae one way, AE Aurigae the other. Each now moves at more than 100 km/s.

stops.name: Kapteyn’s Star

getThere.text: From Mu Columbae, slide up and to the right roughly two fields of view, toward Pictor.

stops.whyHere: This one tests your skills and your sky. Give it a fair try, and skip it without guilt.
stops.transitionText: Kapteyn’s Star is about 2,000,000 times less luminous than Mu Columbae, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.glance: A faint reddish dot near the threshold of 50 mm binoculars; you need a detailed chart to be sure of it.
card.see: This is a challenge: use the app’s chart at high zoom and star-hop from the faint stars of Pictor. Kapteyn’s Star is a dim, slightly reddish point, among the faintest in the field. Once found, you are looking at one of the oldest stars you will ever see.
card.understand: Most nearby stars, like the Sun, circle the Galaxy in its flat disk. Kapteyn’s Star belongs to the halo, a sparse cloud of ancient stars that swing through the disk on steep, looping orbits. It is a small red dwarf and, like most halo stars, poor in heavy elements: it formed before the Galaxy had made many.

stops.name: Beta Pictoris

getThere.text: From Kapteyn’s Star, slide down and to the right roughly one and a half fields of view (about 8°).

stops.whyHere: Record holder: Beta Pictoris is the first star around which a dusty planet-forming disk was photographed (1984) (historical, all stars).
stops.transitionText: Line them up by true output: Kapteyn’s Star at about 0.018 times the Sun's light, Beta Pictoris at about 8.3 times the Sun's light.

card.glance: A modest white star in faint Pictor, about 6° west of brilliant Canopus.
card.see: Start at Canopus and sweep about 6° west to a lone, modest white star in an empty-looking area. That is Beta Pictoris. Nothing in binoculars hints at its planets; the wonder is knowing what is there. Compare its faintness with Canopus, a star five times farther away.
card.understand: Beta Pictoris is only about 23 million years old, a toddler among stars. Around it swirls a flat disk of dust and rock, like a young version of our own Kuiper belt. Two giant planets, each several times Jupiter’s mass, have been photographed orbiting inside it. We are seeing a planetary system in the making.

image.credit: ESO/A.-M. Lagrange

stops.name: Canopus

getThere.text: Move about 6° (one fields) down, toward Carina.

stops.whyHere: Canopus holds a record: the second-brightest star in the night sky, after Sirius (whole night sky).
stops.transitionText: From the second-brightest star in the sky to a modest one six degrees away that is actually much nearer.

card.glance: The second-brightest star of the night: a dazzling white point well south of Sirius.
card.see: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers through colors as our air splits its light; higher up it is a steady white. Then sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer.
card.understand: Canopus is a giant (a star swollen past its long, steady adult life) of roughly nine or ten Suns’ mass and 73 times the Sun’s width. It now burns helium in its core. A star that big and that hot gives out about 16,000 times the Sun’s light, enough to look dazzling from 310 light-years.

journeys.label: D
journeys.title: Ember to Blue-White: Orion
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars.
journeys.story: Red is cool, blue is hot. Test it on tonight's brightest stars. In 5 stops and about 40 minutes you go from W Orionis to θ¹ Orionis C, all in the sky around Orion.
journeys.regionLabel: In the east, around Orion

stops.name: W Orionis

getThere.text: Look 40° up in the north-east. Eyes first: locate Orion’s Belt, then a short binocular hop brings in W Orionis.

stops.whyHere: First stop: you can find W Orionis quickly, and it raises the question we'll answer. One thing first: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

card.glance: A 6th-magnitude orange-red star in western Orion, easy in binoculars.
card.see: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix. Among white field stars it stands out as orange-red; defocus slightly to boost the color.
card.understand: W Orionis is an old giant that has dredged up carbon from its core. That carbon forms molecules in its cool atmosphere that soak up blue light, so it glows warm red. It slowly varies in brightness over about seven months.

stops.name: Alnilam

getThere.text: Take one field-widths right (about 8°); Alnilam is waiting there.

stops.whyHere: Alnilam adds the next piece of the story. Quick background: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: W Orionis burns at about 2,700 K; Alnilam at about 25,000 K. That temperature gap is the color difference you see.

card.glance: The middle star of Orion’s Belt, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. Notice the curving string of fainter stars winding through the Belt; many were born in the same burst. Alnilam shares the same icy blue-white as its two neighbours.
card.understand: Alnilam is a blue supergiant of about 28 Suns, roughly 1,250 light-years away. ESO’s Very Large Telescope interferometer recently measured it: about 28 times the Sun’s width, a surface near 25,000 K, and spinning so fast it is close to flinging gas off its equator. A star this heavy lives only a few million years.

stops.name: Mintaka

getThere.text: Stay put: Mintaka is in the same view, above and to the left of Alnilam.

stops.whyHere: Mintaka shows the next idea you need.
stops.transitionText: Alnilam and Mintaka, the Belt’s middle and western stars, were born in the same wave of star formation.

card.glance: The western (right-hand) star of Orion’s Belt, with an easy companion to its north.
card.see: Center Mintaka, the Belt star nearest Rigel’s side. Look about 50 arcseconds due north for a 7th-magnitude companion: binoculars split it with steady hands.
card.understand: Mintaka is a group of hot, heavy stars. Its inner pair eclipses every 5.7 days, dimming it slightly. Careful modelling suggests it lies about twice as far as early satellite measurements implied, near the young σ Orionis cluster.

stops.name: σ Orionis

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars. σ Orionis is already in the field, above and to the right of Mintaka.

stops.whyHere: This stop takes the story one step further.
stops.transitionText: Careful modelling puts σ Orionis near the distance of Mintaka: neighbours in Orion’s young family.

card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the eastern Belt star.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; brace the binoculars and look for a second, closer one due east. A small, faint triangle of stars sits a few arcminutes away. A telescope splits the scene into many more.
card.understand: The bright point is really at least five stars. The central pair, far too close for any ordinary telescope, holds about 17 and 13 times the Sun’s mass. Interferometers tracked their orbit, and that orbit also gave a very precise distance, about 1,260 light-years, for the young cluster around them.

stops.name: θ¹ Orionis C

getThere.text: Stay put: θ¹ Orionis C is in the same view, just above σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: The answer stop: θ¹ Orionis C is where tonight's question comes together.
stops.transitionText: Both σ Orionis and θ¹ Orionis C hide pairs of very heavy stars whose orbits, tracked with interferometers, let astronomers weigh them.

card.glance: One bright point inside the glowing heart of the Orion Nebula.
card.see: Center the Orion Nebula and look at the bright knot in its core. At binocular power the four Trapezium stars merge into one point, and θ¹ Orionis C is the brightest of them. Just south-east, θ² Orionis adds an easier pair of points.
card.understand: θ¹ Orionis C is a young pair of very heavy stars, together about 44 times the Sun’s mass. Stars this heavy are fiercely hot and flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light. That light energizes the hydrogen gas around them, and the gas glows, much like the gas in a neon sign. Without this one system, most of the nebula would be dark.
